passages: Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users.
Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions".
A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered.
Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks.
Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate.
A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".

Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last."

Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock".
"After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian."
Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland.
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".

Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.

While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

extraction.body: Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users. Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv. A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered. It was unclear who was behind the cyberattacks or whether the two incidents were connected. Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks. Some told the BBC that, four and a half years into the war, they have disabled the app altogether. After Sunday night's hack, the country's air force urged people to consult other official channels. In a post on Telegram, the air force said: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our [Telegram] channel." The government said it had temporarily disabled the app for maintenance, saying it had "apparently been compromised". Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate. But Olena, a Kyiv resident, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been alarmed, saying: "The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'. "I'm prepared for blackouts, for a cut in central heating and water supply, but not for nuclear attack." Olena says her husband then received alerts for "street fighting attacks in Kyiv" and another alert, written in Russian. "After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian." In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public". A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory. It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia". The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide". On Monday morning there was no sense the messages had caused widespread panic in Russia and the incident did not feature prominently on media outlets. Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock". He said the proliferation of AI technology was contributing to an increase in cyberattacks. Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system. While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government. Those responsible for the hack on Russia's system have likely had the capability to launch such an attack for some time but decided to hold off until Ukraine's alert app was compromised, cyber experts told the BBC. Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions. Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions". He continued: "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities." Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last." The alerts in Ukraine were sent minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's frontline Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday. It had been brokered in part by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. Fighting continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place. In the city of Dnipro alone, 15 people were killed in an attack on a train platform on Thursday. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Additional reporting by Jamie Whitehead and Helen Davidson Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland. Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.

sources.title: Hackers send fake nuclear threat alert to Ukraine emergency app - The Guardian
passages: Unknown hackers have targeted Ukraine’s nationwide emergency alert mobile app, sending residents in Kyiv a warning that they were at risk of an imminent nuclear strike.

The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky.
He declined to say how many Oleskhy residents had chosen to go to Ukraine and how many to Russia, citing an agreement with Moscow to keep the figure secret.
Ukrainian media have reported that most of the evacuation buses headed to Ukraine through Crimea, from where a plane took them to Gomel, a city in Belarus.
Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left.
Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow.
A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads.
The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv.

According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”.
Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success.
Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere.
He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same.
It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting.
Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised.

This article is an automated aggregation of coverage from news outlets. Our editorials offer in-depth analysis curated by the NewsCord team.
Russia and Ukraine reported hacks of emergency alert apps triggering nuclear, radiation, and chemical warnings. Occurred Sunday night with messages sent to users across capitals and regions.

Russia said its Emergencies Ministry app came under a “massive cyberattack”, hours after Kyiv said Ukraine’s air raid alert app was hacked and began spreading “false information” about incoming drone attacks.

The Ukrainian Air Force told users in a Telegram post that “The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” adding, “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”

Russia’s Emergencies Ministry said hackers used its mobile app to send a false alert in 33 of Russia’s 89 regions at about 2:45 a.m., Moscow time, while the ministry did not say who was behind the cyberattack. The BBC reported that the Air Force urged people to consult other official channels and quoted the Air Force saying, "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference." Developers of the Air Alert app stated that “unauthorized interference” had occurred and that they temporarily disabled push notifications and the app itself.

The BBC described a purported screenshot of a fake alert shared on Telegram by Atesh, warning that “nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns had been launched at all regions of Russia.” CBS News said Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, stated the hack had no impact on Ukraine’s security operations and that the Air Alert app was not affiliated with the country’s military command systems.

The cyberattacks unfolded as a limited ceasefire in the southern Ukrainian region of Kherson was expiring on Monday, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X that “This is yet another test that Russia does not want any de-escalation.” Russia bombed a aid distribution center and a neighboring shelter in the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, killing 24 people, and Zelenskyy said 10 guided bombs hit an area that included a school building used to distribute humanitarian aid. Emergency teams searched rubble with flashlights as about 20 people were missing and the death toll could rise, while Russian drones launched additional strikes that hindered rescue efforts.
Ukraine Oleshky ceasefire expired as events unfolded

In Russia, the BBC said there was “no sense the messages had caused widespread panic,” and it quoted Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov saying Russian government internet resources were “under constant cyberattacks”. In Ukraine, the BBC said the air force urged calm and follow official updates, while CBS News reported that the Air Alert app was gradually being restored with new yellow and red alert levels on the map.

extraction.body: Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users. Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv. A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered. It was unclear who was behind the cyberattacks or whether the two incidents were connected. Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks. Some told the BBC that, four and a half years into the war, they have disabled the app altogether. After Sunday night's hack, the country's air force urged people to consult other official channels. In a post on Telegram, the air force said: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our [Telegram] channel." The government said it had temporarily disabled the app for maintenance, saying it had "apparently been compromised". Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate. But Olena, a Kyiv resident, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been alarmed, saying: "The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'. "I'm prepared for blackouts, for a cut in central heating and water supply, but not for nuclear attack." Olena says her husband then received alerts for "street fighting attacks in Kyiv" and another alert, written in Russian. "After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian." In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public". A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory. It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia". The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide". On Monday morning there was no sense the messages had caused widespread panic in Russia and the incident did not feature prominently on media outlets. Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock". He said the proliferation of AI technology was contributing to an increase in cyberattacks. Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system. While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government. Those responsible for the hack on Russia's system have likely had the capability to launch such an attack for some time but decided to hold off until Ukraine's alert app was compromised, cyber experts told the BBC. Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions. Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions". He continued: "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities." Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last." The alerts in Ukraine were sent minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's frontline Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday. It had been brokered in part by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. Fighting continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place. In the city of Dnipro alone, 15 people were killed in an attack on a train platform on Thursday. Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Dozens of shops across European countries have been hit by a cyber-attack affecting their fridges.

The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian. Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised. Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.” A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv. In a post on Sunday, the Ukrainian emergency app said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with its operation. The channel had been temporarily suspended, it said, warning users not to click on links in “suspicious notifications”. It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow. One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified. The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky. Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said. There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue. Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burnt-out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported. Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones. According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”. “Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News. The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated in other occupied cities in the Kherson region. He declined to say how many Oleskhy residents had chosen to go to Ukraine and how many to Russia, citing an agreement with Moscow to keep the figure secret. Ukrainian media have reported that most of the evacuation buses headed to Ukraine through Crimea, from where a plane took them to Gomel, a city in Belarus. Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left. Lubinets paid tribute to the US first lady and said he had been in daily contact with her via her aide Marc Beckman. He said he hoped to bring back some of the “thousands of people” who had disappeared, as well as prisoners of war and bodies retrieved last week from Oleshky’s morgue. There were millions of Ukrainian citizens living in occupied territory, he said. Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same. Meanwhile, officials in the western region of Vinnytsia said two civilians had been killed in a drone strike next to an education facility. The victims were a 13-year-old girl, who died at the scene from her injuries, and a woman, who died later in hospital. Several other children were wounded, the officials said.

sources.title: Hackers hit Ukraine, Russia's emergency apps, send fake nuclear, chemical attack alerts
passages: Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert apps had been hacked overnight, sending false warnings to citizens about impending air raids and chemical and nuclear attacks.The warnings coincided with the expiry of a six-day local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in a small area of southern Ukraine - the longest such pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.Ukraine's public air raid app started to send false alerts just before 11 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Sunday for the capital Kyiv and other areas, warning of radiation and chemical attacks and also the risk of street combat in some areas.Hours later, Russian state news agency TASS quoted the Emergencies Ministry in Moscow as saying that its own mobile app had also been hit by a cyberattack that resulted in fake public warnings being transmitted.Reuters was unable to verify which groups were responsible.

Experts have linked previous cyber security incidents during the almost five-year-old war to activist hackers as well as intelligence agencies on both sides.In Ukraine, one of the alarms said Russia had launched a hypersonic Oreshnik missile - which is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead - and that a nuclear alert had been declared.Ukraine's air force said shortly after on the Telegram messaging app that the alert system appeared to have been hacked by Russia, noting that the alerts were broadcast in Russian.

The US on Friday announced a $2.1 billion deal to supply 500 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, but two people briefed on the decision said it could take years for the missiles to arrive.On the streets of Kyiv, residents played down the impact of the hack.Artem Pyndyk, 37, a businessman, said he was briefly surprised to see the messages but then realized what had happened."This didn't trigger the kind of reaction in society that they expected," said Pyndyk, adding that family members and friends he had checked in with had also not panicked."You can laugh about it but, on the other hand, they gained a certain level of access and were able to hack the program."Oksana Vostrykova, 48, also shrugged off the incident."I am calm about it, I kind of immediately understood that it might be a false message," the pizzeria employee said.

The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian. Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised. Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.” A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv. In a post on Sunday, the Ukrainian emergency app said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with its operation. The channel had been temporarily suspended, it said, warning users not to click on links in “suspicious notifications”. It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow. One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified. The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky. Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said. There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue. Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burnt-out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported. Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones. According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”. “Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News. The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated in other occupied cities in the Kherson region. He declined to say how many Oleskhy residents had chosen to go to Ukraine and how many to Russia, citing an agreement with Moscow to keep the figure secret. Ukrainian media have reported that most of the evacuation buses headed to Ukraine through Crimea, from where a plane took them to Gomel, a city in Belarus. Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left. Lubinets paid tribute to the US first lady and said he had been in daily contact with her via her aide Marc Beckman. He said he hoped to bring back some of the “thousands of people” who had disappeared, as well as prisoners of war and bodies retrieved last week from Oleshky’s morgue. There were millions of Ukrainian citizens living in occupied territory, he said. Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same. Meanwhile, officials in the western region of Vinnytsia said two civilians had been killed in a drone strike next to an education facility. The victims were a 13-year-old girl, who died at the scene from her injuries, and a woman, who died later in hospital. Several other children were wounded, the officials said.

extraction.body: Emergency warning apps in Russia and Ukraine were hacked overnight Sunday into Monday, according to authorities in both countries. It’s not clear whether the hacking of the apps is linked. The apps warn the public of missile, drone and other threats. But rather than spread panic, the fake messages appear to have had little impact on war-weary civilians – and instead began to generate some imaginative memes. The messages posted on Ukraine’s public air raid app late on Sunday claimed that the capital Kyiv and other areas were subject to nuclear ⁠and chemical alerts as well as the threat of street combat. Another fake message said Russia’s ⁠hypersonic Oreshnik missile had been deployed. “The air alert app appears to have been subjected to enemy influence,” the Ukrainian air force said ‌on Telegram. Stepan Tanasiychuk, who leads Ukraine’s Air Raid Alert project, said Monday it was gradually being restored, with new yellow and red alert levels currently available on the map. “The team is taking additional measures to secure the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future, Tanasiychuk said on Instagram. “We realise how much unnecessary worry and inconvenience this has caused.” In a separate event, ⁠the mobile app of Russia’s emergencies ministry – Emercom – was hit by a “massive cyberattack” early Monday that resulted in ⁠”the spread of false information to the public,” state news agency TASS quoted ⁠the ‌ministry as saying. A fake alert was sent to 33 Russian regions, the ministry said. The message claimed that “NUCLEAR WARHEADS ON P1-SUN DELIVERY SYSTEMS have been launched across ALL regions of Russia,” and added an expletive-laden warning. “The app is currently operational, and its full functionality will be restored by the end of the day,” the emergencies ministry said later Monday. “EMERCOM specialists have analyzed the incident and identified the vulnerability exploited by the attacker.” The ministry played down the significance of the incident, saying that alerts are distributed through regional and municipal systems such as sirens and loudspeakers, SMS messages and media broadcasts. “All electronic resources belonging to our government agencies are under constant threat of cyberattacks,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Monday. “As technologies, including AI, continue to evolve, the threat of cyberattacks is growing,” he said. Few people appear to have fallen for the false messages. Some suggested it had undermined their trust in official warnings. One Russian user said they had deleted the Emercom app “and I won’t be installing anything like that again. How can they leave apps like this vulnerable? It’s complete nonsense, of course, but what if it weren’t?” Among comments on Instagram among Russian users of the app, one said the fake alert “was written in such a way that it’s impossible to believe it’s real.” Another wrote: “It was hard to believe such nonsense. … How did (the Emergencies ministry) even let this happen.. let themselves get hacked.” “You wake up, open Threads and see tons of posts like this,” another commented. “BUT THANKFULLY IT’S FAKE!” Others joked that they had not even received the warning, with one writing: “This information was reserved for the chosen ones, don’t worry, you’re not important enough to be hacked.” One resident of Kyiv responded to the alert about street fighting by posting: “Good thing our mayor is a boxer.” Despite the lighthearted responses, residents in Ukraine and Russia know all too well the importance of reliable early warning systems, as Moscow and Kyiv continue to trade strikes and the United States continues efforts to broker peace. US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday that the US would mediate working-level negotiations between Ukraine and Russia in Abu Dhabi from November 10 to 11. He posted to X saying American negotiators would also meet with representatives from France, Germany, the UK, EU and NATO in Brussels this week to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine. Witkoff’s announcement came hours after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that at least 26 people were killed in an “utterly horrific” Russian aerial bomb attack which he said targeted a school used for humanitarian purposes. As of Monday evening local time, search and rescue operations were ongoing in the village of Komyshuvakha, southeastern Zaporizhzhia region, with emergency personnel working to locate missing people feared trapped under the rubble. A strong and tough response,” Zelensky posted on X.

sources.title: Hackers hit Ukraine, Russia's emergency apps, send fake nuclear, chemical attack alerts
passages: Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert apps had been hacked overnight, sending false warnings to citizens about impending air raids and chemical and nuclear attacks.The warnings coincided with the expiry of a six-day local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in a small area of southern Ukraine - the longest such pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.Ukraine's public air raid app started to send false alerts just before 11 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Sunday for the capital Kyiv and other areas, warning of radiation and chemical attacks and also the risk of street combat in some areas.Hours later, Russian state news agency TASS quoted the Emergencies Ministry in Moscow as saying that its own mobile app had also been hit by a cyberattack that resulted in fake public warnings being transmitted.Reuters was unable to verify which groups were responsible.

Experts have linked previous cyber security incidents during the almost five-year-old war to activist hackers as well as intelligence agencies on both sides.In Ukraine, one of the alarms said Russia had launched a hypersonic Oreshnik missile - which is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead - and that a nuclear alert had been declared.Ukraine's air force said shortly after on the Telegram messaging app that the alert system appeared to have been hacked by Russia, noting that the alerts were broadcast in Russian.

The US on Friday announced a $2.1 billion deal to supply 500 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, but two people briefed on the decision said it could take years for the missiles to arrive.On the streets of Kyiv, residents played down the impact of the hack.Artem Pyndyk, 37, a businessman, said he was briefly surprised to see the messages but then realized what had happened."This didn't trigger the kind of reaction in society that they expected," said Pyndyk, adding that family members and friends he had checked in with had also not panicked."You can laugh about it but, on the other hand, they gained a certain level of access and were able to hack the program."Oksana Vostrykova, 48, also shrugged off the incident."I am calm about it, I kind of immediately understood that it might be a false message," the pizzeria employee said.

extraction.body: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save * Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. * If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off). * Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it.

extraction.body: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save * Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. * If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off). * Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it.

sources.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
passages: “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay.

It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.

extraction.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

extraction.body: Just days after General Motors agreed to settle a lawsuit over selling customers' data without their consent, Ford announced a new "Privacy Promise" policy . In a statement shared on a new website from the manufacturer, Ford promised owners that they are in the driver's seat when it comes to their data. The site offers guidance on data sharing and collection and how to deactivate and opt out of sharing various types of data, whether on the automaker's webpages, in its app or within the car itself. "We design and build our products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use and storage and even disposal. This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect your privacy," the statement began. "We strive to provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information. This empowers you to navigate your privacy choices with confidence. Once you make those choices, we respect your decision," the statement continued. Calling the move the "right thing to do," Ford shared that its updated vehicle privacy settings will allow users "to control what data you want to share, subject to the features and services you wish to enjoy." "We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers," Ford maintained, a sticking point following General Motors' lawsuit , which saw the Ford rival agree to pay $200 million in a settlement with 36 states following the incident, after it illegally sold drivers' personal information to third parties without their consent, per a Washington State release regarding the suit. As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share. "A value our survey respondents kept returning to was control: the ability to adjust their settings on demand and in detail," Ford added. But, as automotive outlet The Drive notes, there is no one place to turn everything off, forcing Ford owners to do lots of reading and searching to fully opt out of data sharing and customize their Ford experience. While some found the timing of Ford's new website launch uncoincidental amid its longtime feud with GM, in a statement to TechCrunch , Ford's chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said she wouldn't be commenting "on what our competitors are doing, or anything that's sort of been in the news." She did say, however, that as more and more consumers grow wary of whether companies will "take care with their data," Ford wants to make sure it's "building that trust relationship with them." The automaker uses this information to power features such as embedded navigation, real-time traffic updates, and Roadside Assistance. This data also helps Ford troubleshoot problems, improve future vehicles, and personalize your driving experience. Ford says it has built privacy protections for the data, such as anonymizing or grouping data to reduce exposure of personal information. Meanwhile, Ford surveyed over 1,000 consumers for this launch and found 91% believe data privacy is a key consideration when choosing a vehicle. Chief Privacy Officer Kristin Jones told TechCrunch it felt important to be upfront with customers, not just about Ford’s practices but with an actual commitment behind them. The timing is also notable, since Ford’s upcoming connected EVs will generate even more data than before. Ford says it will never sell your driving data to brokers or insurers, and its new website lets you adjust privacy settings anytime. However, opting out comes with trade-offs. Ford CPO Kristin Jones pledges no driving-behavior data sales to brokers, but gaps on insurers and default settings remain General Motors agreed to pay $220 million across 36 states to resolve allegations that it shared driving and location data with data brokers and insurers without adequate consent. Ford’s new “Privacy Promise” arrives in that context. Ford Chief Privacy Officer Kristin Jones framed the initiative as an active commitment to customers, not a legal formality. Jones described the motivation plainly. “I personally think that it’s super important for us to be making it very clear to our customers what our data practices are, and not only that, but making a commitment to them about it,” she told TechCrunch . According to Ford’s announcement, the initiative addresses privacy considerations across the data lifecycle, including collection, use, storage, and disposal. Ford’s connected vehicles can gather a range of information, and that data may be linked to the owner. Ford says it uses that data for connected services such as navigation, traffic updates, and roadside assistance, as well as for maintenance diagnostics , product development, and personalizing features to individual drivers. Ford’s most direct commitment targets the conduct that drew regulatory action against GM. “We also do not share information about how our customers are driving their vehicles to data brokers,” Jones told TechCrunch. Ford’s announcement states that the company does not sell driving-behavior data to data brokers, though the materials do not address every form of third-party data sharing. Ford says both the vehicle itself and the Ford app give drivers a path to adjust what they share. Ford says customers can adjust data-sharing preferences through the vehicle’s center display or the Ford app. The control mechanism exists; what matters is what happens when a driver uses it. Choosing privacy over connectivity comes with concrete feature losses, according to Ford’s own materials. Choosing not to share connected-vehicle data with Ford limits connected features. Real-time navigation, built-in roadside assistance, BlueCruise hands-free driving assistance, internet connectivity, and location functions within the Ford app may all be affected, depending on the vehicle and selected settings, according to Ford’s materials. Ford’s announcement is clear about what it prohibits but leaves several practical questions unresolved. The cited Ford announcement does not clarify whether connected-vehicle data is shared with insurers, advertisers, analytics contractors, or dealers . The available materials reviewed for this article do not specify which data uses require affirmative opt-in consent versus which are active by default. The announcement also does not identify an independent auditing mechanism to verify that the Privacy Promise is honored in practice. Those are open questions, not proven violations. They are, however, the same categories of ambiguity that drew regulatory scrutiny to GM’s data practices. Ford has named the privacy trade-off clearly; fully resolving it will require answers the company has not yet provided. Whether the Privacy Promise constitutes meaningful protection depends on details not yet addressed publicly. Those details include what third-party data sharing covers, which settings are active by default, and how long location and diagnostic data is retained. The trade-off between convenience and data exposure is real for drivers using FordPass, BlueCruise, or built-in navigation. Ford has named that trade-off. It has not yet fully resolved it. coreStoryFacts.text: “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay.

It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.
They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.
Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers.
This story Ford Promises Not to Sell Drivers' Data After General Motors Privacy Scandal first appeared on First for Autos .

"We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers," Ford maintained, a sticking point following General Motors' lawsuit , which saw the Ford rival agree to pay $200 million in a settlement with 36 states following the incident, after it illegally sold drivers' personal information to third parties without their consent, per a Washington State release regarding the suit.

As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share.

While some found the timing of Ford's new website launch uncoincidental amid its longtime feud with GM, in a statement to TechCrunch , Ford's chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said she wouldn't be commenting "on what our competitors are doing, or anything that's sort of been in the news."
Ford says it will never sell your driving data to brokers or insurers, and its new website lets you adjust privacy settings anytime.

According to industry polling , only 14% of customers fully understand what their car collects.
Meanwhile, Ford surveyed over 1,000 consumers for this launch and found 91% believe data privacy is a key consideration when choosing a vehicle.

This data also helps Ford troubleshoot problems, improve future vehicles, and personalize your driving experience.

extraction.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

extraction.body: Just days after General Motors agreed to settle a lawsuit over selling customers' data without their consent, Ford announced a new "Privacy Promise" policy . In a statement shared on a new website from the manufacturer, Ford promised owners that they are in the driver's seat when it comes to their data. The site offers guidance on data sharing and collection and how to deactivate and opt out of sharing various types of data, whether on the automaker's webpages, in its app or within the car itself. "We design and build our products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use and storage and even disposal. This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect your privacy," the statement began. "We strive to provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information. This empowers you to navigate your privacy choices with confidence. Once you make those choices, we respect your decision," the statement continued. Calling the move the "right thing to do," Ford shared that its updated vehicle privacy settings will allow users "to control what data you want to share, subject to the features and services you wish to enjoy." "We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers," Ford maintained, a sticking point following General Motors' lawsuit , which saw the Ford rival agree to pay $200 million in a settlement with 36 states following the incident, after it illegally sold drivers' personal information to third parties without their consent, per a Washington State release regarding the suit. As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share. "A value our survey respondents kept returning to was control: the ability to adjust their settings on demand and in detail," Ford added. But, as automotive outlet The Drive notes, there is no one place to turn everything off, forcing Ford owners to do lots of reading and searching to fully opt out of data sharing and customize their Ford experience. While some found the timing of Ford's new website launch uncoincidental amid its longtime feud with GM, in a statement to TechCrunch , Ford's chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said she wouldn't be commenting "on what our competitors are doing, or anything that's sort of been in the news." She did say, however, that as more and more consumers grow wary of whether companies will "take care with their data," Ford wants to make sure it's "building that trust relationship with them." The timing is also notable, since Ford’s upcoming connected EVs will generate even more data than before. Ford CPO Kristin Jones pledges no driving-behavior data sales to brokers, but gaps on insurers and default settings remain General Motors agreed to pay $220 million across 36 states to resolve allegations that it shared driving and location data with data brokers and insurers without adequate consent. Ford’s new “Privacy Promise” arrives in that context. Ford Chief Privacy Officer Kristin Jones framed the initiative as an active commitment to customers, not a legal formality. Jones described the motivation plainly. “I personally think that it’s super important for us to be making it very clear to our customers what our data practices are, and not only that, but making a commitment to them about it,” she told TechCrunch . According to Ford’s announcement, the initiative addresses privacy considerations across the data lifecycle, including collection, use, storage, and disposal. Ford’s connected vehicles can gather a range of information, and that data may be linked to the owner. Ford says it uses that data for connected services such as navigation, traffic updates, and roadside assistance, as well as for maintenance diagnostics , product development, and personalizing features to individual drivers. Ford’s most direct commitment targets the conduct that drew regulatory action against GM. “We also do not share information about how our customers are driving their vehicles to data brokers,” Jones told TechCrunch. Ford’s announcement states that the company does not sell driving-behavior data to data brokers, though the materials do not address every form of third-party data sharing. Ford says both the vehicle itself and the Ford app give drivers a path to adjust what they share. Ford says customers can adjust data-sharing preferences through the vehicle’s center display or the Ford app. The control mechanism exists; what matters is what happens when a driver uses it. Choosing privacy over connectivity comes with concrete feature losses, according to Ford’s own materials. Choosing not to share connected-vehicle data with Ford limits connected features. Real-time navigation, built-in roadside assistance, BlueCruise hands-free driving assistance, internet connectivity, and location functions within the Ford app may all be affected, depending on the vehicle and selected settings, according to Ford’s materials. Ford’s announcement is clear about what it prohibits but leaves several practical questions unresolved. The cited Ford announcement does not clarify whether connected-vehicle data is shared with insurers, advertisers, analytics contractors, or dealers . The available materials reviewed for this article do not specify which data uses require affirmative opt-in consent versus which are active by default. The announcement also does not identify an independent auditing mechanism to verify that the Privacy Promise is honored in practice. Those are open questions, not proven violations. They are, however, the same categories of ambiguity that drew regulatory scrutiny to GM’s data practices. sources.title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
passages: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project.

The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information.

The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years.
The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.

The core idea across the coverage stays consistent: a camera-and-sensor system that senses what is happening in a room, switches on lights when someone walks in, and supports video calls.

This analysis separates what is reported from what is confirmed, tests the $1,000 and 2027 claims against Apple’s recent hardware pattern, and looks at where an Apple home robot would sit next to products like the HomeView smart display we covered earlier . The headline claim is simple. Apple is working on a home robot, it would sell for roughly $1,000 in the United States, and it is aimed at 2027. Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.

MacRumors published its own piece on November 02 and describes the HomeView Ultra name with a 9-inch screen. That matches the roughly 9-inch display in the other reporting. Nobody in the coverage cites an Apple spokesperson, and we found no on-record quote from Apple or a named Apple representative.

J595 is the internal code name that appears in the reporting. Apple uses alphanumeric identifiers like it for unreleased hardware, and they rarely tell you much about the final marketing name. HomeView Ultra is the product name some reports use, and Apple has not confirmed it.

The name matters because it signals positioning. An Ultra label attached to HomeView would place the robot as the top tier of a home line, not as a separate product family. That reading is our inference. The reports do not say how Apple will brand the device, and Apple could pick something else entirely.

Two use cases dominate the coverage. The first is FaceTime. The second is turning on lights when someone enters a room. Both rely on the same underlying idea, which is that the device carries a camera-and-sensor system and uses it to understand the room around it.

FaceTime is the more natural fit. Apple owns the call experience end to end, and a home screen built for calls plays to that strength. The reports do not describe call features in detail, so how the device would frame or follow a speaker remains outside what any outlet has confirmed.

iThinkDiff reports the HomeView Ultra robot at about $1,000. FourWeekMBA says a tabletop version could cost about the same, citing a report. Ars Technica uses the same round number in its headline framing. Every outlet qualifies it as reported and subject to change.

A four-figure sticker puts the device in an unusual spot. It would cost far more than a typical smart display, and it would land in the price range Apple normally reserves for its top-tier products. Apple has shown it will charge that much when it believes a product is new. It has also shown it will cut features to hit a target price.

Our read is that $1,000 works as a planning anchor, not a promise. Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch. If the price holds, Apple is betting that buyers see the robot as a new category and not a pricey screen. If it climbs, the device narrows to early adopters, which may be exactly the point for a first generation.

The target in the reports is 2027. The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028. That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.

We did not find a stated reason for the possible slip in the verified coverage, so we will not assign one. The pattern in the industry is that sensing, on-device intelligence and reliability testing eat schedules faster than industrial design. That is general context, not a claim about J595 specifically.

For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case. For competitors, the gap is a window. Anyone selling a home robot or a premium display has at least a year to establish habits before Apple shows a finished product.

Apple’s home business has looked like a soft spot. A Yahoo Finance analysis ties the robot plan to the state of Apple’s home segment and asks what it means for AAPL stock. That framing is useful. A robot at this price signals that Apple wants to reset the home category with a flagship, not just refresh the speakers.

The broader industry is also watching robotics shift from lab demos to factory floors. Our look at how Tesla cleared a Model S line for Optimus robots shows how seriously large hardware makers now treat the field. Home robots are a different problem from factory humanoids, but investor attention to both is rising together.

A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot. Apple’s answer, based on the reports, is awareness and hands-free calls, and that case has to feel obvious in a store demo.

Retail strategy will matter as much as hardware. Apple stores let shoppers try a device in a staged room, which suits a product built around reacting to people. A boxed robot on a shelf sells poorly, while a live demo of lights switching on as a visitor walks in sells itself. Expect Apple to lean on that kind of showing if the project reaches launch.

A device that watches a room to decide when to act raises obvious privacy questions. Apple has built a brand on privacy, and it will have to explain where camera data is processed, what is stored, and who can see it. None of the reports address these points, so they remain open.

The bar here is higher than for a phone. A phone camera points where the owner points it. A home device with autonomous awareness can capture guests, children and routines without anyone choosing to record. Buyers and regulators will want clear indicators, easy off switches and plain disclosures.

This is also where the hardware category meets policy. Home cameras have already drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and security researchers, and a $1,000 Apple device would draw more. How Apple answers will shape trust in the whole premium home segment.

Support and repair raise a final question. Our coverage of the foldable line already shows how repair costs shape perception of a new Apple category. A robot with moving or sensing parts would add service complexity, and buyers at this price expect strong support. Apple has not said anything about warranty or service for the device, so that stays an open item.

A device with a camera-and-sensor system and a screen creates a new surface for software. If Apple opens it to third parties, developers could build call, reminder and household-routine experiences for a display that reacts to people. If Apple keeps it closed, the robot stays a showcase for first-party features.

The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open. Apple’s pattern with new hardware is to launch with a tight first-party feature set and widen access later. The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.

For accessory makers and smart-home brands, the question is compatibility. Anyone selling lights, locks or sensors will want to know whether the robot can control their devices. The light-control capability in the reports suggests Apple plans some home-control support, but the scope is unconfirmed. Vendors should watch Apple’s developer documentation for clues, since new hardware often shows up there before it ships.

Also track how the reported price evolves. If outlets converge on a different figure, that is a stronger signal than any single report. And watch whether Apple comments at all, because silence is the default until the company is ready to sell.

sources.title: Apple's Robot Ambitions: $1,000 HomeView Ultra Could Land in 2027 - BigGo Finance
passages: Apple is preparing to enter the home robotics market, with a robotic smart-home device code-named J595 that could carry a price tag of roughly $1,000 or more and reach customers as early as 2027, according to reporting from The Information.

The product, which people familiar with the effort expect to be branded HomeView Ultra, would sit alongside Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display, a device that arrives in users' homes within days.
For Apple investors, the project represents a long-horizon bet on a category the company has never sold into, and one whose revenue would not materialize before the end of the decade.
The timing also matters because Apple has been selective about extending its "Ultra" branding to new products.
Component prices could push the final retail figure above the $1,000 target, and the launch could slip to 2028 if software work falls behind.
Rivals in home automation and consumer robotics would have time to respond, and any delay would leave Apple's smart-home lineup anchored by the HomeView display shipping this month.

Beyond the HomeView Ultra, he is backing a separate effort aimed at machines that can handle household chores such as folding laundry, a project that would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators.
It is unclear whether that work points toward a general-purpose humanoid robot of the kind being developed by startups 1X and Figure AI.

The report describes a core group of only about 10 "true roboticists," with many members of the original engineering team having left over the years, while the software organization counts roughly 300 people.
Apple has not publicly confirmed the project, the name, or the price.
Much of the physical hardware has been ready for about two years, but software remains the bottleneck.

The delay stems from Apple's decision to pursue a more ambitious set of AI-powered capabilities than it originally planned, when the device was conceived mostly as a way to make FaceTime calls more engaging by following a person from room to room.
The project's origins trace back to 2018 prototypes, and former Apple chief executive Tim Cook approved continued work on it.
Equipped with cameras and sensors, the robot is meant to understand its surroundings and act on its own, such as turning on lights when someone walks in or shooing a cat off a table.

The open question is commercial rather than technical: whether buyers will pay four figures for a moving screen whose demonstrated functions overlap with far cheaper smart-home gear and robot vacuums.
