relevantPassages.text: Apple is preparing to enter the home robotics market, with a robotic smart-home device code-named J595 that could carry a price tag of roughly $1,000 or more and reach customers as early as 2027, according to reporting from The Information.

The product, which people familiar with the effort expect to be branded HomeView Ultra, would sit alongside Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display, a device that arrives in users' homes within days.
For Apple investors, the project represents a long-horizon bet on a category the company has never sold into, and one whose revenue would not materialize before the end of the decade.
The timing also matters because Apple has been selective about extending its "Ultra" branding to new products.
Component prices could push the final retail figure above the $1,000 target, and the launch could slip to 2028 if software work falls behind.
Rivals in home automation and consumer robotics would have time to respond, and any delay would leave Apple's smart-home lineup anchored by the HomeView display shipping this month.

Beyond the HomeView Ultra, he is backing a separate effort aimed at machines that can handle household chores such as folding laundry, a project that would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators.
It is unclear whether that work points toward a general-purpose humanoid robot of the kind being developed by startups 1X and Figure AI.

The report describes a core group of only about 10 "true roboticists," with many members of the original engineering team having left over the years, while the software organization counts roughly 300 people.
Apple has not publicly confirmed the project, the name, or the price.
Much of the physical hardware has been ready for about two years, but software remains the bottleneck.

The delay stems from Apple's decision to pursue a more ambitious set of AI-powered capabilities than it originally planned, when the device was conceived mostly as a way to make FaceTime calls more engaging by following a person from room to room.
The project's origins trace back to 2018 prototypes, and former Apple chief executive Tim Cook approved continued work on it.
Equipped with cameras and sensors, the robot is meant to understand its surroundings and act on its own, such as turning on lights when someone walks in or shooing a cat off a table.

The open question is commercial rather than technical: whether buyers will pay four figures for a moving screen whose demonstrated functions overlap with far cheaper smart-home gear and robot vacuums.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project.

The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information.

The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years.
The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.
Apple is reportedly building a home robot that would cost around $1,000 and handle FaceTime calls and light control, and Ars Technica frames the device as a 2027 product.
No name, price, specification or date has come from the company, so everything below rests on press reports as of November 02, 2026.
Where we offer judgment instead of reporting, we say so.
Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.
The takeaway: Apple’s home robot is a credible report with a lot of unknowns.
For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case.
Buyers will compare it against what they already own.
A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot.
The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open.
The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.
The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028.
That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.
Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch.
The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes.

iThinkDiff reports the HomeView Ultra robot at about $1,000. FourWeekMBA says a tabletop version could cost about the same, citing a report. Ars Technica uses the same round number in its headline framing. Every outlet qualifies it as reported and subject to change.

A four-figure sticker puts the device in an unusual spot. It would cost far more than a typical smart display, and it would land in the price range Apple normally reserves for its top-tier products. Apple has shown it will charge that much when it believes a product is new. It has also shown it will cut features to hit a target price.

Our read is that $1,000 works as a planning anchor, not a promise. Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch. If the price holds, Apple is betting that buyers see the robot as a new category and not a pricey screen. If it climbs, the device narrows to early adopters, which may be exactly the point for a first generation.

The target in the reports is 2027. The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028. That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.

We did not find a stated reason for the possible slip in the verified coverage, so we will not assign one. The pattern in the industry is that sensing, on-device intelligence and reliability testing eat schedules faster than industrial design. That is general context, not a claim about J595 specifically.

For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case. For competitors, the gap is a window. Anyone selling a home robot or a premium display has at least a year to establish habits before Apple shows a finished product.

Apple’s home business has looked like a soft spot. A Yahoo Finance analysis ties the robot plan to the state of Apple’s home segment and asks what it means for AAPL stock. That framing is useful. A robot at this price signals that Apple wants to reset the home category with a flagship, not just refresh the speakers.

The broader industry is also watching robotics shift from lab demos to factory floors. Our look at how Tesla cleared a Model S line for Optimus robots shows how seriously large hardware makers now treat the field. Home robots are a different problem from factory humanoids, but investor attention to both is rising together.

The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes. That suggests the J595 is the product that survived a wider exploration, not Apple’s only idea. It fits the company’s habit of testing many prototypes and shipping few.

A $1,000 device will not move Apple’s revenue on its own. Apple’s scale is large enough that a first-generation home robot is a rounding error against its core lines. Our breakdown of Apple’s first earnings under Ternus shows where the company’s margin pressure actually sits.

The real signal is strategic. Investors read new categories as proof that Apple can find growth beyond the phone. The same logic drove attention to the foldable line, which our analysis of the iPhone Duo growth case covers. A home robot would extend that story into a different part of the house.

Rivals face a different calculation. If Apple legitimizes the premium home robot, competitors gain a category reference point. If it stumbles, the whole segment looks riskier. Either outcome reshapes how smart-home vendors pitch their next generation.

One more thing about the price. At $1,000, an Apple home robot competes with a laptop or a mid-range phone for the same household budget. Buyers will compare it against what they already own. A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot. Apple’s answer, based on the reports, is awareness and hands-free calls, and that case has to feel obvious in a store demo.

Retail strategy will matter as much as hardware. Apple stores let shoppers try a device in a staged room, which suits a product built around reacting to people. A boxed robot on a shelf sells poorly, while a live demo of lights switching on as a visitor walks in sells itself. Expect Apple to lean on that kind of showing if the project reaches launch.

A device that watches a room to decide when to act raises obvious privacy questions. Apple has built a brand on privacy, and it will have to explain where camera data is processed, what is stored, and who can see it. None of the reports address these points, so they remain open.

The bar here is higher than for a phone. A phone camera points where the owner points it. A home device with autonomous awareness can capture guests, children and routines without anyone choosing to record. Buyers and regulators will want clear indicators, easy off switches and plain disclosures.

This is also where the hardware category meets policy. Home cameras have already drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and security researchers, and a $1,000 Apple device would draw more. How Apple answers will shape trust in the whole premium home segment.

Support and repair raise a final question. Our coverage of the foldable line already shows how repair costs shape perception of a new Apple category. A robot with moving or sensing parts would add service complexity, and buyers at this price expect strong support. Apple has not said anything about warranty or service for the device, so that stays an open item.

A device with a camera-and-sensor system and a screen creates a new surface for software. If Apple opens it to third parties, developers could build call, reminder and household-routine experiences for a display that reacts to people. If Apple keeps it closed, the robot stays a showcase for first-party features.

The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open. Apple’s pattern with new hardware is to launch with a tight first-party feature set and widen access later. The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.

For accessory makers and smart-home brands, the question is compatibility. Anyone selling lights, locks or sensors will want to know whether the robot can control their devices. The light-control capability in the reports suggests Apple plans some home-control support, but the scope is unconfirmed. Vendors should watch Apple’s developer documentation for clues, since new hardware often shows up there before it ships.

Also track how the reported price evolves. If outlets converge on a different figure, that is a stronger signal than any single report. And watch whether Apple comments at all, because silence is the default until the company is ready to sell.

The takeaway: Apple’s home robot is a credible report with a lot of unknowns. A roughly $1,000 device with FaceTime and light control, aimed at 2027 and possibly slipping to 2028, is the version in circulation. Until Apple confirms the name, price, specifications or date, plan around the uncertainty.

sources.title: Apple's Robot Ambitions: $1,000 HomeView Ultra Could Land in 2027 - BigGo Finance
passages: Apple is preparing to enter the home robotics market, with a robotic smart-home device code-named J595 that could carry a price tag of roughly $1,000 or more and reach customers as early as 2027, according to reporting from The Information.

The product, which people familiar with the effort expect to be branded HomeView Ultra, would sit alongside Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display, a device that arrives in users' homes within days.
For Apple investors, the project represents a long-horizon bet on a category the company has never sold into, and one whose revenue would not materialize before the end of the decade.
The timing also matters because Apple has been selective about extending its "Ultra" branding to new products.
Component prices could push the final retail figure above the $1,000 target, and the launch could slip to 2028 if software work falls behind.
Rivals in home automation and consumer robotics would have time to respond, and any delay would leave Apple's smart-home lineup anchored by the HomeView display shipping this month.

Beyond the HomeView Ultra, he is backing a separate effort aimed at machines that can handle household chores such as folding laundry, a project that would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators.
It is unclear whether that work points toward a general-purpose humanoid robot of the kind being developed by startups 1X and Figure AI.

The report describes a core group of only about 10 "true roboticists," with many members of the original engineering team having left over the years, while the software organization counts roughly 300 people.
Apple has not publicly confirmed the project, the name, or the price.
Much of the physical hardware has been ready for about two years, but software remains the bottleneck.

The delay stems from Apple's decision to pursue a more ambitious set of AI-powered capabilities than it originally planned, when the device was conceived mostly as a way to make FaceTime calls more engaging by following a person from room to room.
The project's origins trace back to 2018 prototypes, and former Apple chief executive Tim Cook approved continued work on it.
Equipped with cameras and sensors, the robot is meant to understand its surroundings and act on its own, such as turning on lights when someone walks in or shooing a cat off a table.

The open question is commercial rather than technical: whether buyers will pay four figures for a moving screen whose demonstrated functions overlap with far cheaper smart-home gear and robot vacuums.

passages: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .

Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.
Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.

Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.
Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance.
"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.

The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets. Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber-attack . The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack. Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion." There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added. Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance. The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.3bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack. Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed. Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back. "We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme. "The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added. The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 . The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them. The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets. Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions. The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue. Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. extraction.body: Customers of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, withdrew approximately $3.6bn in digital assets after the platform resumed operations on Sunday following a cyberattack that affected $6.3bn worth of cryptocurrencies. The withdrawals came after Binance suspended transactions in response to the breach, which has been blamed on North Korea by major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Binance disclosed that it processed $4.649bn in withdrawals and $1.01bn in deposits between 06:00 and 15:30 GMT on November 1, leaving the exchange with a net outflow of approximately $3.64bn. The company announced the figures on X, saying: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion." According to the exchange, withdrawals initially surged following the resumption of services but subsequently slowed, with activity "stabilising as expected". Despite the significant outflow, Binance said the withdrawals represented just over two per cent of the $171bn in assets under its management. The company has also assured customers that it is working to recover from the breach, maintaining that it will bear the full financial consequences of the incident. Binance said it had already replaced approximately 95 per cent of the stolen assets, although recovering the outstanding amount could take additional time. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. Last week, the exchange disclosed that it had set aside more than $6.3bn to manage the consequences of the attack. It also confirmed that withdrawals involving more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, had resumed. Other services are expected to return in stages after completing the necessary security checks. Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis, which is assisting Binance and government agencies with the recovery effort, said the attackers were actively moving the stolen assets through multiple cryptocurrency wallets. "We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme. "The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added. The group was previously linked to the theft of $1.5bn from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in 2025, then considered a record-breaking cryptocurrency heist. On Saturday, the FBI released a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses associated with the group, asking industry partners to help prevent the movement of stolen funds by blocking transactions connected to the addresses. ALSO READ: US: All nine on board killed as jet crashes near Trump’s Florida home Binance also called on cryptocurrency issuers to freeze assets believed to be linked to the breach. The exchange's preliminary investigation indicated that the attack may have originated from an engineer's compromised laptop, which hackers allegedly exploited to gain access to unauthorised transactions. The incident affected Binance.com, the company's global centralised exchange. However, Binance's US-facing platform said it was not impacted. Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide. The platform allows customers to buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies, which are digital assets that exist electronically rather than in physical form.

Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."

Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.

Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alex Zebrick, a senior investigator at Chainalysis who has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.

The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.

Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.

extraction.body: Binance customers withdrew a net $3.64bn (£2.72bn) of assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following a record hack last week. The firm suspended all transactions in the wake of the incident, which impacted $6.3bn worth of digital assets. Major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), have accused North Korea of being responsible for the cyber attack, which is said to be the largest hack in history. The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach, but that the remaining amount may take longer to source. Binance has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack. "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion," Binance posted on X. There was an "initial spike" in withdrawals, which later declined and "are stabilising as expected", it added. It also said withdrawals for more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed. The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025. The FBI on Saturday published a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses linked to the group and urged partners in the industry to help by blocking transactions involving them. The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it has not been affected by the issue. The exchange scrambled to urge cryptocurrency issuers to freeze affected assets. Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions. The crypto withdrawn represents just a fraction of the total value of assets held by Binance. The exact valuation of Binance is unclear as the firm is privately held, though the company said in 2024 that it had more than $160bn in assets in its custody. The firm said last week that it has reserved more than $6.34bn in funds, to deal with ​the fallout of the attack. Binance said it replaced customers' assets using a combination of channels that include its corporate treasury and its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. Cryptocurrencies are digital assets traded on exchanges such as Binance. Unlike cash, they do not exist in physical form and are managed on computers, smartphones and other digital devices. extraction.body: Customers of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, withdrew approximately $3.6bn in digital assets after the platform resumed operations on Sunday following a cyberattack that affected $6.3bn worth of cryptocurrencies. The withdrawals came after Binance suspended transactions in response to the breach, which has been blamed on North Korea by major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Binance disclosed that it processed $4.649bn in withdrawals and $1.01bn in deposits between 06:00 and 15:30 GMT on November 1, leaving the exchange with a net outflow of approximately $3.64bn. The company announced the figures on X, saying: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion." According to the exchange, withdrawals initially surged following the resumption of services but subsequently slowed, with activity "stabilising as expected". Despite the significant outflow, Binance said the withdrawals represented just over two per cent of the $171bn in assets under its management. The company has also assured customers that it is working to recover from the breach, maintaining that it will bear the full financial consequences of the incident. Binance said it had already replaced approximately 95 per cent of the stolen assets, although recovering the outstanding amount could take additional time. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. Last week, the exchange disclosed that it had set aside more than $6.3bn to manage the consequences of the attack. It also confirmed that withdrawals involving more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, had resumed. Other services are expected to return in stages after completing the necessary security checks. Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis, which is assisting Binance and government agencies with the recovery effort, said the attackers were actively moving the stolen assets through multiple cryptocurrency wallets. "We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme. "The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added. The group was previously linked to the theft of $1.5bn from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in 2025, then considered a record-breaking cryptocurrency heist. On Saturday, the FBI released a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses associated with the group, asking industry partners to help prevent the movement of stolen funds by blocking transactions connected to the addresses. ALSO READ: US: All nine on board killed as jet crashes near Trump’s Florida home Binance also called on cryptocurrency issuers to freeze assets believed to be linked to the breach. The exchange's preliminary investigation indicated that the attack may have originated from an engineer's compromised laptop, which hackers allegedly exploited to gain access to unauthorised transactions. The incident affected Binance.com, the company's global centralised exchange. However, Binance's US-facing platform said it was not impacted. Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide. The platform allows customers to buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies, which are digital assets that exist electronically rather than in physical form.

sources.title: Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone
passages: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model.
Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products.
Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

With the standard iPhone 18 delayed until spring 2027, the iPhone 17 is set to become the longest-lived standard model in the company’s history. The move comes alongside Apple’s best-ever March quarter revenue, driven by what CEO Tim Cook described as “extraordinary demand” for the iPhone 17 series. For years, Apple has followed a predictable rhythm: new iPhones every September. That rhythm is about to change. According to multiple reports, Apple will launch only the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the much-anticipated iPhone Ultra foldable at its September 2026 event. The standard iPhone 18 will not appear until the following spring. This delay means the iPhone 17, which debuted in September 2025, will remain on sale for roughly 18 months—an unusually long lifecycle for a non-Pro model. Apple has already ramped up production capacity for the iPhone 17, signaling its intention to keep the device in the spotlight through the 2026 holiday season and beyond. The extended production run is expected to allow the phone to participate in major sales events like China’s Double 11 shopping festival later this year. The iPhone 17’s staying power is not just about timing—it is also about hardware. For the first time, a standard iPhone model includes ProMotion technology, giving it a 120Hz variable refresh rate display that matches the Pro lineup. This upgrade addresses one of the most persistent criticisms of Apple’s base models. Apple also eliminated the 128GB entry-level storage tier, starting the iPhone 17 at 256GB. Despite the upgrade, the starting price remains at $876 USD (converted from CNY 5,999 at the reference rate of 0.146). In China, government subsidies of up to $73 USD (CNY 500) can bring the effective price down to about $803 USD. This pricing strategy positions the iPhone 17 as a value-driven option in the premium segment. The strategy is working. According to Counterpoint Research, iPhone sales surged 22% in the first month after the iPhone 17’s launch, even as the overall smartphone market contracted by 2.7%. This growth helped Apple report its best March quarter ever, with total revenue of $111.2 billion—a 17% year-over-year increase. iPhone-specific revenue reached $56.99 billion, slightly above analyst expectations. Tim Cook attributed the results to double-digit growth across every geographic segment and strong demand for the entire iPhone 17 lineup, including the iPhone 17e, which launched during the quarter. Apple also set new March quarter records for operating cash flow (over $28 billion) and earnings per share. Not everything is smooth sailing. Cook warned that memory costs are expected to rise significantly in the coming quarter, driven by an ongoing memory shortage that has already impacted other tech companies. Rising component prices could pressure Apple’s margins, especially as it continues to offer competitive pricing on the iPhone 17. Additionally, Cook is set to step down as CEO later this year, marking the end of an era. His departure adds an element of uncertainty to Apple’s future product and pricing strategies, though the company’s current momentum remains strong. The iPhone 17’s extended lifecycle is a clear sign that Apple is willing to break its own traditions to maximize returns on a winning product. For consumers, it means a well-equipped phone at a stable price—and a longer wait before the next standard model arrives. North Korea on Tuesday dismissed as "absurd rhetoric" US allegations that it was behind a $6 billion cryptocurrency heist on the Binance platform , saying they proved Washington remained hostile towards it, state news agency KCNA said. The denial issued by Kim Yo Jong , the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un , comes as Pyongyang has stayed silent on US President Donald Trump's overtures to resume summit diplomacy. Kim Yo Jong warned that North Korea had "issues to reconsider" over what it calls US hostility. The FBI said at the weekend that North Korea was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cybercriminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organisation 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," KCNA quoted Kim Yo Jong, a ruling party official, as saying. DPRK is a short form for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. "But the US assertion is absurd rhetoric and nothing new," Kim said. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cybercrimes in different parts of the world are our deeds." Cybersecurity experts say North Korean hackers are among the world's most prolific crypto thieves and the proceeds help fund the country's weapons programmes. North Korea denies all allegations of its links to cryptocurrency theft and other cybercrimes. North Korea is one of the world's most impoverished countries but has poured resources secured through illicit means and activities banned under UN Security Council resolutions into its ballistic missile and nuclear weapons programmes . Kim Yo Jong said North Korea would "reconsider" unspecified issues in light of the "very unpleasant US hostile attitude". While she did not elaborate, North Korea has not publicly responded to Trump's offers to resume summit diplomacy, and experts have said Pyongyang may be weighing its options. The FBI said members of a North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor were responsible for the Binance attack. extraction.body: Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denied North Korea’s involvement in the $6.3 billion Binance hack and appeared to suggest, without evidence, that the US could have been behind the theft. In a statement released via the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Tuesday, Kim rejected the FBI’s attribution of the attack to a North Korean-backed hacking group. “The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a ‘cyber criminal state’, claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization ‘supported’ by the DPRK was involved in the incident,” said Kim. “But the US assertion is an absurd rhetoric and nothing new.” She described the allegations as a political provocation intended to damage North Korea’s international standing. The FBI also blamed North Korea for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, an accusation Kim also rejected on Tuesday. “This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the ‘cyber crime’ incidents whenever they occur on an international scale,” said Kim. Kim has also pointed the finger at the US for involvement in the hack, without supplying any evidence. “If it carefully examines who will get the large amount of the so-called stolen cryptocurrency when the latter is retrieved, it may get a clue about who is behind the hacking incident,” she said. The statement provided no evidence connecting Washington to the attack. Cointelegraph reached out to the FBI for comment. Kim has also pointed the finger at the US for involvement in the hack, without supplying any evidence. “If it carefully examines who will get the large amount of the so-called stolen cryptocurrency when the latter is retrieved, it may get a clue about who is behind the hacking incident,” she said. Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea. The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits. Binance detailed that the resulting net outflows represent just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets under management. Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen. On Monday, the exchange said it has covered approximately 95% of the impacted amount. The outstanding 5% consists of smaller tokens outside of the top 10 cryptocurrencies, whose assets are less liquid and will take longer to source. "We continue working with industry partners to complete the remaining acquisitions," Binance said in an update on X. Over the weekend, the FBI said the attack was linked to North Korea. "The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," a press release said. Customer withdrawals were temporarily suspended, and co-CEO Richard Teng promised the exchange will cover all losses. Teng said the hack was not carried out by one person. Initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but further review revealed broader security breaches. "This was a complex attack," Teng said. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers." Around $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, according to Tom Robinson, chief scientist and co-founder at blockchain analytics company Elliptic. The attack has rattled crypto markets, and bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) traded at around $77,700 on Monday. Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data. Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.

On the other chains the funds left through ordinary signed transfers rather than any delegation trick.

28, and the attack code rehearsed on other wallets about four hours before it ran.

Market makers disclosed their exposure quickly.

Three blockchain analytics firms have pointed at North Korea.
Chainalysis CEO Jonathan Levin said TraderTraitor likely carried it out.

Co-CEO Yi He said the exchange was buying altcoins in quantities matching what was taken ahead of an updated proof of reserves.
Founder Changpeng Zhao said that as a shareholder he expects user funds to be covered in full.
Binance's explanation has developed over the day, and the times matter.

30 it said its initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, which may have let an attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
It said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked.
At 07:37 UTC co-CEO Richard Teng wrote that the attack involved a more complex process than a single click and that the investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual.
The 50 signatures covered 50 consecutive transaction counts so that one would be valid at execution.
Because the delegation stayed in place, the attacker swept new deposits into the same wallet at least six more times over the next three and a half hours.

Figures for stolen, frozen and moving funds are dated estimates and should not be treated as live balances.

29, when five Binance wallets on the XRP Ledger sent 233 million XRP to a single attacker address.

TRM counts ten chains; Elliptic counts eleven, adding NEAR.

And the money that was saved was saved by issuers who could freeze within minutes, which is an argument for knowing, before an incident, who can freeze what and how to reach them.

extraction.body: By Rae Wee, Elizabeth Howcroft and Hannah Lang SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning. The ​theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay ‌customers in full. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX. The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so ‌far in ​2026. Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the ⁠last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit ​did not respond to requests for comment. Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to ​withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the ‌FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether also rebounded from a two-month low. Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday. The FBI said on Saturday that the North ⁠Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Researchers describe the group as highly sophisticated and say its activities help fund the country’s weapons programs. Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, ⁠according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said. About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by ​issuers including Circle, ‌which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control ​around $3.28 billion, mostly ⁠in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.” Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear. “The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency. (Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by ​Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so ‌far in ​2026.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the ⁠last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit ​did not respond to requests for comment.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.
Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to ​withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago.
“After the ‌FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old.
After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether also rebounded from a two-month low.

“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.

Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear.

“The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency.

sources.title: Binance customers withdraw more than $4.6 billion after crypto heist
passages: Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”
The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

A second wave hit Avalanche and Polygon wallets around 23:00 UTC, and sweeps on Ethereum continued until just before midnight. TRM counts ten chains; Elliptic counts eleven, adding NEAR. The Ethereum leg is the most unusual. According to TRM, a single transaction at 20:20 UTC carried 50 authorizations signed by a Binance hot wallet under EIP-7702, a 2025 Ethereum change that lets an ordinary wallet hand control to a smart contract. About three and a half minutes later the wallet's full balance, 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens including 1.6 billion USDT, went to the attacker. The Ethereum leg is the most unusual. According to TRM, a single transaction at 20:20 UTC carried 50 authorizations signed by a Binance hot wallet under EIP-7702, a 2025 Ethereum change that lets an ordinary wallet hand control to a smart contract. The 50 signatures covered 50 consecutive transaction counts so that one would be valid at execution. One was. About three and a half minutes later the wallet's full balance, 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens including 1.6 billion USDT, went to the attacker. Because the delegation stayed in place, the attacker swept new deposits into the same wallet at least six more times over the next three and a half hours.

On the other chains the funds left through ordinary signed transfers rather than any delegation trick. TRM's conclusion is that this points to a compromise of Binance's hot wallet signing infrastructure rather than its cryptography, a pattern Elliptic compares to the Bybit theft of about $1.5 billion in February 2025. Elliptic also found preparation the day before: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet on Oct. 28, and the attack code rehearsed on other wallets about four hours before it ran.

The headline figures differ because the firms value the assets at different moments. Binance's own estimate is about $6.3 billion. TRM counts $6.36 billion at the price of each asset when it was taken, or about $6.23 billion at current prices. Elliptic counts $6.43 billion, excluding $169 million that left Binance after withdrawals were paused and that it believes was Binance moving its own money. Chainalysis has put the figure at roughly $5.9 billion at the time of theft, according to CoinDesk . By Elliptic's count, stablecoins made up $3.46 billion of the total, and USDT on Ethereum, Bitcoin, USDC and USDT on Tron together accounted for 74% of it.

The most useful operational detail in the trackers' reports is how fast issuers moved. Elliptic says Tether froze the main attacker wallet 37 minutes after the USDT arrived, locking 1.18 billion USDT, then froze four more addresses within 17 minutes. Circle froze 823 million USDC in the same wallet three minutes after Tether acted. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino later put his company's total above $1.567 billion, and Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said his firm had frozen more than $800 million in coordination with law enforcement.

Ripple froze RLUSD, World Liberty Financial froze USD1, Paxos and First Digital froze their stablecoins, Tether froze tokenized gold, and the Arbitrum Security Council moved about $30 million in ETH and ARB out of the attacker's reach. Aave froze the affected lending markets, which blocked new activity but seized nothing. Binance puts the verified frozen total at about $3 billion; Elliptic verifies $2.84 billion, or 44% of the theft, and says stablecoins were 94% of what was frozen.

The attacker converted some stablecoins before the freezes landed. TRM saw about 325 million USDT sold through intent-based swap contracts for roughly 122,300 ETH at about 10% below market, 300 million USDT parked in a Tron lending protocol, and about 48 million RLUSD sold before Ripple froze the rest. Elliptic estimates about $786 million of stablecoins became ETH and TRX, with implied losses of 12% to 26% on some swaps, which it reads as the attacker trading price for speed. Roughly $3.3 billion, including about 18,270 BTC split across 19 addresses, remains outside any issuer's reach.

Three blockchain analytics firms have pointed at North Korea. TRM Labs attributes the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, the unit the FBI named for the Bybit theft, citing shared patterns with Bybit and the April 2026 KelpDAO exploit: small Tornado Cash withdrawals, staging well before the theft, and pre-obtained signatures executed in one burst. Chainalysis CEO Jonathan Levin said TraderTraitor likely carried it out. Elliptic says North Korean actors are likely responsible, citing funds from Binance and the September 2026 Bitget exploit reaching the same Ethereum address, but it lists caveats: the overlap is small, the laundering has been slower than usual for the group, and Binance has not published a root cause.

Update, November 2: The FBI’s October 31 cyber alert attributes the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance to North Korea and names the activity TraderTraitor. This supersedes the earlier statement here that no government had attributed the attack. The FBI says it and partner agencies observed stolen assets being converted primarily into Ether.

CoinDesk reported on Thursday evening that bitcoin fell 4.8% to below $77,000, ether 5.7%, BNB 8% and AAVE 11%. By Friday morning, Yahoo Finance had bitcoin at $78,106 after a low of $76,518, ether down 3.7% at $2,232, and Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy each down about 5% in premarket trading. Glassnode's breakdown of the stolen assets, cited by Yahoo Finance, said Binance's BNB holdings were untouched.

Market makers disclosed their exposure quickly. Wintermute's Evgeny Gaevoy said the firm's Binance exposure was under 20% of net equity, and GSR's Xin Song put its exposure under 5%; neither expected major disruption, according to Cointelegraph . Standard Chartered's Geoffrey Kendrick said the hack could accelerate the shift to decentralized exchanges. Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan told CoinDesk the tactics were consistent with North Korean operations and suggested signing-infrastructure compromise rather than key theft.

The next checkpoint is the scope of restored withdrawals: Elliptic reports that Binance began with the Bitcoin network on November 1, rather than reopening every network at once. The promised post-mortem and updated proof of reserves remain important evidence for the cause and coverage of losses. Figures for stolen, frozen and moving funds are dated estimates and should not be treated as live balances. For formal attribution and addresses linked to the laundering, consult the FBI’s October 31 alert.

For anyone running custody or treasury operations, two details from the trackers stand out. The attack did not break any cryptography; it got Binance's own signing infrastructure to sign for the attacker, and the Ethereum delegation kept working until it was revoked. And the money that was saved was saved by issuers who could freeze within minutes, which is an argument for knowing, before an incident, who can freeze what and how to reach them.

sources.title: Binance says customers pulled net $4.7 billion after hack as crypto world weighs risk - The Mighty 790 KFGO
passages: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”
The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets.
Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.

extraction.body: By Rae Wee, Elizabeth Howcroft and Hannah Lang SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning. The ​theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay ‌customers in full. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX. The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so ‌far in ​2026. Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the ⁠last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit ​did not respond to requests for comment. Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to ​withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the ‌FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether also rebounded from a two-month low. Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday. The FBI said on Saturday that the North ⁠Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Researchers describe the group as highly sophisticated and say its activities help fund the country’s weapons programs. Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, ⁠according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said. About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by ​issuers including Circle, ‌which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control ​around $3.28 billion, mostly ⁠in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.” Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear. “The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency. (Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by ​Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.
The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning.
The ​theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay ‌customers in full.

Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added.

The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX.
The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so ‌far in ​2026.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the ⁠last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit ​did not respond to requests for comment.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.
Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to ​withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago.
“After the ‌FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old.
After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether also rebounded from a two-month low.

Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.

The FBI said on Saturday that the North ⁠Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Researchers describe the group as highly sophisticated and say its activities help fund the country’s weapons programs.

Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, ⁠according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by ​issuers including Circle, ‌which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC.

According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control ​around $3.28 billion, mostly ⁠in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.”

Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear.

“The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency.

(Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by ​Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

passages: Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.
