Mizzou Athletics announced a partnership with World Wide Technology that will add a new patch to Mizzou basketball uniforms. Mizzou Athletics and Learfield announced Monday that World Wide Technology will be the new jersey patch partner for Mizzou Basketball. As part of the partnership, the St. Louis based companies' acronym, WWT, will be featured on both the women's and men's uniforms. WWT’s logo will also appear on Norm Stewart Court at Mizzou Arena as part of the Tiger’s expanded partnership. "We are proud to welcome World Wide Technology as a partner of Mizzou Athletics and Mizzou Basketball," said Laird Veatch, Mizzou Director of Athletics. "WWT’s founder and chairman David Steward, its co-founder and CEO Jim Kavanaugh and their team have built an extraordinary company with a global reach and deep Missouri roots. When you have the opportunity to partner with a brand of WWT’s caliber, you put them at the top of your draft board. WWT's investment in our basketball programs demonstrates a strong belief in Mizzou and our commitment to competing for championships. We’re excited to continue to build this partnership with an organization that shares our pride in Missouri and our ambition to demand excellence" said Laird Veatch. To report an error or typo, email news@komu.com .

The sponsorship builds upon the company’s deep and long-standing connection to its home state university through cybersecurity, AI and digital transformation. Over many years, WWT has partnered with the university on its technology modernization efforts across all University of Missouri System campuses and University of Missouri Health Care. "Missouri is home, and World Wide Technology is blessed and honored to support the institutions and people who make our state special," said Steward, WWT's founder and chairman. Supporting Mizzou Basketball is another way we can give back to our home state and encourage the next generation of leaders on and off the court.” “World Wide Technology is an outstanding example of what can be accomplished through vision and teamwork. I have really appreciated my relationship with Mr. Steward over the years and know how much he values giving back to the community,” Mizzou’s Whitten Family Men's Basketball Head Coach Dennis Gates said. “He has continually demonstrated that with his exceptional work with the Steward Family Foundation and with his partnership at Mizzou. Steward’s support and friendship as we continue to build a championship program in Columbia.” "We're so grateful for World Wide Technology's investment in Mizzou and Mr. Steward’s belief in our programs and student-athletes," Mizzou Women’s Basketball coach Kellie Harper said. "Having a Missouri-based technology company with WWT's reputation and history support our team is incredibly exciting, and we're proud to represent this university and our state together." The sponsorship with World Wide Technology was created with Mizzou Athletics in collaboration with Learfield’s Mizzou Sports Properties. “World Wide Technology is a natural fit for this opportunity. As a Missouri-based industry leader with deep ties to Mizzou, WWT shares a commitment to excellence, innovation and elevating the student-athlete experience,” said Josh Pell, General Manager of Mizzou Sports Properties. “We’re proud to work alongside Mizzou Athletics to bring WWT’s brand to the forefront of Mizzou Basketball and create meaningful connections with Tiger fans.” About World Wide TechnologyWorld Wide Technology (WWT) is a global technology solutions provider helping organizations make a new world happen by turning ambition into real-world outcomes. Founded in 1990, WWT brings together strategy, deep technical expertise and world-class technology partnerships to help public- and private-sector organizations design, build and scale intelligent AI, digital, cybersecurity, cloud and infrastructure solutions. Through its Advanced Technology Center (ATC), a collaborative ecosystem featuring state-of-the-art hardware and software, WWT enables clients and partners to conceptualize, test and validate innovative technology and then deploy solutions at scale using its global integration and distribution capabilities. With more than 14,000 team members and over 60 locations worldwide, WWT's culture— grounded in core values and leadership philosophies— has been recognized by Fortune and Great Place to Work® for its commitment to innovation, trust and creating a great place to work for all. Softchoice, a World Wide Technology company, supports commercial and SMB markets in the U.S. and Canada. About LearfieldLearfield is the leading media and technology company powering college athletics. With ties to over 1,200 collegiate institutions and over 12,000 local and national brand partners, Learfield’s presence in college sports and live events delivers influence and maximizes reach to target audiences. With solutions for a 365-day, 24/7 fan experience, Learfield enables schools and brands to connect with fans through licensed merchandise, game ticketing, donor identification for athletic programs, exclusive custom content, innovative marketing initiatives, student-athlete marketing initiatives , and advanced digital platforms. Since 2008, it has served as title sponsor for the acclaimed Learfield Directors’ Cup, supporting athletic departments across all divisions About Mizzou AthleticsMizzou Athletics supports 450 student-athletes across 20 varsity programs while competing at the highest level of intercollegiate athletics in the Southeastern Conference. Guided by its core values — Earn Trust & Respect, Live Our Will to Win, Dare to Demand Excellence and Believe Every Step Matters — Mizzou is committed to developing championship-level programs, creating transformative student-athlete experiences and uniting the state of Missouri through competitive excellence.COLUMBIA, Mo. – Mizzou Athletics and Learfield today announced St. Louis-based World Wide Technology (WWT) as the new jersey patch partner of Mizzou Basketball. This expands upon WWT’s existing innovative relationship with Mizzou as the University’s Official Technology Solutions Partner of Athletics. As part of the partnership , the WWT brand mark will be featured on the uniforms of both men’s and women’s Tiger basketball programs beginning this fall. WWT’s logo will also appear on Norm Stewart Court at Mizzou Arena as part of the university’s expanded partnership with the St. "We are proud to welcome World Wide Technology as a partner of Mizzou Athletics and Mizzou Basketball," said Laird Veatch, Mizzou Director of Athletics. "WWT’s founder and chairman David Steward, its co-founder and CEO Jim Kavanaugh and their team have built an extraordinary company with a global reach and deep Missouri roots. When you have the opportunity to partner with a brand of WWT’s caliber, you put them at the top of your draft board. WWT's investment in our basketball programs demonstrates a strong belief in Mizzou and our commitment to competing for championships. We’re excited to continue to build this partnership with an organization that shares our pride in Missouri and our ambition to demand excellence."

extraction.body: The top reason analytics agents produce substandard insights is a lack of business context, prompting investment in semantic layers and governance, rather than bigger models. In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired. Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed. Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business. Some key findings from the report include the following: Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses. Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights. Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.

Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.

Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.
Some key findings from the report include the following:

Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.

Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.

Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.

Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.

Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.

extraction.body: AI analytics agents are generating recommendations faster than organizations can evaluate them. New global research, based on a survey of 400 data and technology executives, explores what separates the organizations getting real business value from agentic analytics from the rest. 48% of agent-generated insights lead to actions that improve the business — up from 37% a year ago, but still leaving more than half unused or not helpful. 55% of executives cite lack of business context as the primary reason agent insights fall short. 60% say orchestrating teams of AI agents will be a primary analyst role within two years. Agentic analytics has made real progress, but performance varies sharply depending on the type of insight. When it comes to describing what happened, agents perform well: 83% of respondents rate their descriptive insights as good or excellent. For prescriptive insights — recommendations on what to do next — only 45% say the same. A small group of organizations, 7% of those surveyed, report that 77% of their agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. What sets them apart isn't a matter of technology. When analytics agents deliver substandard insights, the most common explanation is straightforward: They lack sufficient understanding of the business. “When agents don't have enough understanding of the business needs, requirements and priorities, they struggle to determine the true value of the insights they generate." The research examines how eight industries compare on agent performance. Technology, financial services and retail organizations outperform others in key dimensions — including the share of insights that lead to business improvement. Even when insight quality improves, organizations face a second challenge: determining which insights to trust and act on. Only 24% can evaluate all the insights their agents generate. Most decide on a case-by-case basis, prioritizing by risk or reviewing only when resources allow. That's beginning to change. Two years from now, 53% of executives expect automated evaluation by AI agents to be their primary method — up from 29% today. “Many organizations still rely on expert review and anecdotal testing because evaluating insights' quality is fundamentally harder than evaluating traditional software. The challenge is not just determining whether an answer is correct, but whether it is trustworthy, contextual and valuable." Two years ago, the primary analyst activities were documenting requirements and mapping processes. Today, analysts spend more of their time interpreting AI-generated insights, validating agent outputs and feeding corrections back into the system to improve accuracy over time. The role is shifting from producing analysis to governing, directing and refining it. “Prescriptive insights are hard, because they require a translation step: from 'what will happen' to 'what we should do about it.' This requires the agent to incorporate business constraints, risk preferences and decision authority that are frequently undocumented and contextually variable." In addition to the survey, in-depth interviews with senior technology executives offer firsthand insights into how organizations are striving to improve the quality of AI agent insights. passages: Snap has reached a settlement in a lawsuit brought by two teenagers who accused the company of designing its platform to be addictive and contributing to their depression, anxiety, and eating disorders, as first reported by Reuters .
The plaintiffs had previously reached settlements with Meta, TikTok, and YouTube.

Social media giants are facing thousands of lawsuits in federal and state courts over claims that they knowingly designed their platforms to hook young users and fuel a youth mental health crisis involving anxiety, depression, and suicide.

“The Parties are pleased to have been able to resolve this matter in an amicable manner,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement to TechCrunch. “We’ve built safeguards, launched safety tutorials, and partnered with experts and because safety is never finished, we remain committed to continually strengthening the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community.”
The company had already settled its other cases scheduled for trial.
Snap CEO Evan Spiegel was expected to take the stand.

extraction.body: Results from the 2026 Nebraska Rural Poll show that the number of Nebraskans who have used generative AI tools has more than doubled in just the past two years, from 27% in 2024 to 55% this year. Heather Akin, associate professor of strategic communication at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, said this increase is in line with national trends. “We’re seeing just a rapid uptake of those tools over the last year or so, I think in general across the country,” she said. A 2025 survey from YouGov found that 56% of American adults use AI tools. Akin said the poll findings were likely a “conservative estimate” of AI use in rural Nebraska because the average age of respondents was about 51. Among respondents ages 50-64, 51% indicated that they had ever used AI tools. That’s compared to about 75% of respondents aged 19-39. Akin also said that some respondents may have unknowingly used AI, leading them to respond inaccurately. She pointed to the Google Gemini “AI Overview” results that accompany every Google search as an example. “I’m not sure whether people always know that they’re using generative AI in their searches, but in fact it’s running in the background,” she said. The poll found that women were more likely than men to use AI chatbots, although the report did not indicate how large the AI usage gap between men and women was. Akin said that while she can only speculate as to why women are more likely to use chatbots than men, a June 2026 study from Pew Research Center found the nationwide “gender gap” in chatbot use closed between 2024 and 2026. Forty-seven percent of women reported having ever used chatbots in 2026, up from 28% in 2024. Meanwhile, men’s chatbot use increased less sharply, from 39% in 2024 to 50% in 2026. Akin said the closing gender gap could explain why more women than men use chatbots in rural Nebraska. Akin said AI tools can help people find information in areas where access to medical and legal advice is limited. However, she said this can become harmful when chatbots give out inaccurate information. A little more than one-third of poll respondents said they were somewhat or extremely interested in learning how to evaluate response accuracy from generative AI. “Of course, we want to be really cautious and conscious of the accuracy of the information that people get,” Akin said. The poll results indicated that rural Nebraskans' biggest concern about AI is privacy, with 45% of respondents saying they were somewhat or extremely interested in learning how to protect their privacy when using AI. “We’re hearing a lot of very valid concerns about it,” Akin said. “I think we’re going to hit a point where, as a society, we kind of have to negotiate how much we’re willing to accept this technology being used.” Nebraska Extension and Rural Prosperity Nebraska mailed questionnaires to nearly 6,900 Nebraska households in April and May 2026. The poll captured 881 responses from 86 of Nebraska’s 93 counties. Cass, Douglas, Lancaster, Sarpy, Saunders, Seward and Washington counties were not surveyed. Heather Akin, associate professor of strategic communication at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, said this increase is in line with national trends. “We’re seeing just a rapid uptake of those tools over the last year or so, I think in general across the country,” she said. A 2025 survey from YouGov found that 56% of American adults use AI tools. Akin said the poll findings were likely a “conservative estimate” of AI use in rural Nebraska because the average age of respondents was about 51. Among respondents ages 50-64, 51% indicated that they had ever used AI tools. That’s compared to about 75% of respondents aged 19-39. Akin also said that some respondents may have unknowingly used AI, leading them to respond inaccurately. She pointed to the Google Gemini “AI Overview” results that accompany every Google search as an example. “I’m not sure whether people always know that they’re using generative AI in their searches, but in fact it’s running in the background,” she said. The poll found that women were more likely than men to use AI chatbots, although the report did not indicate how large the AI usage gap between men and women was. Akin said that while she can only speculate as to why women are more likely to use chatbots than men, a June 2026 study from Pew Research Center found the nationwide “gender gap” in chatbot use closed between 2024 and 2026. Forty-seven percent of women reported having ever used chatbots in 2026, up from 28% in 2024. Meanwhile, men’s chatbot use increased less sharply, from 39% in 2024 to 50% in 2026. Akin said the closing gender gap could explain why more women than men use chatbots in rural Nebraska. Akin said AI tools can help people find information in areas where access to medical and legal advice is limited. However, she said this can become harmful when chatbots give out inaccurate information. sources.title: Jets' Aaron Glenn not fretting job security - AOL.com
passages: Aaron Glenn lost for the 20th time in 25 games as head coach of the Jets on Sunday, but the former NFL defensive back has no time to fret his future in New York.
According to the embattled coach, there is no fire sale coming before the trade deadline.
The Jets hired Glenn to get the team back to the playoffs, but a stretch of losing seasons could run to 11 in a row.
"There's so much that I think about when it comes to us improving each week that it really doesn't come across my mind, to be honest with you," Glenn said on a media video call Monday.

"There's so much that I think about when it comes to us improving each week that it really doesn't come across my mind, to be honest with you," Glenn said on a media video call Monday. "I understand how this league is. I understand what this business is about, but my first job is each week improving this team. And that's the only thing that I think about." The Jets hired Glenn to get the team back to the playoffs, but a stretch of losing seasons could run to 11 in a row. The Jets (2-6) have lost three consecutive games and now hit the road for a game against the Kansas City Chiefs (5-2) before returning home to face the Buffalo Bills (6-1). The Jets are finding ways to lose close games. Their six losses this season are by a total of 36 points, all but one of them a one-score game. According to the embattled coach, there is no fire sale coming before the trade deadline. With a treasure trove of draft picks from marquee trades for defensive lineman Quinnen Williams and cornerback Sauce Gardner at the trade deadline last year, he believes the Jets will be "in the business of keeping good players," adding running back Breece Hall "will still be here" next week. Glenn said the run of defeats underscores the need for a change in "mindset" or losses will continue piling up. "I mean, that's what this is," Glenn said. "It's a bottom-line business and we have to win, but we still have nine games left. So we still have an opportunity to win nine games."

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. The largest crypto hack on record hit Binance last week. Bitcoin's (BTC) charts, however, show little sign of a broken bull market. Three signals point that way, from the weekly close to monthly momentum. One group of investors still has reason for caution before the US midterm elections. The Binance hack on October 29 drained about $6.3 billion from 10 blockchains. Binance pledged to cover all losses and began phased withdrawals on November 1. Even so, Bitcoin closed the week down only 2.9%, according to on-chain analyst Willy Woo. Gold fell 3% over the same stretch, per Woo's figures. Woo contrasted this with the FTX collapse, which knocked Bitcoin down 25% in the 2022 bear market. A drop of that size failed to repeat here. Ash Crypto also argues that a 20% drop is normal during a Bitcoin bull market. The hack-week loss stayed far below that threshold. Bitcoin's longer-term chart points in the same direction. Bitcoin posted its 7th straight weekly close above the 50-week moving average (MA), Ash Crypto noted. The streak began in September, when Bitcoin reclaimed the average for the first time in 45 weeks. Alex Thorn, who heads firmwide research at Galaxy, tied that reclaim to past cycle bottoms at the time. "Regaining the 50w MA has historically served as strong confirmation that bear market lows are 'in,'" he said. At press time, Bitcoin traded at $78,307, up 0.65% over the past 24 hours, per BeInCrypto Markets. That puts it about 3.6% above the 50-week MA, which currently stands near $75,602. A slower monthly gauge offers a third reading. Bitcoin gained about 43% across July, August, and September, Coinglass data show. It then closed October down 7.32%, its first monthly loss since June. That loss still left Bitcoin's monthly momentum above a key line, according to analyst PlanB. His chart shows the 14-month relative strength index (RSI) above 50 for a 3rd straight month. RSI measures momentum on a 0 to 100 scale. Readings above 50 mean gains have outweighed losses over the lookback period. PlanB reads the streak as the start of a new bull market. Still, Bitcoin ETF outflows tell a weaker story than the price chart. US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $643.33 million on October 30, the first full session after the hack. That outflow erased four days of inflows and left the week about $202 million negative. Glassnode data place the average cost basis of US spot ETF holders near $82,308. Bitcoin sits about 4.9% below that line, leaving the average ETF buyer at a loss. Bitcoin also remains 10.4% below its January 1 level, per Coinglass. Those levels frame the next test, which arrives with the midterm vote. US voters head to the polls on November 3. Bitcoin has closed November higher in 10 of 16 years, with a median gain of 10.3%, Coinglass data show. Midterm years split evenly, however, with two November gains and two losses. The losses came in 2018 and 2022, when Bitcoin fell 36.41% and 16.23%. Both were bear market years. A weekly close above the 50-week MA after the vote may separate 2026 from those two years. A move back above $82,308 would put the average ETF holder back in profit. Ash Crypto's monthly analysis marks $87,500 as resistance. The largest crypto hack on record hit Binance last week. Bitcoin's (BTC) charts, however, show little sign of a broken bull market.
Three signals point that way, from the weekly close to monthly momentum. One group of investors still has reason for caution before the US midterm elections.
The Binance hack on October 29 drained about $6.3 billion from 10 blockchains. Binance pledged to cover all losses and began phased withdrawals on November 1.
Even so, Bitcoin closed the week down only 2.9%, according to on-chain analyst Willy Woo. Gold fell 3% over the same stretch, per Woo's figures.
Woo contrasted this with the FTX collapse, which knocked Bitcoin down 25% in the 2022 bear market. A drop of that size failed to repeat here.
Ash Crypto also argues that a 20% drop is normal during a Bitcoin bull market. The hack-week loss stayed far below that threshold.
Bitcoin's longer-term chart points in the same direction.
Bitcoin posted its 7th straight weekly close above the 50-week moving average (MA), Ash Crypto noted.

The streak began in September, when Bitcoin reclaimed the average for the first time in 45 weeks. Alex Thorn, who heads firmwide research at Galaxy, tied that reclaim to past cycle bottoms at the time.
"Regaining the 50w MA has historically served as strong confirmation that bear market lows are 'in,'" he said.
At press time, Bitcoin traded at $78,307, up 0.65% over the past 24 hours, per BeInCrypto Markets. That puts it about 3.6% above the 50-week MA, which currently stands near $75,602.
A slower monthly gauge offers a third reading.
Bitcoin gained about 43% across July, August, and September, Coinglass data show. It then closed October down 7.32%, its first monthly loss since June.
That loss still left Bitcoin's monthly momentum above a key line, according to analyst PlanB. His chart shows the 14-month relative strength index (RSI) above 50 for a 3rd straight month.
RSI measures momentum on a 0 to 100 scale. Readings above 50 mean gains have outweighed losses over the lookback period. PlanB reads the streak as the start of a new bull market.
Still, Bitcoin ETF outflows tell a weaker story than the price chart.
US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $643.33 million on October 30, the first full session after the hack. That outflow erased four days of inflows and left the week about $202 million negative.
Glassnode data place the average cost basis of US spot ETF holders near $82,308. Bitcoin sits about 4.9% below that line, leaving the average ETF buyer at a loss.
Bitcoin also remains 10.4% below its January 1 level, per Coinglass. Those levels frame the next test, which arrives with the midterm vote.
US voters head to the polls on November 3. Bitcoin has closed November higher in 10 of 16 years, with a median gain of 10.3%, Coinglass data show.
Midterm years split evenly, however, with two November gains and two losses. The losses came in 2018 and 2022, when Bitcoin fell 36.41% and 16.23%. Both were bear market years.

A weekly close above the 50-week MA after the vote may separate 2026 from those two years. A move back above $82,308 would put the average ETF holder back in profit. Ash Crypto's monthly analysis marks $87,500 as resistance.

Google Cloud takes the cake as the fastest-growing, delivering 103% revenue growth during Q3. That helped boost Alphabet's overall growth rate to 25%, but the market didn't care. Instead, the market sold the stock off by over 10% the day following earnings. That's short-sighted thinking by the market, as the huge investments that Alphabet is making in cloud computing will provide strong and steady cash flows for years, if not decades.

The same goes for AWS. While it didn't grow as fast as Google Cloud, it still grew at a 39% year-over-year pace. The bigger deal with Amazon is that AWS makes up 63% of Amazon's operating profits. So, as AWS grows quicker, so do Amazon's operating profits as a whole. This will cause Amazon's earnings to grow faster than revenue, which is an excellent setup for long-term outperformance of the market. However, because the market is focused on short-term profitability, it sold Amazon's stock off following earnings.
Buying opportunities rarely come around for these two, and investors should take advantage of the market's short-sightedness and buy them in November .

Nvidia may be an even bigger buying opportunity than Amazon and Alphabet. Nvidia has been vocal about how strong long-term demand is for its GPUs, yet the market is pricing none of that in. During its Q2 earnings report, it told investors to expect 70% revenue growth in 2027. If you've followed Nvidia for any period of time, you know that it consistently underprojects and overperforms, which is a good thing. So the 70% growth call for 2027 is likely an underestimation. Still, the market hasn't priced any of that into its stock.

Nvidia trades for just 26 times trailing earnings, which is an average price to pay for a big tech stock. However, Nvidia's growth is anything but average. If you utilize next year's earnings projections to value the stock, Nvidia trades for just 13 times next year's earnings. So, if it hits analyst expectations and returns to its current 26 times earnings level, the stock would have to double.
That's a pretty promising rate of return in just a bit over a year, and makes Nvidia a top stock to buy in November.

sources.title: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked - BBC
passages: Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users.
Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions".
A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered.
Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks.
Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate.
A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".

Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last."

Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock".
"After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian."
Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Calls are being made for the defence of the Shetland Isles to be strengthened after increased sightings of Russian trawlers off the coast of Scotland.
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".

Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.

While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Nobody was hurt, officials said. There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue. Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burnt-out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported. Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated in other occupied cities in the Kherson region. Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left. Lubinets paid tribute to the US first lady and said he had been in daily contact with her via her aide Marc Beckman. He said he hoped to bring back some of the “thousands of people” who had disappeared, as well as prisoners of war and bodies retrieved last week from Oleshky’s morgue. There were millions of Ukrainian citizens living in occupied territory, he said. Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same. Meanwhile, officials in the western region of Vinnytsia said two civilians had been killed in a drone strike next to an education facility. The app reported a high possibility of nuclear radiation late on Sunday. It also wrongly warned of a chemical threat to the Ukrainian capital and street-to-street fighting. The messages were written in English with spelling mistakes, as well as in Ukrainian. Many residents ignored the alerts, which began shortly before 11pm local time, assuming that the app had been compromised. Others were scared. “I was briefly terrified,” one woman, Nina, said. “I lay on my bed and wondered what was coming.” A message written in Russian also claimed Ukraine was about to be hit by Oreshnik missiles, which can carry nuclear warheads. The Kremlin has used the ballistic weapon three times before, hitting the Kyiv region and the cities of Dnipro and Lviv. In a post on Sunday, the Ukrainian emergency app said “unauthorised parties” had interfered with its operation. The channel had been temporarily suspended, it said, warning users not to click on links in “suspicious notifications”. It was unclear on Monday who might have carried out the cyber-raid, or why. Russian officials claimed hackers had also sent fake emergency alerts there after gaining access to the app of the ministry for emergencies, based in Moscow. One of their posts mentioned the hacking group Hitcore. Mash, a Russian Telegram channel with links to the security services, said it had spoken to representatives of Hitcore and that they had claimed responsibility for the attack. The report could not be verified. The fake nuclear threats to Ukraine came as Russia resumed its attacks on the southern city of Kherson, hours after the end of a ceasefire during which hundreds of people were evacuated from the nearby Kremlin-controlled town of Oleshky. Kherson’s military administration said a Russian drone hit a hospital at 7.40am. Video footage showed wrecked rooms, with windows blown out, doors broken, and debris on the street. Nobody was hurt, officials said. There is evidence that the Russian army used the six-day ceasefire, which the White House said was brokered by the first lady, Melania Trump, to strengthen its positions in Oleskhy and to rotate in new troops. Bodies of dead civilians were also removed from a hospital morgue. Footage shared with Sky News showed Russian soldiers deploying heavy military equipment and delivering ammunition. They carried large bags into burnt-out houses and buildings and disappeared into basements, the broadcaster reported. Armoured vehicles were spotted moving around Oleshky’s streets. The occupied city is 3 miles from Kherson, on the opposite bank of the Dnipro River. Before last week’s truce, resupply was difficult because of the threat from Ukrainian kamikaze drones. According to the commander of Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade, Dmitry Pulinets, Russian soldiers were previously unable to drive in the city, “neither during the day, nor at night, nor in bad weather”. “Now they have this opportunity. And for the last few days this movement has been happening constantly,” he told Sky News. The ceasefire expired at 11pm on Sunday. Both sides hailed the local pause in the fighting – the most significant since 2022 – as a success. Ukraine’s ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who visited Oleshky to coordinate the mission, said it could be repeated in other occupied cities in the Kherson region. He declined to say how many Oleskhy residents had chosen to go to Ukraine and how many to Russia, citing an agreement with Moscow to keep the figure secret. Ukrainian media have reported that most of the evacuation buses headed to Ukraine through Crimea, from where a plane took them to Gomel, a city in Belarus. Melania Trump said in a post that more than 750 people had left. Lubinets paid tribute to the US first lady and said he had been in daily contact with her via her aide Marc Beckman. He said he hoped to bring back some of the “thousands of people” who had disappeared, as well as prisoners of war and bodies retrieved last week from Oleshky’s morgue. There were millions of Ukrainian citizens living in occupied territory, he said. Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov, however, said on Monday that there were no immediate plans for another truce elsewhere. He said it was standard practice for army units to regroup in such circumstances and that he assumed Ukraine’s armed forces had done the same. Meanwhile, officials in the western region of Vinnytsia said two civilians had been killed in a drone strike next to an education facility. The victims were a 13-year-old girl, who died at the scene from her injuries, and a woman, who died later in hospital. Several other children were wounded, the officials said.

sources.title: Hackers hit Ukraine, Russia's emergency apps, send fake nuclear, chemical attack alerts
passages: Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert apps had been hacked overnight, sending false warnings to citizens about impending air raids and chemical and nuclear attacks.The warnings coincided with the expiry of a six-day local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in a small area of southern Ukraine - the longest such pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.Ukraine's public air raid app started to send false alerts just before 11 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Sunday for the capital Kyiv and other areas, warning of radiation and chemical attacks and also the risk of street combat in some areas.Hours later, Russian state news agency TASS quoted the Emergencies Ministry in Moscow as saying that its own mobile app had also been hit by a cyberattack that resulted in fake public warnings being transmitted.Reuters was unable to verify which groups were responsible.

Experts have linked previous cyber security incidents during the almost five-year-old war to activist hackers as well as intelligence agencies on both sides.In Ukraine, one of the alarms said Russia had launched a hypersonic Oreshnik missile - which is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead - and that a nuclear alert had been declared.Ukraine's air force said shortly after on the Telegram messaging app that the alert system appeared to have been hacked by Russia, noting that the alerts were broadcast in Russian.

The US on Friday announced a $2.1 billion deal to supply 500 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, but two people briefed on the decision said it could take years for the missiles to arrive.On the streets of Kyiv, residents played down the impact of the hack.Artem Pyndyk, 37, a businessman, said he was briefly surprised to see the messages but then realized what had happened."This didn't trigger the kind of reaction in society that they expected," said Pyndyk, adding that family members and friends he had checked in with had also not panicked."You can laugh about it but, on the other hand, they gained a certain level of access and were able to hack the program."Oksana Vostrykova, 48, also shrugged off the incident."I am calm about it, I kind of immediately understood that it might be a false message," the pizzeria employee said.

sources.title: Hackers hit Ukraine, Russia's emergency apps, send fake nuclear, chemical attack alerts
passages: Ukraine and Russia said their emergency alert apps had been hacked overnight, sending false warnings to citizens about impending air raids and chemical and nuclear attacks.The warnings coincided with the expiry of a six-day local ceasefire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump in a small area of southern Ukraine - the longest such pause in fighting since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.Ukraine's public air raid app started to send false alerts just before 11 p.m. (2100 GMT) on Sunday for the capital Kyiv and other areas, warning of radiation and chemical attacks and also the risk of street combat in some areas.Hours later, Russian state news agency TASS quoted the Emergencies Ministry in Moscow as saying that its own mobile app had also been hit by a cyberattack that resulted in fake public warnings being transmitted.Reuters was unable to verify which groups were responsible.

Experts have linked previous cyber security incidents during the almost five-year-old war to activist hackers as well as intelligence agencies on both sides.In Ukraine, one of the alarms said Russia had launched a hypersonic Oreshnik missile - which is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead - and that a nuclear alert had been declared.Ukraine's air force said shortly after on the Telegram messaging app that the alert system appeared to have been hacked by Russia, noting that the alerts were broadcast in Russian.

The US on Friday announced a $2.1 billion deal to supply 500 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, but two people briefed on the decision said it could take years for the missiles to arrive.On the streets of Kyiv, residents played down the impact of the hack.Artem Pyndyk, 37, a businessman, said he was briefly surprised to see the messages but then realized what had happened."This didn't trigger the kind of reaction in society that they expected," said Pyndyk, adding that family members and friends he had checked in with had also not panicked."You can laugh about it but, on the other hand, they gained a certain level of access and were able to hack the program."Oksana Vostrykova, 48, also shrugged off the incident."I am calm about it, I kind of immediately understood that it might be a false message," the pizzeria employee said.

extraction.body: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save * Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. * If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off). * Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it.

extraction.body: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is the company’s most capable smartwatch. Of note, those include Sound Recognition, which alerts you to noises like alarms and doorbells, and the Live Rewind feature that lets you revisit the last 15 seconds of an in-person conversation. This model has broader health and fitness capabilities than previous models, too. Its sensors promise more accurate EKG measurements, while the watch can track your heart rate as often as every five seconds. The new Readiness feature (not available on the Ultra 3 and earlier models) also analyzes your recent activity, sleep quality, and other health metrics to generate a score from zero to 10, helping you determine whether to push yourself or take it easy. On the hardware front, battery life is perhaps the biggest highlight, with Apple promising up to 50 hours on a charge — twice as long as the Series 12. Like its predecessor, this model features Apple’s brightest watch display and a rugged design that’s water-resistant up to 100 meters and IP6X-rated for dust resistance. It also retains conveniences like the second-generation Ultra Wideband chip for Precision Finding, and helpful gesture controls so you can you can perform actions with a double tap or flick of your wrist. Read our hands-on impressions of the Apple Watch Ultra 4. Three more ways to save * Ugreen’s FineTrack2 Bluetooth tracker is on sale for $13.99 at Amazon, just a few cents shy of its best price to date. The soccer ball-shaped tracker stands out with its playful design, but it also offers some useful features including a non-rechargeable battery can last up to seven years. It works with Apple’s expansive Find My network to help you locate misplaced belongings, while its lanyard makes it easy to attach to your keys, bag, or other items. * If you’re looking to spruce up your Apple Watch Ultra or Series smartwatch, a variety of Apple’s official bands are on sale for up to 69 percent off at Woot. The silicone Sport Band is down to $14.99 ($35 off), while the soft, breathable Sport Loop is available for $19.99 ($29 off). You can also grab the rugged Trail Loop for $34.99 ($64 off). * Hoto’s new Pulse 4-in-1 Cordless Staple Gun is on sale for $69.99 ($10 off) at Amazon. It works with four types of staples and nails, letting you switch between them depending on the task, while offering two firing modes. It also features a built-in display that shows battery life and alerts you when you can safely fire the stapler and when it’s time to reload it.

sources.title: Ford promises not to sell your driving habits to data brokers
passages: “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay.

It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share.
They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.
Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers.

extraction.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share.

extraction.body: Just days after General Motors agreed to settle a lawsuit over selling customers' data without their consent, Ford announced a new "Privacy Promise" policy . In a statement shared on a new website from the manufacturer, Ford promised owners that they are in the driver's seat when it comes to their data. The site offers guidance on data sharing and collection and how to deactivate and opt out of sharing various types of data, whether on the automaker's webpages, in its app or within the car itself. "We design and build our products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use and storage and even disposal. This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect your privacy," the statement began. "We strive to provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information. This empowers you to navigate your privacy choices with confidence. Once you make those choices, we respect your decision," the statement continued. Calling the move the "right thing to do," Ford shared that its updated vehicle privacy settings will allow users "to control what data you want to share, subject to the features and services you wish to enjoy." extraction.body: When you buy through our links, you’re supporting our mission . Ford CPO Kristin Jones pledges no driving-behavior data sales to brokers, but gaps on insurers and default settings remain General Motors agreed to pay $220 million across 36 states to resolve allegations that it shared driving and location data with data brokers and insurers without adequate consent. Ford’s new “Privacy Promise” arrives in that context. Ford Chief Privacy Officer Kristin Jones framed the initiative as an active commitment to customers, not a legal formality. Jones described the motivation plainly. “I personally think that it’s super important for us to be making it very clear to our customers what our data practices are, and not only that, but making a commitment to them about it,” she told TechCrunch . According to Ford’s announcement, the initiative addresses privacy considerations across the data lifecycle, including collection, use, storage, and disposal. Ford’s connected vehicles can gather a range of information, and that data may be linked to the owner. Ford says it uses that data for connected services such as navigation, traffic updates, and roadside assistance, as well as for maintenance diagnostics , product development, and personalizing features to individual drivers. Ford’s most direct commitment targets the conduct that drew regulatory action against GM. “We also do not share information about how our customers are driving their vehicles to data brokers,” Jones told TechCrunch. Ford’s announcement states that the company does not sell driving-behavior data to data brokers, though the materials do not address every form of third-party data sharing. Ford says both the vehicle itself and the Ford app give drivers a path to adjust what they share. Ford says customers can adjust data-sharing preferences through the vehicle’s center display or the Ford app. The control mechanism exists; what matters is what happens when a driver uses it. Choosing privacy over connectivity comes with concrete feature losses, according to Ford’s own materials. Choosing not to share connected-vehicle data with Ford limits connected features. Real-time navigation, built-in roadside assistance, BlueCruise hands-free driving assistance, internet connectivity, and location functions within the Ford app may all be affected, depending on the vehicle and selected settings, according to Ford’s materials. Ford’s announcement is clear about what it prohibits but leaves several practical questions unresolved. The cited Ford announcement does not clarify whether connected-vehicle data is shared with insurers, advertisers, analytics contractors, or dealers . The available materials reviewed for this article do not specify which data uses require affirmative opt-in consent versus which are active by default. The announcement also does not identify an independent auditing mechanism to verify that the Privacy Promise is honored in practice. Those are open questions, not proven violations. They are, however, the same categories of ambiguity that drew regulatory scrutiny to GM’s data practices. Ford has named the privacy trade-off clearly; fully resolving it will require answers the company has not yet provided. Whether the Privacy Promise constitutes meaningful protection depends on details not yet addressed publicly. Those details include what third-party data sharing covers, which settings are active by default, and how long location and diagnostic data is retained. The trade-off between convenience and data exposure is real for drivers using FordPass, BlueCruise, or built-in navigation. Ford has named that trade-off. It has not yet fully resolved it. extraction.body: Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization. As part of its new promise, Ford says it will strive to protect customer data by using aggregating and anonymizing techniques. It will also “provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information.” And while Ford says it will still use data to improve safety, it will allow customers to adjust how much or how little data they would prefer to share. In making an explicit pledge not to sell customer data to outside firms, Ford is trying to position itself as one of the better actors in an industry rife with shady practices. “We know that trust is earned,” Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer at Ford, writes in a blog post. “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers. The agreement requires GM to limit the driving data it collects and obtain “express consent” from drivers before collecting their information. Other automakers have been caught with their hands in the customer data cookie jar. A recent examination of 21 vehicle brands found that every single one transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. In a recent report, Mozilla crowned modern connected cars “the worst category of products for privacy” ever reviewed. The global nonprofit found that 92 percent of the reviewed automakers provide drivers with little (if any) control over their personal data, with 84 percent sharing user data with outside parties. Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay. If Ford publicly promises something like, “We never sell your driving data to brokers” but breaks that promise, the FTC and state attorneys general can step in. They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines. It should be noted that a company’s blog post or public promise is not a legal contract. Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers. Also, opting out of data sharing does come with tradeoffs. While Ford states that data collection depends on the features you want to use, turning off vehicle tracking or location sharing often disables key features like built-in navigation, remote start, and wireless software updates.

extraction.body: Just days after General Motors agreed to settle a lawsuit over selling customers' data without their consent, Ford announced a new "Privacy Promise" policy . In a statement shared on a new website from the manufacturer, Ford promised owners that they are in the driver's seat when it comes to their data. The site offers guidance on data sharing and collection and how to deactivate and opt out of sharing various types of data, whether on the automaker's webpages, in its app or within the car itself. "We design and build our products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use and storage and even disposal. This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect your privacy," the statement began. "We strive to provide clear and easy-to-understand information about how we use your personal information. This empowers you to navigate your privacy choices with confidence. Once you make those choices, we respect your decision," the statement continued. Calling the move the "right thing to do," Ford shared that its updated vehicle privacy settings will allow users "to control what data you want to share, subject to the features and services you wish to enjoy." "We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers," Ford maintained, a sticking point following General Motors' lawsuit , which saw the Ford rival agree to pay $200 million in a settlement with 36 states following the incident, after it illegally sold drivers' personal information to third parties without their consent, per a Washington State release regarding the suit. As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share. "A value our survey respondents kept returning to was control: the ability to adjust their settings on demand and in detail," Ford added. But, as automotive outlet The Drive notes, there is no one place to turn everything off, forcing Ford owners to do lots of reading and searching to fully opt out of data sharing and customize their Ford experience. While some found the timing of Ford's new website launch uncoincidental amid its longtime feud with GM, in a statement to TechCrunch , Ford's chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said she wouldn't be commenting "on what our competitors are doing, or anything that's sort of been in the news." She did say, however, that as more and more consumers grow wary of whether companies will "take care with their data," Ford wants to make sure it's "building that trust relationship with them." Ford CPO Kristin Jones pledges no driving-behavior data sales to brokers, but gaps on insurers and default settings remain General Motors agreed to pay $220 million across 36 states to resolve allegations that it shared driving and location data with data brokers and insurers without adequate consent. Ford’s new “Privacy Promise” arrives in that context. Ford Chief Privacy Officer Kristin Jones framed the initiative as an active commitment to customers, not a legal formality. Jones described the motivation plainly. “I personally think that it’s super important for us to be making it very clear to our customers what our data practices are, and not only that, but making a commitment to them about it,” she told TechCrunch . According to Ford’s announcement, the initiative addresses privacy considerations across the data lifecycle, including collection, use, storage, and disposal. Ford’s connected vehicles can gather a range of information, and that data may be linked to the owner. Ford says it uses that data for connected services such as navigation, traffic updates, and roadside assistance, as well as for maintenance diagnostics , product development, and personalizing features to individual drivers. Ford’s most direct commitment targets the conduct that drew regulatory action against GM. “We also do not share information about how our customers are driving their vehicles to data brokers,” Jones told TechCrunch. Ford’s announcement states that the company does not sell driving-behavior data to data brokers, though the materials do not address every form of third-party data sharing. Ford says both the vehicle itself and the Ford app give drivers a path to adjust what they share. Ford says customers can adjust data-sharing preferences through the vehicle’s center display or the Ford app. The control mechanism exists; what matters is what happens when a driver uses it. Choosing privacy over connectivity comes with concrete feature losses, according to Ford’s own materials. Choosing not to share connected-vehicle data with Ford limits connected features. Real-time navigation, built-in roadside assistance, BlueCruise hands-free driving assistance, internet connectivity, and location functions within the Ford app may all be affected, depending on the vehicle and selected settings, according to Ford’s materials. Ford’s announcement is clear about what it prohibits but leaves several practical questions unresolved. The cited Ford announcement does not clarify whether connected-vehicle data is shared with insurers, advertisers, analytics contractors, or dealers . The available materials reviewed for this article do not specify which data uses require affirmative opt-in consent versus which are active by default. The announcement also does not identify an independent auditing mechanism to verify that the Privacy Promise is honored in practice. Those are open questions, not proven violations. They are, however, the same categories of ambiguity that drew regulatory scrutiny to GM’s data practices. Ford has named the privacy trade-off clearly; fully resolving it will require answers the company has not yet provided. Whether the Privacy Promise constitutes meaningful protection depends on details not yet addressed publicly. Those details include what third-party data sharing covers, which settings are active by default, and how long location and diagnostic data is retained. The trade-off between convenience and data exposure is real for drivers using FordPass, BlueCruise, or built-in navigation. Ford has named that trade-off. It has not yet fully resolved it. facts.text: “Protecting your personal information is one way we intend to earn it every day.” "“We know that trust is earned.”" - Kristin Jones, Ford’s chief privacy officer The promise comes in the wake of General Motors agreeing to pay $220 million to settle claims that it illegally sold driver and location information to data brokers.

Ford vowed to never sell customer driving data to third-party data brokers as part of a new privacy promise aimed at setting the automaker apart from competitors that have faced legal and regulatory blowback for sharing telematics with data brokers without authorization.

Over half contacted domains that specialize in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA), like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, which gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads.

Ford said it surveyed over 1,000 US customers, both Ford and non-Ford owners, who agreed that privacy is a top concern while over half of the respondents said they understand that some data sharing is okay.
They can sue Ford, force the company to sign legally binding agreements to correct the issue, and impose substantial financial fines.
Those legal agreements contain standard exceptions that allow Ford to share your data, such as complying with police requests or working with outside service providers.
This story Ford Promises Not to Sell Drivers' Data After General Motors Privacy Scandal first appeared on First for Autos .

"We also never sell data about how you drive your vehicle to data brokers," Ford maintained, a sticking point following General Motors' lawsuit , which saw the Ford rival agree to pay $200 million in a settlement with 36 states following the incident, after it illegally sold drivers' personal information to third parties without their consent, per a Washington State release regarding the suit.

As much as Ford said it acknowledged user privacy, it noted that after surveying just over 1,000 Ford customers, it found customers also "understand the value of data sharing" and want to be the ones making the ultimate decision when it comes to what they want to share.

While some found the timing of Ford's new website launch uncoincidental amid its longtime feud with GM, in a statement to TechCrunch , Ford's chief privacy officer Kristin Jones said she wouldn't be commenting "on what our competitors are doing, or anything that's sort of been in the news."

sources.title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights
passages: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project.

The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information.

The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years.
The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.

extraction.body: Apple robot backed by CEO John Ternus may have hefty price tag and limited uses. Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room. People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display . The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028. The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies. However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households. Is there a market for a smart home device costing more than $1,000 that moves around while hosting FaceTime calls, automatically handling room lights, and occasionally ordering the family cat to get off the dining table? One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years. The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people. Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information. The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI . From a technical and safety standpoint, Apple’s initial focus on a limited-purpose home robot still makes much more sense right now than any attempt to develop a general-purpose autonomous robot that could pose greater risks when operating near humans . The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
