passages: Apple robot backed by CEO John Ternus may have hefty price tag and limited uses.

Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.

People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display . The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.

The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households. Is there a market for a smart home device costing more than $1,000 that moves around while hosting FaceTime calls, automatically handling room lights, and occasionally ordering the family cat to get off the dining table?

One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years. The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.

Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information. The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .

From a technical and safety standpoint, Apple’s initial focus on a limited-purpose home robot still makes much more sense right now than any attempt to develop a general-purpose autonomous robot that could pose greater risks when operating near humans . The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.

sources.title: Apple's Robot Ambitions: $1,000 HomeView Ultra Could Land in 2027 - BigGo Finance
passages: Apple is preparing to enter the home robotics market, with a robotic smart-home device code-named J595 that could carry a price tag of roughly $1,000 or more and reach customers as early as 2027, according to reporting from The Information.

The product, which people familiar with the effort expect to be branded HomeView Ultra, would sit alongside Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display, a device that arrives in users' homes within days.
For Apple investors, the project represents a long-horizon bet on a category the company has never sold into, and one whose revenue would not materialize before the end of the decade.
The timing also matters because Apple has been selective about extending its "Ultra" branding to new products.
Component prices could push the final retail figure above the $1,000 target, and the launch could slip to 2028 if software work falls behind.
Rivals in home automation and consumer robotics would have time to respond, and any delay would leave Apple's smart-home lineup anchored by the HomeView display shipping this month.

Beyond the HomeView Ultra, he is backing a separate effort aimed at machines that can handle household chores such as folding laundry, a project that would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators.
It is unclear whether that work points toward a general-purpose humanoid robot of the kind being developed by startups 1X and Figure AI.

The report describes a core group of only about 10 "true roboticists," with many members of the original engineering team having left over the years, while the software organization counts roughly 300 people.
Apple has not publicly confirmed the project, the name, or the price.
Much of the physical hardware has been ready for about two years, but software remains the bottleneck.

The delay stems from Apple's decision to pursue a more ambitious set of AI-powered capabilities than it originally planned, when the device was conceived mostly as a way to make FaceTime calls more engaging by following a person from room to room.
The project's origins trace back to 2018 prototypes, and former Apple chief executive Tim Cook approved continued work on it.
Equipped with cameras and sensors, the robot is meant to understand its surroundings and act on its own, such as turning on lights when someone walks in or shooing a cat off a table.

The open question is commercial rather than technical: whether buyers will pay four figures for a moving screen whose demonstrated functions overlap with far cheaper smart-home gear and robot vacuums.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project.

The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information.

The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years.
The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.
Apple is reportedly building a home robot that would cost around $1,000 and handle FaceTime calls and light control, and Ars Technica frames the device as a 2027 product.
No name, price, specification or date has come from the company, so everything below rests on press reports as of November 02, 2026.
Where we offer judgment instead of reporting, we say so.
Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.
The takeaway: Apple’s home robot is a credible report with a lot of unknowns.
For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case.
Buyers will compare it against what they already own.
A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot.
The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open.
The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.
The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028.
That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.
Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch.
The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes.

Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room. People who worked on Apple’s robotic projects told The Information that the AI-driven home robot, code-named J595, could be named HomeView Ultra in line with Apple’s new HomeView stationary smart display . The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028. The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project. The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies. However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households. Is there a market for a smart home device costing more than $1,000 that moves around while hosting FaceTime calls, automatically handling room lights, and occasionally ordering the family cat to get off the dining table? One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years. The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people. Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information. The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI . From a technical and safety standpoint, Apple’s initial focus on a limited-purpose home robot still makes much more sense right now than any attempt to develop a general-purpose autonomous robot that could pose greater risks when operating near humans . The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot. relevantPassages.text: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project.

The Information describes Apple’s engineers as trying to give the robot more capabilities beyond being a “fancy way to make FaceTime calls” in order to justify a high price tag, even as the team has spent years refining the software and incorporating more AI technologies.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information.

The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years.
The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.

Apple has not announced it. No name, price, specification or date has come from the company, so everything below rests on press reports as of November 02, 2026.

This analysis separates what is reported from what is confirmed, tests the $1,000 and 2027 claims against Apple’s recent hardware pattern, and looks at where an Apple home robot would sit next to products like the HomeView smart display we covered earlier . Where we offer judgment instead of reporting, we say so.
Add Shattered once in the Google app and our stories show up in your news suggestions.

The headline claim is simple. Apple is working on a home robot, it would sell for roughly $1,000 in the United States, and it is aimed at 2027. Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.

MacRumors published its own piece on November 02 and describes the HomeView Ultra name with a 9-inch screen. That matches the roughly 9-inch display in the other reporting. Nobody in the coverage cites an Apple spokesperson, and we found no on-record quote from Apple or a named Apple representative.

J595 is the internal code name that appears in the reporting. Apple uses alphanumeric identifiers like it for unreleased hardware, and they rarely tell you much about the final marketing name. HomeView Ultra is the product name some reports use, and Apple has not confirmed it.

The name matters because it signals positioning. An Ultra label attached to HomeView would place the robot as the top tier of a home line, not as a separate product family. That reading is our inference. The reports do not say how Apple will brand the device, and Apple could pick something else entirely.

Two use cases dominate the coverage. The first is FaceTime. The second is turning on lights when someone enters a room. Both rely on the same underlying idea, which is that the device carries a camera-and-sensor system and uses it to understand the room around it.

FaceTime is the more natural fit. Apple owns the call experience end to end, and a home screen built for calls plays to that strength. The reports do not describe call features in detail, so how the device would frame or follow a speaker remains outside what any outlet has confirmed.

iThinkDiff reports the HomeView Ultra robot at about $1,000. FourWeekMBA says a tabletop version could cost about the same, citing a report. Ars Technica uses the same round number in its headline framing. Every outlet qualifies it as reported and subject to change.

A four-figure sticker puts the device in an unusual spot. It would cost far more than a typical smart display, and it would land in the price range Apple normally reserves for its top-tier products. Apple has shown it will charge that much when it believes a product is new. It has also shown it will cut features to hit a target price.

Our read is that $1,000 works as a planning anchor, not a promise. Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch. If the price holds, Apple is betting that buyers see the robot as a new category and not a pricey screen. If it climbs, the device narrows to early adopters, which may be exactly the point for a first generation.

The target in the reports is 2027. The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028. That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.

We did not find a stated reason for the possible slip in the verified coverage, so we will not assign one. The pattern in the industry is that sensing, on-device intelligence and reliability testing eat schedules faster than industrial design. That is general context, not a claim about J595 specifically.

For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case. For competitors, the gap is a window. Anyone selling a home robot or a premium display has at least a year to establish habits before Apple shows a finished product.

Apple’s home business has looked like a soft spot. A Yahoo Finance analysis ties the robot plan to the state of Apple’s home segment and asks what it means for AAPL stock. That framing is useful. A robot at this price signals that Apple wants to reset the home category with a flagship, not just refresh the speakers.

The broader industry is also watching robotics shift from lab demos to factory floors. Our look at how Tesla cleared a Model S line for Optimus robots shows how seriously large hardware makers now treat the field. Home robots are a different problem from factory humanoids, but investor attention to both is rising together.

The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes. That suggests the J595 is the product that survived a wider exploration, not Apple’s only idea. It fits the company’s habit of testing many prototypes and shipping few.

A $1,000 device will not move Apple’s revenue on its own. Apple’s scale is large enough that a first-generation home robot is a rounding error against its core lines. Our breakdown of Apple’s first earnings under Ternus shows where the company’s margin pressure actually sits.

The real signal is strategic. Investors read new categories as proof that Apple can find growth beyond the phone. The same logic drove attention to the foldable line, which our analysis of the iPhone Duo growth case covers. A home robot would extend that story into a different part of the house.

Rivals face a different calculation. If Apple legitimizes the premium home robot, competitors gain a category reference point. If it stumbles, the whole segment looks riskier. Either outcome reshapes how smart-home vendors pitch their next generation.

One more thing about the price. At $1,000, an Apple home robot competes with a laptop or a mid-range phone for the same household budget. Buyers will compare it against what they already own. A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot. Apple’s answer, based on the reports, is awareness and hands-free calls, and that case has to feel obvious in a store demo.

Retail strategy will matter as much as hardware. Apple stores let shoppers try a device in a staged room, which suits a product built around reacting to people. A boxed robot on a shelf sells poorly, while a live demo of lights switching on as a visitor walks in sells itself. Expect Apple to lean on that kind of showing if the project reaches launch.

A device that watches a room to decide when to act raises obvious privacy questions. Apple has built a brand on privacy, and it will have to explain where camera data is processed, what is stored, and who can see it. None of the reports address these points, so they remain open.

The bar here is higher than for a phone. A phone camera points where the owner points it. A home device with autonomous awareness can capture guests, children and routines without anyone choosing to record. Buyers and regulators will want clear indicators, easy off switches and plain disclosures.

This is also where the hardware category meets policy. Home cameras have already drawn scrutiny from lawmakers and security researchers, and a $1,000 Apple device would draw more. How Apple answers will shape trust in the whole premium home segment.

Support and repair raise a final question. Our coverage of the foldable line already shows how repair costs shape perception of a new Apple category. A robot with moving or sensing parts would add service complexity, and buyers at this price expect strong support. Apple has not said anything about warranty or service for the device, so that stays an open item.

A device with a camera-and-sensor system and a screen creates a new surface for software. If Apple opens it to third parties, developers could build call, reminder and household-routine experiences for a display that reacts to people. If Apple keeps it closed, the robot stays a showcase for first-party features.

The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open. Apple’s pattern with new hardware is to launch with a tight first-party feature set and widen access later. The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.

For accessory makers and smart-home brands, the question is compatibility. Anyone selling lights, locks or sensors will want to know whether the robot can control their devices. The light-control capability in the reports suggests Apple plans some home-control support, but the scope is unconfirmed. Vendors should watch Apple’s developer documentation for clues, since new hardware often shows up there before it ships.

Also track how the reported price evolves. If outlets converge on a different figure, that is a stronger signal than any single report. And watch whether Apple comments at all, because silence is the default until the company is ready to sell.

passages: Apple is preparing to enter the home robotics market, with a robotic smart-home device code-named J595 that could carry a price tag of roughly $1,000 or more and reach customers as early as 2027, according to reporting from The Information.

The product, which people familiar with the effort expect to be branded HomeView Ultra, would sit alongside Apple's new HomeView stationary smart display, a device that arrives in users' homes within days.
For Apple investors, the project represents a long-horizon bet on a category the company has never sold into, and one whose revenue would not materialize before the end of the decade.
The timing also matters because Apple has been selective about extending its "Ultra" branding to new products.
Component prices could push the final retail figure above the $1,000 target, and the launch could slip to 2028 if software work falls behind.
Rivals in home automation and consumer robotics would have time to respond, and any delay would leave Apple's smart-home lineup anchored by the HomeView display shipping this month.

Beyond the HomeView Ultra, he is backing a separate effort aimed at machines that can handle household chores such as folding laundry, a project that would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators.
It is unclear whether that work points toward a general-purpose humanoid robot of the kind being developed by startups 1X and Figure AI.

The report describes a core group of only about 10 "true roboticists," with many members of the original engineering team having left over the years, while the software organization counts roughly 300 people.
Apple has not publicly confirmed the project, the name, or the price.
Much of the physical hardware has been ready for about two years, but software remains the bottleneck.

The delay stems from Apple's decision to pursue a more ambitious set of AI-powered capabilities than it originally planned, when the device was conceived mostly as a way to make FaceTime calls more engaging by following a person from room to room.
The project's origins trace back to 2018 prototypes, and former Apple chief executive Tim Cook approved continued work on it.
Equipped with cameras and sensors, the robot is meant to understand its surroundings and act on its own, such as turning on lights when someone walks in or shooing a cat off a table.

The open question is commercial rather than technical: whether buyers will pay four figures for a moving screen whose demonstrated functions overlap with far cheaper smart-home gear and robot vacuums.

story.title: Coming in 2027: Apple’s $1,000 home robot for FaceTime and switching on lights

facts.text: Apple’s new CEO, John Ternus, is apparently pushing the tech company’s development of household robots—and the first to debut may be a home robot designed to autonomously roam around while supporting FaceTime calls and switching lights on whenever a person enters the room.
The company is reportedly aiming to launch the robotic product with a possible price tag of $1,000 or more by 2027, although development delays may push that back to 2028.
The earliest prototypes of the home robot first came out in 2018 and received approval from former Apple CEO Tim Cook to continue the project.

However, the robot’s few reported features seem underwhelming so far when compared with existing smart home devices and systems, or even a run-of-the-mill robot vacuum with a clearer use case for households.
Still, Ternus has been backing this home robot as well as a separate Apple project focused on developing robots for household tasks like folding clothes, according to The Information.

The latter would presumably require robotic arms and manipulators, though it’s unclear if that means Apple has ambitions to develop a general-purpose humanoid robot for household use like robotics startups 1X and Figure AI .
The question is whether Apple can find enough customers willing to pay whatever it charges for a limited-purpose home robot.
One of the Information’s sources also described Apple as having a very small team of about 10 “true roboticists,” with many members of the initial engineering team having departed over the years.
The software side boasts a significantly larger team of approximately 300 people.
Apple is reportedly building a home robot that would cost around $1,000 and handle FaceTime calls and light control, and Ars Technica frames the device as a 2027 product.
No name, price, specification or date has come from the company, so everything below rests on press reports as of November 02, 2026.
Where we offer judgment instead of reporting, we say so.
Ars Technica carries that framing, and iThinkDiff and FourWeekMBA both ran price-focused write-ups around the same figure.
The takeaway: Apple’s home robot is a credible report with a lot of unknowns.
For buyers, the practical takeaway is to plan around 2028 and treat 2027 as the optimistic case.
Buyers will compare it against what they already own.
A family that has a tablet on the kitchen counter and a speaker in the living room will ask what the robot does that those two cannot.
The reports do not say which path Apple will take, so we treat both as open.
The Apple Watch and the home speaker line both followed that arc, and a robot at $1,000 would likely start the same way.
The same reports say development could delay the release until 2028.
That is a normal spread for a first-of-its-kind Apple device, and it echoes how other new categories at the company slid when the hardware outran the software.
Component costs, tariffs and the final feature set all move before launch.
The Apple Post, per its headline, reports that Apple has explored other home-robot concepts, including ones that follow users around and fold clothes.
It fits the company’s habit of testing many prototypes and shipping few.
This is also where the hardware category meets policy.
How Apple answers will shape trust in the whole premium home segment.
J595 is the reported internal code name for the home robot project.
Investors read new categories as proof that Apple can find growth beyond the phone.
The same logic drove attention to the foldable line, which our analysis of the iPhone Duo growth case covers.
The name matters because it signals positioning.
For accessory makers and smart-home brands, the question is compatibility.
Anyone selling lights, locks or sensors will want to know whether the robot can control their devices.
The light-control capability in the reports suggests Apple plans some home-control support, but the scope is unconfirmed.

That matches the roughly 9-inch display in the other reporting.

Every outlet qualifies it as reported and subject to change.

passages: Binance customers withdrew $3.6bn (£2.7bn) of assets from the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange as it reopened on Sunday following what is believed to be the largest hack in history.
The attack on Binance has been attributed to TraderTraitor, a North Korean cybercrime group also known as the Lazarus Group, which stole a then-record $1.5bn from crypto exchange Bybit in 2025 .

Funds linked to the Binance hack continue to be laundered, according to Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at Chainalysis, which has been working with the firm and governments to get the stolen money back.
Binance said on X: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 [GMT] on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion."
Sunday's net withdrawals account for just over 2% of the $171bn of assets under its management, said Binance.
The hack hit Binance's global centralised exchange, Binance.com, while its US-facing platform has said it was not affected by the issue.
The company said it has covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach but the remaining amount may take longer to source.
Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users globally.
Binance also said withdrawals of more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum have resumed and that more services will resume in phases once security checks are completed.

Binance said last week that early checks suggest the incident may have started with a compromised laptop that belonged to an engineer, allowing hackers to find a way to make unauthorised transactions.
Binance said it had replaced customers' assets using a combination of sources, including its corporate treasury as well as its futures insurance and emergency reserve funds.

"We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme.

extraction.body: Customers of Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, withdrew approximately $3.6bn in digital assets after the platform resumed operations on Sunday following a cyberattack that affected $6.3bn worth of cryptocurrencies. The withdrawals came after Binance suspended transactions in response to the breach, which has been blamed on North Korea by major organisations, including the US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI). Binance disclosed that it processed $4.649bn in withdrawals and $1.01bn in deposits between 06:00 and 15:30 GMT on November 1, leaving the exchange with a net outflow of approximately $3.64bn. The company announced the figures on X, saying: "Between 06:00 and 15:30 on November 1, we processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits, resulting in a net outflow of approximately $3.64 billion." According to the exchange, withdrawals initially surged following the resumption of services but subsequently slowed, with activity "stabilising as expected". Despite the significant outflow, Binance said the withdrawals represented just over two per cent of the $171bn in assets under its management. The company has also assured customers that it is working to recover from the breach, maintaining that it will bear the full financial consequences of the incident. Binance said it had already replaced approximately 95 per cent of the stolen assets, although recovering the outstanding amount could take additional time. "Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident," the firm said. Last week, the exchange disclosed that it had set aside more than $6.3bn to manage the consequences of the attack. It also confirmed that withdrawals involving more than two dozen major cryptocurrencies, including Bitcoin and Ethereum, had resumed. Other services are expected to return in stages after completing the necessary security checks. Alec Zebrick, senior manager in global services at blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis, which is assisting Binance and government agencies with the recovery effort, said the attackers were actively moving the stolen assets through multiple cryptocurrency wallets. "We continue to see funds being laundered quite actively," he told the BBC's Today Programme. "The attackers are layering these funds across many thousands of addresses, across thousands of deposits," he added. The group was previously linked to the theft of $1.5bn from cryptocurrency exchange Bybit in 2025, then considered a record-breaking cryptocurrency heist. On Saturday, the FBI released a list of cryptocurrency wallet addresses associated with the group, asking industry partners to help prevent the movement of stolen funds by blocking transactions connected to the addresses. ALSO READ: US: All nine on board killed as jet crashes near Trump’s Florida home Binance also called on cryptocurrency issuers to freeze assets believed to be linked to the breach. The exchange's preliminary investigation indicated that the attack may have originated from an engineer's compromised laptop, which hackers allegedly exploited to gain access to unauthorised transactions. The incident affected Binance.com, the company's global centralised exchange. However, Binance's US-facing platform said it was not impacted. Binance was founded in China and has hundreds of millions of registered users worldwide. The platform allows customers to buy, sell and trade cryptocurrencies, which are digital assets that exist electronically rather than in physical form.

sources.title: Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone
passages: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model.
Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products.
Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Notably, the company reported US$57.58 billion (about C$80.5 billion) in iPhone revenue, a 17 per cent jump from the same time last year. For context, this was achieved with a smaller-than-usual phone lineup. Traditionally, Apple has launched the standard and premium versions of its phones in the same September window, but for this year’s iPhone 18 family, it only debuted the 18 Pro and Pro Max , as well as its first-ever foldable, the Duo . The base iPhone 18 has yet to be released, with reports suggesting it will come in early 2027 alongside the lower-cost 18e and Air 2. In other words, Apple still managed to have a record iPhone quarter on the back of its more expensive phones. It’s also important to stress that the Duo, which starts at a whopping $3,000 in Canada, isn’t included in this report since its pre-orders and launch took place in October. Overall, Apple reported US$114.5 billion (about C$160 billion) in revenue, marking a 12 percent increase. The Mac and services businesses grew during Q4, the latter of which actually reaching an all-time high of US$31.57 billion (about C$44.1 billion), although iPad revenue declined 10 per cent year-over-year. Looking ahead to the next quarter, Apple has the aforementioned Duo and a new touchscreen MacBook . It will also be John Ternus’ first full quarter as CEO, as he took over from Apple veteran Tim Cook on Sept. 1 . extraction.body: Apple is rewriting its playbook for the iPhone lineup, and the iPhone 17 is the unexpected beneficiary. With the standard iPhone 18 delayed until spring 2027, the iPhone 17 is set to become the longest-lived standard model in the company’s history. The move comes alongside Apple’s best-ever March quarter revenue, driven by what CEO Tim Cook described as “extraordinary demand” for the iPhone 17 series. For years, Apple has followed a predictable rhythm: new iPhones every September. That rhythm is about to change. According to multiple reports, Apple will launch only the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the much-anticipated iPhone Ultra foldable at its September 2026 event. The standard iPhone 18 will not appear until the following spring. This delay means the iPhone 17, which debuted in September 2025, will remain on sale for roughly 18 months—an unusually long lifecycle for a non-Pro model. Apple has already ramped up production capacity for the iPhone 17, signaling its intention to keep the device in the spotlight through the 2026 holiday season and beyond. The extended production run is expected to allow the phone to participate in major sales events like China’s Double 11 shopping festival later this year. The iPhone 17’s staying power is not just about timing—it is also about hardware. For the first time, a standard iPhone model includes ProMotion technology, giving it a 120Hz variable refresh rate display that matches the Pro lineup. This upgrade addresses one of the most persistent criticisms of Apple’s base models. Apple also eliminated the 128GB entry-level storage tier, starting the iPhone 17 at 256GB. Despite the upgrade, the starting price remains at $876 USD (converted from CNY 5,999 at the reference rate of 0.146). In China, government subsidies of up to $73 USD (CNY 500) can bring the effective price down to about $803 USD. This pricing strategy positions the iPhone 17 as a value-driven option in the premium segment. The strategy is working. According to Counterpoint Research, iPhone sales surged 22% in the first month after the iPhone 17’s launch, even as the overall smartphone market contracted by 2.7%. This growth helped Apple report its best March quarter ever, with total revenue of $111.2 billion—a 17% year-over-year increase. iPhone-specific revenue reached $56.99 billion, slightly above analyst expectations. Tim Cook attributed the results to double-digit growth across every geographic segment and strong demand for the entire iPhone 17 lineup, including the iPhone 17e, which launched during the quarter. Apple also set new March quarter records for operating cash flow (over $28 billion) and earnings per share. Not everything is smooth sailing. Cook warned that memory costs are expected to rise significantly in the coming quarter, driven by an ongoing memory shortage that has already impacted other tech companies. Rising component prices could pressure Apple’s margins, especially as it continues to offer competitive pricing on the iPhone 17. Additionally, Cook is set to step down as CEO later this year, marking the end of an era. His departure adds an element of uncertainty to Apple’s future product and pricing strategies, though the company’s current momentum remains strong. The iPhone 17’s extended lifecycle is a clear sign that Apple is willing to break its own traditions to maximize returns on a winning product. For consumers, it means a well-equipped phone at a stable price—and a longer wait before the next standard model arrives. passages: Apple is rewriting its playbook for the iPhone lineup, and the iPhone 17 is the unexpected beneficiary. With the standard iPhone 18 delayed until spring 2027, the iPhone 17 is set to become the longest-lived standard model in the company’s history. The move comes alongside Apple’s best-ever March quarter revenue, driven by what CEO Tim Cook described as “extraordinary demand” for the iPhone 17 series.

For years, Apple has followed a predictable rhythm: new iPhones every September. That rhythm is about to change. According to multiple reports, Apple will launch only the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the much-anticipated iPhone Ultra foldable at its September 2026 event. The standard iPhone 18 will not appear until the following spring. This delay means the iPhone 17, which debuted in September 2025, will remain on sale for roughly 18 months—an unusually long lifecycle for a non-Pro model.

Apple has already ramped up production capacity for the iPhone 17, signaling its intention to keep the device in the spotlight through the 2026 holiday season and beyond. The extended production run is expected to allow the phone to participate in major sales events like China’s Double 11 shopping festival later this year.

The iPhone 17’s staying power is not just about timing—it is also about hardware. For the first time, a standard iPhone model includes ProMotion technology, giving it a 120Hz variable refresh rate display that matches the Pro lineup. This upgrade addresses one of the most persistent criticisms of Apple’s base models.

Apple also eliminated the 128GB entry-level storage tier, starting the iPhone 17 at 256GB. Despite the upgrade, the starting price remains at $876 USD (converted from CNY 5,999 at the reference rate of 0.146). In China, government subsidies of up to $73 USD (CNY 500) can bring the effective price down to about $803 USD. This pricing strategy positions the iPhone 17 as a value-driven option in the premium segment.

The strategy is working. According to Counterpoint Research, iPhone sales surged 22% in the first month after the iPhone 17’s launch, even as the overall smartphone market contracted by 2.7%. This growth helped Apple report its best March quarter ever, with total revenue of $111.2 billion—a 17% year-over-year increase. iPhone-specific revenue reached $56.99 billion, slightly above analyst expectations.

Tim Cook attributed the results to double-digit growth across every geographic segment and strong demand for the entire iPhone 17 lineup, including the iPhone 17e, which launched during the quarter. Apple also set new March quarter records for operating cash flow (over $28 billion) and earnings per share.

Not everything is smooth sailing. Cook warned that memory costs are expected to rise significantly in the coming quarter, driven by an ongoing memory shortage that has already impacted other tech companies. Rising component prices could pressure Apple’s margins, especially as it continues to offer competitive pricing on the iPhone 17.

Additionally, Cook is set to step down as CEO later this year, marking the end of an era. His departure adds an element of uncertainty to Apple’s future product and pricing strategies, though the company’s current momentum remains strong.

The iPhone 17’s extended lifecycle is a clear sign that Apple is willing to break its own traditions to maximize returns on a winning product. For consumers, it means a well-equipped phone at a stable price—and a longer wait before the next standard model arrives.

coreStoryFacts.text: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model.
Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products.
Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Traditionally, Apple has launched the standard and premium versions of its phones in the same September window, but for this year’s iPhone 18 family, it only debuted the 18 Pro and Pro Max , as well as its first-ever foldable, the Duo .
The base iPhone 18 has yet to be released, with reports suggesting it will come in early 2027 alongside the lower-cost 18e and Air 2.
In other words, Apple still managed to have a record iPhone quarter on the back of its more expensive phones.
Looking ahead to the next quarter, Apple has the aforementioned Duo and a new touchscreen MacBook .
It will also be John Ternus’ first full quarter as CEO, as he took over from Apple veteran Tim Cook on Sept.
Apple just had released its fourth-quarter earnings report, and it was a particularly big one.
Overall, Apple reported US$114.5 billion (about C$160 billion) in revenue, marking a 12 percent increase.

The Mac and services businesses grew during Q4, the latter of which actually reaching an all-time high of US$31.57 billion (about C$44.1 billion), although iPad revenue declined 10 per cent year-over-year. Looking ahead to the next quarter, Apple has the aforementioned Duo and a new touchscreen MacBook . It will also be John Ternus’ first full quarter as CEO, as he took over from Apple veteran Tim Cook on Sept. 1 . With the standard iPhone 18 delayed until spring 2027, the iPhone 17 is set to become the longest-lived standard model in the company’s history. The move comes alongside Apple’s best-ever March quarter revenue, driven by what CEO Tim Cook described as “extraordinary demand” for the iPhone 17 series. For years, Apple has followed a predictable rhythm: new iPhones every September. That rhythm is about to change. According to multiple reports, Apple will launch only the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and the much-anticipated iPhone Ultra foldable at its September 2026 event. The standard iPhone 18 will not appear until the following spring. This delay means the iPhone 17, which debuted in September 2025, will remain on sale for roughly 18 months—an unusually long lifecycle for a non-Pro model. Apple has already ramped up production capacity for the iPhone 17, signaling its intention to keep the device in the spotlight through the 2026 holiday season and beyond. The extended production run is expected to allow the phone to participate in major sales events like China’s Double 11 shopping festival later this year. The iPhone 17’s staying power is not just about timing—it is also about hardware. For the first time, a standard iPhone model includes ProMotion technology, giving it a 120Hz variable refresh rate display that matches the Pro lineup. This upgrade addresses one of the most persistent criticisms of Apple’s base models. Apple also eliminated the 128GB entry-level storage tier, starting the iPhone 17 at 256GB. Despite the upgrade, the starting price remains at $876 USD (converted from CNY 5,999 at the reference rate of 0.146). In China, government subsidies of up to $73 USD (CNY 500) can bring the effective price down to about $803 USD. This pricing strategy positions the iPhone 17 as a value-driven option in the premium segment. The strategy is working. According to Counterpoint Research, iPhone sales surged 22% in the first month after the iPhone 17’s launch, even as the overall smartphone market contracted by 2.7%. This growth helped Apple report its best March quarter ever, with total revenue of $111.2 billion—a 17% year-over-year increase. iPhone-specific revenue reached $56.99 billion, slightly above analyst expectations. Tim Cook attributed the results to double-digit growth across every geographic segment and strong demand for the entire iPhone 17 lineup, including the iPhone 17e, which launched during the quarter. Apple also set new March quarter records for operating cash flow (over $28 billion) and earnings per share. Not everything is smooth sailing. Cook warned that memory costs are expected to rise significantly in the coming quarter, driven by an ongoing memory shortage that has already impacted other tech companies. Rising component prices could pressure Apple’s margins, especially as it continues to offer competitive pricing on the iPhone 17. Additionally, Cook is set to step down as CEO later this year, marking the end of an era. His departure adds an element of uncertainty to Apple’s future product and pricing strategies, though the company’s current momentum remains strong. The iPhone 17’s extended lifecycle is a clear sign that Apple is willing to break its own traditions to maximize returns on a winning product. story.title: Apple set an iPhone sales record even without a new standard iPhone

facts.text: Apple had a record-breaking quarter for iPhone sales — despite not releasing a standard model during its latest refresh.
In its fourth-quarter earnings report released on Monday, Apple says it earned $57.58 billion in iPhone revenue, a 17 percent jump from the same time last year.

Its Mac business grew 24 percent to $10.79 billion, while Apple’s services division, which includes App Store commissions along with subscriptions to services like Apple TV and Apple Music, grew to $31.57 billion. iPad revenue declined 10 percent year over year, with $6.23 billion in sales.
The increase in revenue follows the launch of Apple’s iPhone 18 lineup in September, which included a pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max model.
Apple also took the wraps off its first folding phone, the iPhone Duo, but its preorder sales aren’t included in this earnings report.
Meanwhile, Apple only had a “limited” number of iPhone Duos available in store at launch, with some estimated shipment dates extending into 2027.
Apple shook up other areas of its product lineup with some other major launches over the past several weeks.
Like other device-makers, Apple has been dealing with supply chain constraints and rising memory costs, leading it to raise prices across its products.
Last week, Apple also revealed a MacBook Pro with a touchscreen — a design choice that its executives famously resisted.

Traditionally, Apple has launched the standard and premium versions of its phones in the same September window, but for this year’s iPhone 18 family, it only debuted the 18 Pro and Pro Max , as well as its first-ever foldable, the Duo .
The base iPhone 18 has yet to be released, with reports suggesting it will come in early 2027 alongside the lower-cost 18e and Air 2.
In other words, Apple still managed to have a record iPhone quarter on the back of its more expensive phones.
Looking ahead to the next quarter, Apple has the aforementioned Duo and a new touchscreen MacBook .
It will also be John Ternus’ first full quarter as CEO, as he took over from Apple veteran Tim Cook on Sept.
Apple just had released its fourth-quarter earnings report, and it was a particularly big one.
Overall, Apple reported US$114.5 billion (about C$160 billion) in revenue, marking a 12 percent increase.

This upgrade addresses one of the most persistent criticisms of Apple’s base models.

extraction.body: North Korea on Tuesday dismissed US allegations that it was behind a $6 billion cryptocurrency theft from Binance as "absurd rhetoric", accusing Washington of seeking to portray the country as a cybercriminal state and warning that US hostility could affect future diplomatic engagement. North Korea on Tuesday dismissed as "absurd rhetoric" US allegations that it was behind a $6 billion cryptocurrency heist on the Binance platform , saying they proved Washington remained hostile towards it, state news agency KCNA said. The denial issued by Kim Yo Jong , the influential sister of leader Kim Jong Un , comes as Pyongyang has stayed silent on US President Donald Trump's overtures to resume summit diplomacy. Kim Yo Jong warned that North Korea had "issues to reconsider" over what it calls US hostility. The FBI said at the weekend that North Korea was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion in virtual assets from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange, in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. "The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a 'cybercriminal state,' claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organisation 'supported' by the DPRK was involved in the incident," KCNA quoted Kim Yo Jong, a ruling party official, as saying. DPRK is a short form for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea. "But the US assertion is absurd rhetoric and nothing new," Kim said. "It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads international public opinion as if all the cybercrimes in different parts of the world are our deeds." Cybersecurity experts say North Korean hackers are among the world's most prolific crypto thieves and the proceeds help fund the country's weapons programmes. North Korea denies all allegations of its links to cryptocurrency theft and other cybercrimes. North Korea is one of the world's most impoverished countries but has poured resources secured through illicit means and activities banned under UN Security Council resolutions into its ballistic missile and nuclear weapons programmes . Kim Yo Jong said North Korea would "reconsider" unspecified issues in light of the "very unpleasant US hostile attitude". While she did not elaborate, North Korea has not publicly responded to Trump's offers to resume summit diplomacy, and experts have said Pyongyang may be weighing its options. The FBI said members of a North Korean state-sponsored unit known as TraderTraitor were responsible for the Binance attack. Law enforcement had observed them converting the stolen assets to the cryptocurrency Ethereum, and expected them to launder the assets further. Binance has said it has covered most of the assets stolen from the platform by using company money. © 2026 Copyright France 24 - All rights reserved. extraction.body: Kim Yo Jong, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, denied North Korea’s involvement in the $6.3 billion Binance hack and appeared to suggest, without evidence, that the US could have been behind the theft. In a statement released via the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA) on Tuesday, Kim rejected the FBI’s attribution of the attack to a North Korean-backed hacking group. “The FBI is trying to brand the DPRK as a ‘cyber criminal state’, claiming that it obtained information that a hacking organization ‘supported’ by the DPRK was involved in the incident,” said Kim. “But the US assertion is an absurd rhetoric and nothing new.” She described the allegations as a political provocation intended to damage North Korea’s international standing. The FBI also blamed North Korea for the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in February 2025, an accusation Kim also rejected on Tuesday. “This is not the first time that the U.S. has attempted to spread misunderstanding of the DPRK in the international community, blindly linking the DPRK with the ‘cyber crime’ incidents whenever they occur on an international scale,” said Kim. Kim has also pointed the finger at the US for involvement in the hack, without supplying any evidence. “If it carefully examines who will get the large amount of the so-called stolen cryptocurrency when the latter is retrieved, it may get a clue about who is behind the hacking incident,” she said. The statement provided no evidence connecting Washington to the attack. Cointelegraph reached out to the FBI for comment. Kim has also pointed the finger at the US for involvement in the hack, without supplying any evidence. “If it carefully examines who will get the large amount of the so-called stolen cryptocurrency when the latter is retrieved, it may get a clue about who is behind the hacking incident,” she said. Market makers disclosed their exposure quickly. Standard Chartered's Geoffrey Kendrick said the hack could accelerate the shift to decentralized exchanges. The promised post-mortem and updated proof of reserves remain important evidence for the cause and coverage of losses. Figures for stolen, frozen and moving funds are dated estimates and should not be treated as live balances. sources.title: Binance says customers pulled net $4.7 billion after hack as crypto world weighs risk - The Mighty 790 KFGO
passages: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”
The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets.
Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.

extraction.body: By Rae Wee, Elizabeth Howcroft and Hannah Lang SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist. The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning. The ​theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay ‌customers in full. Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX. The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so ‌far in ​2026. Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years. “Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the ⁠last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit ​did not respond to requests for comment. Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to ​withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the ‌FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether also rebounded from a two-month low. Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday. The FBI said on Saturday that the North ⁠Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Researchers describe the group as highly sophisticated and say its activities help fund the country’s weapons programs. Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, ⁠according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs. “A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said. About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by ​issuers including Circle, ‌which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC. According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control ​around $3.28 billion, mostly ⁠in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.” Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear. “The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency. (Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by ​Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.
The exchange froze withdrawals for more than two days after the hack, which the FBI said was carried out by North Korea, then started allowing customers to withdraw again on Sunday morning.
The ​theft has underlined the vulnerability of digital assets to attacks and raised questions about the impact of the hack on Binance, which has vowed to repay ‌customers in full.

Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up. Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added.

The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance itself processed net outflows of about $6 billion over 72 hours in 2022 after the collapse of FTX.
The attack marks a step-up in North Korea’s crypto thefts. Blockchain analytics firm TRM Labs said North Korea-linked hackers have stolen $7.4 billion so ‌far in ​2026.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the ⁠last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit ​did not respond to requests for comment.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.
Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to ​withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago.
“After the ‌FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old.
After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether also rebounded from a two-month low.

Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets. Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.

The FBI said on Saturday that the North ⁠Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Researchers describe the group as highly sophisticated and say its activities help fund the country’s weapons programs.

Analysts said the attack’s scale could curb institutional appetite for cryptocurrencies. Spot bitcoin ETFs recorded outflows of $643 million on Friday, the largest daily withdrawal in October, while more than $1.3 billion in leveraged positions were liquidated, ⁠according to Ari Redbord, global head of policy at TRM Labs.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by ​issuers including Circle, ‌which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC.

According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control ​around $3.28 billion, mostly ⁠in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.”

Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear.

“The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency.

(Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by ​Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

sources.title: Binance customers withdraw more than $4.6 billion after crypto heist
passages: Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”
The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets.
Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.

Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”
The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets.
Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.

Both put the start at about 20:05 UTC on Oct. 29, when five Binance wallets on the XRP Ledger sent 233 million XRP to a single attacker address. The Ethereum leg is the most unusual. According to TRM, a single transaction at 20:20 UTC carried 50 authorizations signed by a Binance hot wallet under EIP-7702, a 2025 Ethereum change that lets an ordinary wallet hand control to a smart contract.
