Binance said attackers stole about $6.3 billion from its wallets on October 29, prompting a withdrawal pause. The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor activity in an October 31 alert. Elliptic’s November 1 update reports that Binance began reopening withdrawals at 06:00 UTC that day, starting with the Bitcoin network. That report does not establish that withdrawals had resumed on every network. TRM Labs and Elliptic describe the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

Binance says it will cover every customer loss. In an update on the morning of Oct. 30 it said it had set aside more than $6.34 billion in company funds for that purpose, about $5 billion of it already held in the same tokens that were stolen, with the rest being bought on the open market and through over-the-counter desks. Co-CEO Yi He said the exchange was buying altcoins in quantities matching what was taken ahead of an updated proof of reserves. Founder Changpeng Zhao said that as a shareholder he expects user funds to be covered in full.

Binance's explanation has developed over the day, and the times matter. At 02:25 UTC on Oct. 30 it said its initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, which may have let an attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. It said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked. At 07:37 UTC co-CEO Richard Teng wrote that the attack involved a more complex process than a single click and that the investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual.

At 08:37 UTC Binance said investigators had found additional points of breach and were still establishing the full attack path with law enforcement. It has promised a post-mortem once the facts are verified. The exchange also said it submits weekly fund reports to Abu Dhabi's Financial Services Regulatory Authority under a requirement that predates the hack.

TRM Labs and Elliptic have each published on-chain reconstructions, and they largely agree. Both put the start at about 20:05 UTC on Oct. 29, when five Binance wallets on the XRP Ledger sent 233 million XRP to a single attacker address. Within about 20 minutes, hot wallets on Solana, Bitcoin, Tron, Ethereum, Arbitrum, Optimism, Base and Avalanche had been emptied as well. A second wave hit Avalanche and Polygon wallets around 23:00 UTC, and sweeps on Ethereum continued until just before midnight. TRM counts ten chains; Elliptic counts eleven, adding NEAR.

The Ethereum leg is the most unusual. According to TRM, a single transaction at 20:20 UTC carried 50 authorizations signed by a Binance hot wallet under EIP-7702, a 2025 Ethereum change that lets an ordinary wallet hand control to a smart contract. The 50 signatures covered 50 consecutive transaction counts so that one would be valid at execution. One was. About three and a half minutes later the wallet's full balance, 167,464 ETH and 63 tokens including 1.6 billion USDT, went to the attacker. Because the delegation stayed in place, the attacker swept new deposits into the same wallet at least six more times over the next three and a half hours.

On the other chains the funds left through ordinary signed transfers rather than any delegation trick. TRM's conclusion is that this points to a compromise of Binance's hot wallet signing infrastructure rather than its cryptography, a pattern Elliptic compares to the Bybit theft of about $1.5 billion in February 2025. Elliptic also found preparation the day before: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet on Oct. 28, and the attack code rehearsed on other wallets about four hours before it ran.

The headline figures differ because the firms value the assets at different moments. Binance's own estimate is about $6.3 billion. TRM counts $6.36 billion at the price of each asset when it was taken, or about $6.23 billion at current prices. Elliptic counts $6.43 billion, excluding $169 million that left Binance after withdrawals were paused and that it believes was Binance moving its own money. Chainalysis has put the figure at roughly $5.9 billion at the time of theft, according to CoinDesk . By Elliptic's count, stablecoins made up $3.46 billion of the total, and USDT on Ethereum, Bitcoin, USDC and USDT on Tron together accounted for 74% of it.

The most useful operational detail in the trackers' reports is how fast issuers moved. Elliptic says Tether froze the main attacker wallet 37 minutes after the USDT arrived, locking 1.18 billion USDT, then froze four more addresses within 17 minutes. Circle froze 823 million USDC in the same wallet three minutes after Tether acted. Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino later put his company's total above $1.567 billion, and Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire said his firm had frozen more than $800 million in coordination with law enforcement.

Ripple froze RLUSD, World Liberty Financial froze USD1, Paxos and First Digital froze their stablecoins, Tether froze tokenized gold, and the Arbitrum Security Council moved about $30 million in ETH and ARB out of the attacker's reach. Aave froze the affected lending markets, which blocked new activity but seized nothing. Binance puts the verified frozen total at about $3 billion; Elliptic verifies $2.84 billion, or 44% of the theft, and says stablecoins were 94% of what was frozen.

The attacker converted some stablecoins before the freezes landed. TRM saw about 325 million USDT sold through intent-based swap contracts for roughly 122,300 ETH at about 10% below market, 300 million USDT parked in a Tron lending protocol, and about 48 million RLUSD sold before Ripple froze the rest. Elliptic estimates about $786 million of stablecoins became ETH and TRX, with implied losses of 12% to 26% on some swaps, which it reads as the attacker trading price for speed. Roughly $3.3 billion, including about 18,270 BTC split across 19 addresses, remains outside any issuer's reach.

Three blockchain analytics firms have pointed at North Korea. TRM Labs attributes the attack with high confidence to TraderTraitor, the unit the FBI named for the Bybit theft, citing shared patterns with Bybit and the April 2026 KelpDAO exploit: small Tornado Cash withdrawals, staging well before the theft, and pre-obtained signatures executed in one burst. Chainalysis CEO Jonathan Levin said TraderTraitor likely carried it out. Elliptic says North Korean actors are likely responsible, citing funds from Binance and the September 2026 Bitget exploit reaching the same Ethereum address, but it lists caveats: the overlap is small, the laundering has been slower than usual for the group, and Binance has not published a root cause.

Update, November 2: The FBI’s October 31 cyber alert attributes the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance to North Korea and names the activity TraderTraitor. This supersedes the earlier statement here that no government had attributed the attack. The FBI says it and partner agencies observed stolen assets being converted primarily into Ether.

CoinDesk reported on Thursday evening that bitcoin fell 4.8% to below $77,000, ether 5.7%, BNB 8% and AAVE 11%. By Friday morning, Yahoo Finance had bitcoin at $78,106 after a low of $76,518, ether down 3.7% at $2,232, and Coinbase, Robinhood and Strategy each down about 5% in premarket trading. Glassnode's breakdown of the stolen assets, cited by Yahoo Finance, said Binance's BNB holdings were untouched.

Market makers disclosed their exposure quickly. Wintermute's Evgeny Gaevoy said the firm's Binance exposure was under 20% of net equity, and GSR's Xin Song put its exposure under 5%; neither expected major disruption, according to Cointelegraph . Standard Chartered's Geoffrey Kendrick said the hack could accelerate the shift to decentralized exchanges. Blockaid CEO Ido Ben-Natan told CoinDesk the tactics were consistent with North Korean operations and suggested signing-infrastructure compromise rather than key theft.

The next checkpoint is the scope of restored withdrawals: Elliptic reports that Binance began with the Bitcoin network on November 1, rather than reopening every network at once. The promised post-mortem and updated proof of reserves remain important evidence for the cause and coverage of losses. Figures for stolen, frozen and moving funds are dated estimates and should not be treated as live balances. For formal attribution and addresses linked to the laundering, consult the FBI’s October 31 alert.

For anyone running custody or treasury operations, two details from the trackers stand out. The attack did not break any cryptography; it got Binance's own signing infrastructure to sign for the attacker, and the Ethereum delegation kept working until it was revoked. And the money that was saved was saved by issuers who could freeze within minutes, which is an argument for knowing, before an incident, who can freeze what and how to reach them.

sources.title: Binance says customers pulled net $4.7 billion after hack as crypto world weighs risk - The Mighty 790 KFGO
passages: SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”
The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets.
Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.

Most withdrawals from the platform were in the form of Tether’s USDT stablecoin, Binance added. The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023. Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches. “It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong. Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.” Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit ​did not respond to requests for comment. Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance. Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to ​withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago. “After the ‌FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old. (Reporting by Rae Wee and Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Elizabeth Howcroft in Paris and Hannah Lang in New York; Writing by Scott Murdoch and Tom Westbrook; Editing by ​Sonali Paul, Xevi Fontdegloria, Mark Potter, Rod Nickel)

“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“It has not yet triggered widespread panic or a massive, concentrated withdrawal,” said Tim Sun, a senior researcher at HashKey Group, a digital asset financial service company in Hong Kong.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

OKX recorded $284.87 million in inflows in the ⁠last 24 hours, followed by Gate with $93.22 million in inflows and Bybit, which saw $29.25 million in inflows. Representatives for OKX, Gate and Bybit ​did not respond to requests for comment.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.
Ryan Tan, a Binance user, said he was in no hurry to ​withdraw his funds from the platform, as he had already kept his account fairly light since the collapse of FTX four years ago.
“After the ‌FTX collapse, I decided to hold everything on my wallet instead of leaving them on exchanges,” said the 39-year-old.
After hitting a six-week low on Friday, bitcoin prices recovered through the weekend to trade above $77,000 on Monday, while ether also rebounded from a two-month low.

The FBI said on Saturday that the North ⁠Korean state-sponsored group TraderTraitor was responsible for the attack. Researchers describe the group as highly sophisticated and say its activities help fund the country’s weapons programs.

“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
About half of the stolen funds were held in stablecoins and have been frozen by ​issuers including Circle, ‌which said on Monday it had frozen more than $1.1 billion in USDC.

According to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, the hackers still control ​around $3.28 billion, mostly ⁠in bitcoin and ether, and only a negligible amount has been cashed out of crypto and into fiat currency. Elliptic described the laundering process as “highly complex and clearly automated.”

Jonathan Benton, founder and chief executive at crypto asset recovery firm iSanctuary, said blockchain technology exists to trace stolen funds, but the challenge is turning that intelligence into rapid, coordinated action before those assets disappear.

“The future of crypto won’t be decided by how much money enters the market, but by how safe that money is once it’s there,” said Benton, former head of the international corruption unit of the UK’s National Crime Agency.

passages: Binance customers withdrew more than $4.6 billion from the cryptocurrency exchange after it suffered what security experts said was the largest digital coin theft ever.In a post on social media, Binance said customers also deposited just over $1 billion after the company allowed people to resume transactions on Sunday for Bitcoin, Ethereum and other cryptocurrencies, resulting in a net outflow of $3.64 billion.

Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange with more than 300 million users, said the value of crypto holdings being withdrawn represents just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets."Our top priority right now is to ensure the environment is secure, after which users can withdraw their funds, and Binance can resume operations," Binance cofounder Yi He said in an X post early Monday.Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The fund withdrawals came after cybercriminals, whom the FBI linked to North Korea, stole $6.3 billion in digital currency from Binance.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

story.title: Binance sees more than $4.6 billion in withdrawals after largest crypto hack in history - Yahoo Finance

facts.text: Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits.

"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," a press release said.
Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200.
Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
"We continue working with industry partners to complete the remaining acquisitions," Binance said in an update on X.
Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data.
Binance said attackers stole about $6.3 billion from its wallets on October 29, prompting a withdrawal pause.
The FBI attributed the theft to North Korea’s TraderTraitor activity in an October 31 alert.
Elliptic’s November 1 update reports that Binance began reopening withdrawals at 06:00 UTC that day, starting with the Bitcoin network.
That report does not establish that withdrawals had resumed on every network.
TRM Labs and Elliptic describe the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.
The headline figures differ because the firms value the assets at different moments.
TRM counts $6.36 billion at the price of each asset when it was taken, or about $6.23 billion at current prices.
Elliptic counts $6.43 billion, excluding $169 million that left Binance after withdrawals were paused and that it believes was Binance moving its own money.
By Elliptic's count, stablecoins made up $3.46 billion of the total, and USDT on Ethereum, Bitcoin, USDC and USDT on Tron together accounted for 74% of it.

Ripple froze RLUSD, World Liberty Financial froze USD1, Paxos and First Digital froze their stablecoins, Tether froze tokenized gold, and the Arbitrum Security Council moved about $30 million in ETH and ARB out of the attacker's reach.
Aave froze the affected lending markets, which blocked new activity but seized nothing.
Binance puts the verified frozen total at about $3 billion; Elliptic verifies $2.84 billion, or 44% of the theft, and says stablecoins were 94% of what was frozen.
On the other chains the funds left through ordinary signed transfers rather than any delegation trick.

TRM's conclusion is that this points to a compromise of Binance's hot wallet signing infrastructure rather than its cryptography, a pattern Elliptic compares to the Bybit theft of about $1.5 billion in February 2025.
Elliptic also found preparation the day before: small Tornado Cash withdrawals funding an operator wallet on Oct.
28, and the attack code rehearsed on other wallets about four hours before it ran.
This supersedes the earlier statement here that no government had attributed the attack.
The FBI says it and partner agencies observed stolen assets being converted primarily into Ether.
Market makers disclosed their exposure quickly.
Wintermute's Evgeny Gaevoy said the firm's Binance exposure was under 20% of net equity, and GSR's Xin Song put its exposure under 5%; neither expected major disruption, according to Cointelegraph .
Standard Chartered's Geoffrey Kendrick said the hack could accelerate the shift to decentralized exchanges.
Three blockchain analytics firms have pointed at North Korea.
Chainalysis CEO Jonathan Levin said TraderTraitor likely carried it out.

Elliptic says North Korean actors are likely responsible, citing funds from Binance and the September 2026 Bitget exploit reaching the same Ethereum address, but it lists caveats: the overlap is small, the laundering has been slower than usual for the group, and Binance has not published a root cause.
Binance says it will cover every customer loss.
Co-CEO Yi He said the exchange was buying altcoins in quantities matching what was taken ahead of an updated proof of reserves.
Founder Changpeng Zhao said that as a shareholder he expects user funds to be covered in full.
Binance's explanation has developed over the day, and the times matter.

30 it said its initial investigation pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to a DevOps engineer, which may have let an attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions.
It said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked.
At 07:37 UTC co-CEO Richard Teng wrote that the attack involved a more complex process than a single click and that the investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual.
The 50 signatures covered 50 consecutive transaction counts so that one would be valid at execution.
Because the delegation stayed in place, the attacker swept new deposits into the same wallet at least six more times over the next three and a half hours.

SINGAPORE/PARIS/NEW YORK, Nov 2 (Reuters) – Binance’s customers have withdrawn a net $4.72 billion from the world’s biggest cryptocurrency exchange since it reopened, after hackers stole around $6.3 billion of crypto from the platform in what could be the largest-ever financial heist.

Binance, which says it ​has more than 335 million users worldwide and average daily trading volumes of $95 billion across digital assets and derivatives, said it had also seen $2.7 billion in customer inflows since Sunday and that withdrawal volumes were stabilising after an “initial spike.”
The outflow compares with about $7 billion withdrawn from Circle’s USDC stablecoin over a week after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in 2023.
Binance said the net outflows amounted to around 3% of the assets on its platform, a relatively modest figure that analysts said suggested customer confidence had largely held up.
Binance said it was covering the losses with company funds and had already raised $6 billion from its corporate treasury, an insurance fund and reserves set aside for security breaches.
“A ‌hack at a crypto exchange is bank robbery at the speed of the internet, which creates an unstable risk profile for anyone ⁠responsible for other people’s capital,” he said.
“Binance will absorb the financial impact of the stolen funds, not our users,” the company said in a statement on X.

Data from data analytics provider DeFiLlama showed several crypto exchanges received notable inflows to their platforms since Binance opened withdrawals, although it ⁠was unclear what share came from users moving funds off Binance.

Stablecoin market capitalizations, often viewed as a gauge of money moving into and out of crypto markets, have fallen since Friday, suggesting some investors have shifted funds into cash or traditional assets.
Binance started allowing US dollar cash withdrawals again on Monday.
Some traders told Reuters they were keeping their accounts on Binance.

Analysts and crypto experts said the fallout appeared limited so far, and there was little sign of an impact on ⁠broader financial markets despite deepening ties between crypto and ⁠mainstream finance in recent years.

TraderTraitor was also responsible for a February 2025 attack on another crypto exchange, Bybit, that resulted in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.Following the Binance attack, the FBI encouraged private-sector entities "to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets."Binance has promised to cover the full losses using company funds.

passages: Pennsylvania has enacted legislation imposing new disclosure requirements on certain advertisements that use artificial intelligence (AI)-generated or AI-modified content.

The statute, titled the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act , establishes a disclosure requirement for advertisers whose use of synthetic content creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised.

Whether a particular advertisement falls within the statute will depend on its content, context, and presentation. What Constitutes a Clear and Conspicuous Disclosure? extraction.body: Across the nation, there appears to be growing frustration with the explosion of AI-generated advertising plaguing small-business storefronts and restaurant interiors. Last Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, mandating that all ads, from million-dollar television commercials to printed flyers passed out on the street, contain a disclosure label in the same format as the ad itself. SEE ALSO: Hackers find a way to turn users' own AI agents and Downloads folders against them The purpose of the bill is to combat false or misleading advertising, which is much easier to engage in with the help of AI-generated content. The bill, as introduced, states:"An advertiser may not create and disseminate or cause to be created and disseminated an advertisement that uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised, without clear and conspicuous disclosure. A disclosure under this section must state that the advertisement contains content that was modified or generated using artificial intelligence."And because it applies to all advertising shown in Pennsylvania, it will impact, for example, television commercials created in other states or advertisements made in other countries, so the consequences of this bill will be far-reaching. According to reporting by The Verge, though, critics of the bill wonder how effective it will be, given the imprecise nature of some of the language used. As The Verge notes, language like "significantly modified" is subjective and open to wide ranges of interpretation, while extensive exceptions made for "parody, satire, commentary, or criticism" offer advertisers legal wiggle room. Whatever the ultimate impacts of the bill or the future interpretations by the court system, it represents another attempt by elected representatives to respond to the overwhelming will of voters to bring artificial intelligence under legislative control, so we expect this bill to initiate a trend.

Pennsylvania has enacted legislation imposing new disclosure requirements on certain advertisements that use artificial intelligence (AI)-generated or AI-modified content. Senate Bill 806, now Act 99 of 2026 , was signed into law by Governor Josh Shapiro on October 22, 2026. The statute, titled the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act , establishes a disclosure requirement for advertisers whose use of synthetic content creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised.

The law is particularly relevant to businesses that use AI-generated images, videos, or audio in their marketing and advertising campaigns, including financial services providers that employ synthetic content to promote lending products, deposit accounts, payment services, or other consumer financial products. Although the statute is directed at deceptive advertising rather than AI use generally, its broad definitions and disclosure requirements warrant attention from businesses using generative AI in consumer-facing advertising.

The statute defines “synthetic content” as information, including an image, video, audio clip, or text, that has been significantly modified or generated by AI. Its definition of AI expressly includes generative AI.

The law does not impose a blanket disclosure requirement whenever an advertiser uses AI. Rather, the disclosure obligation is tied to the use of synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception about the advertised goods or services.

For example, an advertiser using an AI-generated video that appears to depict a real customer describing an actual experience with a financial product could face questions under the statute if the presentation creates a false impression about the authenticity of the testimonial. Similarly, synthetic audio or imagery that falsely suggests a product, service, or endorsement is genuine could trigger the disclosure requirement.
Whether a particular advertisement falls within the statute will depend on its content, context, and presentation.

These requirements make the manner of disclosure as important as its substance. A disclosure that is technically present but difficult to see, hear, or understand may not satisfy the statute.

The text-only exception is notable. Although the statute’s definition of synthetic content encompasses text significantly modified or generated by AI, the disclosure provision expressly excludes content limited to text. Consequently, AI-generated text alone does not trigger this particular disclosure requirement, even though other laws governing deceptive advertising may remain applicable.

The exception for evidently fictional content also suggests that the law is principally concerned with synthetic depictions that could mislead consumers into believing that an advertisement or its underlying representation is authentic. The statute does not, however, define a specific test for determining when content is evidently fictional.

The statute authorizes the Pennsylvania Attorney General or the appropriate district attorney to seek injunctive relief when the official has reason to believe that a prohibited practice is occurring or is about to occur and proceedings would be in the public interest.
The Attorney General or appropriate district attorney may also bring a civil action for violations. A court may award a civil fine of up to $3,000, as well as actual attorney fees and court costs.

The statute does not expressly create a private right of action. Its enforcement provisions identify the Attorney General and appropriate district attorneys as the officials authorized to bring actions under the Act. The provision authorizing a court to award damages does not, standing alone, resolve every question concerning who may pursue a claim, but the text does not expressly authorize consumers to sue directly under the new law.

Importantly, the Act provides that disclosure of AI use does not limit any other recourse available under law. Thus, compliance with the new disclosure requirement does not immunize an advertiser from otherwise applicable claims based on deceptive advertising or other unlawful conduct.

extraction.body: Across the nation, there appears to be growing frustration with the explosion of AI-generated advertising plaguing small-business storefronts and restaurant interiors. Last Thursday, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act into law, mandating that all ads, from million-dollar television commercials to printed flyers passed out on the street, contain a disclosure label in the same format as the ad itself. SEE ALSO: Hackers find a way to turn users' own AI agents and Downloads folders against them The purpose of the bill is to combat false or misleading advertising, which is much easier to engage in with the help of AI-generated content. The bill, as introduced, states:"An advertiser may not create and disseminate or cause to be created and disseminated an advertisement that uses synthetic content in a manner that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services being advertised, without clear and conspicuous disclosure. A disclosure under this section must state that the advertisement contains content that was modified or generated using artificial intelligence."And because it applies to all advertising shown in Pennsylvania, it will impact, for example, television commercials created in other states or advertisements made in other countries, so the consequences of this bill will be far-reaching. According to reporting by The Verge, though, critics of the bill wonder how effective it will be, given the imprecise nature of some of the language used. As The Verge notes, language like "significantly modified" is subjective and open to wide ranges of interpretation, while extensive exceptions made for "parody, satire, commentary, or criticism" offer advertisers legal wiggle room. Whatever the ultimate impacts of the bill or the future interpretations by the court system, it represents another attempt by elected representatives to respond to the overwhelming will of voters to bring artificial intelligence under legislative control, so we expect this bill to initiate a trend.

Pennsylvania Enacts an AI Ad Disclosure Law: What Companies Need to Know Before December 21
Pennsylvania recently joined the group of states regulating AI in advertising when Governor Josh Shapiro signed the Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act (SB 806) into law.
The law takes effect December 21, 2026, so companies have less than two months to prepare.
Companies will need to decide when to include a disclosure.
Based on a strict reading of the law, a disclosure shouldn’t be required if the use of AI doesn’t create a false consumer perception about the nature, origin, or authenticity of what is being sold.

Unlike the California and New York laws we’ve posted about—which focus on synthetic performers and appear designed to protect actors and models—the Pennsylvania law seems to have more of a consumer protection angle. (See this press release from the bill’s sponsor, for example.)

A disclosure under this section must state that the advertisement contains content that was modified or generated using artificial intelligence."And because it applies to all advertising shown in Pennsylvania, it will impact, for example, television commercials created in other states or advertisements made in other countries, so the consequences of this bill will be far-reaching.

The Massachusetts House on Wednesday approved a bill that would bar children under 14 from using social media and require a “bell-to-bell” ban on cellphones in public schools. The measure, which passed 129–25, goes further than the Senate’s version, approved last summer, that banned cellphone use, but did not include the new restrictions on young teens’ access to social media. Under the House bill, children under 14 would be blocked from using social platforms entirely, while 14- and 15-year-olds would need parental permission. Users 16 and older would face no limits. The proposal now heads back to the Senate for further consideration. “The harmful impacts of unregulated technology on our children are something our educators and librarians have long been concerned about,” said Jessica Tang, president of the American Federation of Teachers, Massachusetts, in a statement. Tang continued, “The bills passed by both the House and Senate take important steps to ensure each child has access to a learning experience free of distraction and negative influence.” Under the House bill, social media companies would have to establish age verification systems to vet current and prospective users. School districts would have to implement policies prohibiting cell phone use, with updated policies submitted to the state’s Department of Elementary & Secondary Education by Sept. 1 each year. “This bill will protect children from harmful content and addictive algorithms, and ensure that our students are able to focus in the classroom without the distraction from cell phones,” said House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano, D-Quincy, in a statement. The ban “would be among the most restrictive in the entire country,” Mariano and House Ways and Means Chair Aaron Michlewitz said in a joint statement prior to the vote. The bill’s passage comes as Gov. Maura Healey , Attorney General Andrea Campbell , and many other influential elected officials in Massachusetts have increased their public skepticism of social media companies and the negative impact that they can have on young people. During her State of the Commonwealth address earlier this year, Healey pushed for social media companies to require parental consent and age verification. “These platforms are built with addictive algorithms, and they exploit insecurities, especially in our young people,” Healey said. “We’re going to prevent social media companies from targeting kids for profit. Parents are trying to protect their kids, and we’re going to help them do it.” However, a small coalition of the Massachusetts LGBTQ groups led by the advocacy group Fight for the Future have come out against the age-restriction bans. “Do Massachusetts lawmakers believe that young people have nothing valuable to contribute to society?” questioned Evan Greer, a Boston-based transgender activist and director of Fight for the Future, in a statement. “That’s what this bill seems to say.” Greer argues that the bill would make it less safe for children if they are forced to upload their government ID or submit to a facial recognition scan to post online. In addition, the term “social media” is so broad, it’s unclear where the line will be drawn for users, Greer said. “This legislation would have kicked Greta Thuneberg off social media before she organized her first climate protest,” Greer said. “How does that make kids safer?” Beth Treffeisen is a general assignment reporter for Boston.com, focusing on local news, crime, and business in the New England region. The measure, which passed 129–25, goes further than the Senate’s version, approved last summer, that banned cellphone use, but did not include the new restrictions on young teens’ access to social media.
Under the House bill, children under 14 would be blocked from using social platforms entirely, while 14- and 15-year-olds would need parental permission. Users 16 and older would face no limits.
The proposal now heads back to the Senate for further consideration.

“The harmful impacts of unregulated technology on our children are something our educators and librarians have long been concerned about,” said Jessica Tang, president of the American Federation of Teachers, Massachusetts, in a statement.
Tang continued, “The bills passed by both the House and Senate take important steps to ensure each child has access to a learning experience free of distraction and negative influence.”
Under the House bill, social media companies would have to establish age verification systems to vet current and prospective users.
School districts would have to implement policies prohibiting cell phone use, with updated policies submitted to the state’s Department of Elementary & Secondary Education by Sept. 1 each year.

“This bill will protect children from harmful content and addictive algorithms, and ensure that our students are able to focus in the classroom without the distraction from cell phones,” said House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano, D-Quincy, in a statement.
The ban “would be among the most restrictive in the entire country,” Mariano and House Ways and Means Chair Aaron Michlewitz said in a joint statement prior to the vote.

The bill’s passage comes as Gov. Maura Healey , Attorney General Andrea Campbell , and many other influential elected officials in Massachusetts have increased their public skepticism of social media companies and the negative impact that they can have on young people.
During her State of the Commonwealth address earlier this year, Healey pushed for social media companies to require parental consent and age verification.

“These platforms are built with addictive algorithms, and they exploit insecurities, especially in our young people,” Healey said. “We’re going to prevent social media companies from targeting kids for profit. Parents are trying to protect their kids, and we’re going to help them do it.”
However, a small coalition of the Massachusetts LGBTQ groups led by the advocacy group Fight for the Future have come out against the age-restriction bans.

“Do Massachusetts lawmakers believe that young people have nothing valuable to contribute to society?” questioned Evan Greer, a Boston-based transgender activist and director of Fight for the Future, in a statement. “That’s what this bill seems to say.”
Greer argues that the bill would make it less safe for children if they are forced to upload their government ID or submit to a facial recognition scan to post online.
In addition, the term “social media” is so broad, it’s unclear where the line will be drawn for users, Greer said.
“This legislation would have kicked Greta Thuneberg off social media before she organized her first climate protest,” Greer said. “How does that make kids safer?”

extraction.body: Parents, the next time you are about to send a quick trivial text message to your students while they’re at school—maybe sitting in a classroom—stop. And think about this: it might take them only 10 seconds to respond with a thumbs-up emoji, but their brain will need 20 minutes to refocus on the algebra or history or physics lesson in front of them— 20 minutes . That was just one of the many findings in a recent report from a 14-country study by UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) that prompted this headline in the Washington Post : “Schools should ban smartphones. Parents should help.” The study recommends a ban on smartphones at school for students of all ages, and says the data are unequivocal, showing that countries that enforce restrictions see improved academic performance and less bullying. It’s a fraught debate, one that prompts frustration among educators, who say students are less focused than ever as schools struggle to enforce cell phone limitation policies, and rage from some parents, worrying about a possible shooting when they can’t get in touch, who insist they need to be able to reach their children at all times. And, perhaps surprisingly, it prompts a collective yawn from students. BU Today spoke with Renstrom about the latest study and research. Renstrom: The measure affects cell phone use * in school, * not at home or in other places. Reacting as though this prohibits students from using phones at all misses the point—it’s about what students do in a place where learning is the primary objective. The data is clear that phone use in school is problematic and facilitates everything from distractions to cheating to bullying. Introducing measures to support student learning (and teaching) is entirely appropriate and is long overdue. My hope would be that such a measure draws attention to the seriousness of the problems that stem from social media addiction, which isn’t limited to schools. Phones in themselves aren’t bad, of course, but they provide a portal to platforms that facilitate all kinds of harm, including misinformation and mental health problems that stem from addiction and overuse of social media. Schools often set the tone in their policies, so perhaps enacting this one could get parents and students to think more deeply about their phone use in general, which can only be a net positive. Renstrom: Of course. But it is easier said than done. It’s hard to be consistent. We will always have students with some kind of reason, or a note from someone, that gives them access to technology. And then it becomes hard to explain why some people can have it and some people can’t. But student buy-in to the idea is important. Renstrom: I have made the case before that addiction to phones is kind of like second-hand smoking. If you’re young and people around you are using it, you are going to want it, too. Every baby is like that. They want to reach for it, it’s flashing, their parents are on it all the time. Students openly acknowledge they are addicted. Their digital lives are there. But they also know there is this lack of balance in their lives. I do think buy-in is important. But do it as an experiment. Did it work? What changes did it make? Did it make you anxious or distracted during those 50 minutes in class? I did that for years. I surveyed students for a number of semesters; how do you feel about putting your phone in a pouch? They made some predictions and said what they thought about how annoying it was. But at the end, they talked about how those predictions [played out], and whether they were better able to focus. It was very, very clear they were better able to focus. Also interestingly, not a single student left during class to get a drink or go to the bathroom. They had been 100 percent doing that just so they could use their phone. Renstrom: It’s never going to be universal. Different families, different schools. And there is, on some level, a safety issue. I do not blame parents for thinking, if there’s someone with a gun in school, I need a way to reach my kids. What if all the phones are in pouches when someone with a gun comes in? It’s crazy that we even have to consider that. Renstrom: Parents need to stop calling their kids during the day. Stop doing that. What you are doing is setting that kid up so that they are responding to a bot 24-7 when they shouldn’t be. If you’re a kid who gets a text from your parent in class, you are conditioned to respond and to know that [the parent] expects a response. It adds so much anxiety to people’s lives. It all just ends up in this anxiety loop. When kids are in school, leave them alone. Think about what that phone is actually meant for. When you gave them a phone, you said it’s in case of an emergency or if you need to be picked up in a different place. Make those the parameters. If it’s just to confirm, “I’m still picking you up at 3,” then no, don’t do that. Remember when we didn’t have to confirm? There is a time and place for this, for all technology. Renstrom: Studies show kids’ brains, and their gray matter, are low when they are on screens. School is prime habit-forming time. You should not sit in class within view of the professor, laughing while they are talking about World War II. There is a social appropriateness that needs to be learned. Another habit that needs to be addressed is the misconception of multitasking. We are under this misconception we all can do it. And we can’t. You might think, I can listen to this lecture while my sister texts me. That is not supported by science or studies. It is literally derailing you. Your brain jumps off to another track and has to get back on. If you think you have not left that first track, you are wrong. Renstrom: I would like to see both schools and families be more assertive about this. But also to work together. If the parents are anti-smartphone policy, it doesn’t matter if the school is pro-policy. If there is a war between parents and schools, I am not sure much will happen. Some kind of intervention and restriction is better than just ripping it away from kids. The UNESCO study found it is actually even worse for university students. We are all coming at this problem from all different ways. Pouches or banned phones. Or nothing. passages: Parents, the next time you are about to send a quick trivial text message to your students while they’re at school—maybe sitting in a classroom—stop. And think about this: it might take them only 10 seconds to respond with a thumbs-up emoji, but their brain will need 20 minutes to refocus on the algebra or history or physics lesson in front of them— 20 minutes .

That was just one of the many findings in a recent report from a 14-country study by UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) that prompted this headline in the Washington Post : “Schools should ban smartphones. Parents should help.” The study recommends a ban on smartphones at school for students of all ages, and says the data are unequivocal, showing that countries that enforce restrictions see improved academic performance and less bullying.

It’s a fraught debate, one that prompts frustration among educators, who say students are less focused than ever as schools struggle to enforce cell phone limitation policies, and rage from some parents, worrying about a possible shooting when they can’t get in touch, who insist they need to be able to reach their children at all times. And, perhaps surprisingly, it prompts a collective yawn from students.
BU Today spoke with Renstrom about the latest study and research.

Renstrom: The measure affects cell phone use * in school, * not at home or in other places. Reacting as though this prohibits students from using phones at all misses the point—it’s about what students do in a place where learning is the primary objective. The data is clear that phone use in school is problematic and facilitates everything from distractions to cheating to bullying. Introducing measures to support student learning (and teaching) is entirely appropriate and is long overdue. My hope would be that such a measure draws attention to the seriousness of the problems that stem from social media addiction, which isn’t limited to schools. Phones in themselves aren’t bad, of course, but they provide a portal to platforms that facilitate all kinds of harm, including misinformation and mental health problems that stem from addiction and overuse of social media. Schools often set the tone in their policies, so perhaps enacting this one could get parents and students to think more deeply about their phone use in general, which can only be a net positive.

Renstrom: Of course. But it is easier said than done. It’s hard to be consistent. We will always have students with some kind of reason, or a note from someone, that gives them access to technology. And then it becomes hard to explain why some people can have it and some people can’t. But student buy-in to the idea is important.

Renstrom: I have made the case before that addiction to phones is kind of like second-hand smoking. If you’re young and people around you are using it, you are going to want it, too. Every baby is like that. They want to reach for it, it’s flashing, their parents are on it all the time. Students openly acknowledge they are addicted. Their digital lives are there. But they also know there is this lack of balance in their lives. I do think buy-in is important. But do it as an experiment. Did it work? What changes did it make? Did it make you anxious or distracted during those 50 minutes in class? I did that for years. I surveyed students for a number of semesters; how do you feel about putting your phone in a pouch? They made some predictions and said what they thought about how annoying it was. But at the end, they talked about how those predictions [played out], and whether they were better able to focus. It was very, very clear they were better able to focus. Also interestingly, not a single student left during class to get a drink or go to the bathroom. They had been 100 percent doing that just so they could use their phone.

Renstrom: It’s never going to be universal. Different families, different schools. And there is, on some level, a safety issue. I do not blame parents for thinking, if there’s someone with a gun in school, I need a way to reach my kids. What if all the phones are in pouches when someone with a gun comes in? It’s crazy that we even have to consider that.

Renstrom: Parents need to stop calling their kids during the day. Stop doing that. What you are doing is setting that kid up so that they are responding to a bot 24-7 when they shouldn’t be. If you’re a kid who gets a text from your parent in class, you are conditioned to respond and to know that [the parent] expects a response. It adds so much anxiety to people’s lives. It all just ends up in this anxiety loop. When kids are in school, leave them alone. Think about what that phone is actually meant for. When you gave them a phone, you said it’s in case of an emergency or if you need to be picked up in a different place. Make those the parameters. If it’s just to confirm, “I’m still picking you up at 3,” then no, don’t do that. Remember when we didn’t have to confirm? There is a time and place for this, for all technology.

Renstrom: Studies show kids’ brains, and their gray matter, are low when they are on screens. School is prime habit-forming time. You should not sit in class within view of the professor, laughing while they are talking about World War II. There is a social appropriateness that needs to be learned. Another habit that needs to be addressed is the misconception of multitasking. We are under this misconception we all can do it. And we can’t. You might think, I can listen to this lecture while my sister texts me. That is not supported by science or studies. It is literally derailing you. Your brain jumps off to another track and has to get back on. If you think you have not left that first track, you are wrong.

Renstrom: I would like to see both schools and families be more assertive about this. But also to work together. If the parents are anti-smartphone policy, it doesn’t matter if the school is pro-policy. If there is a war between parents and schools, I am not sure much will happen. Some kind of intervention and restriction is better than just ripping it away from kids. The UNESCO study found it is actually even worse for university students. We are all coming at this problem from all different ways. Pouches or banned phones. Or nothing.
Why Schools Should Ban Cell Phones in the Classroom—and Why Parents Have to Help

extraction.body: It is an ambitious social experiment of our moment in history — one that experts say could accomplish something that parents, schools and other governments have attempted with varying degrees of success: keeping kids off social media until they turn 16. Australia's new law, approved by its Parliament last week, is an attempt to swim against many tides of modern life — formidable forces like technology, marketing, globalization and, of course, the iron will of a teenager. And like efforts of the past to protect kids from things that parents believe they're not ready for, the nation's move is both ambitious and not exactly simple, particularly in a world where young people are often shaped, defined and judged by the online company they keep. Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are. The ban won't go into effect for another year. But how will Australia be able to enforce it? That's not clear, nor will it be easy. TikTok, Snapchat and Instagram have become so ingrained in young people's lives that going cold turkey will be difficult. Other questions loom. Does the ban limit kids' free expression and — especially for those in vulnerable groups — isolate them and curtail their opportunity to connect with members of their community? And how will social sites verify people's ages, anyway? Can't kids just get around such technicalities, as they so often do? This is, after all, the 21st century — an era when social media is the primary communications tool for most of those born in the past 25 years who, in a fragmented world, seek the common cultures of trends, music and memes. What happens when big swaths of that fall away? Is Australia's initiative a good, long-time-coming development that will protect the vulnerable, or could it become a well-meaning experiment with unintended consequences? The law will make platforms including TikTok, Facebook, Snapchat, Reddit, X and Instagram liable for fines of up to 50 million Australian dollars ($33 million) for systemic failures to prevent children younger than 16 from holding accounts. “It’s clear that social media companies have to be held accountable, which is what Australia is trying to do,” said Jim Steyer, president and CEO of the nonprofit Common Sense Media. Leaders and parents in countries around the world are watching Australia’s policy closely as many seek to protect young kids from the internet's dangerous corners — and, not incidentally, from each other. Most nations have taken different routes, from parental consent requirements to minimum age limits. Many child safety experts, parents and even teens who have waited to get on social media consider Australia's move a positive step. They say there’s ample reason to ensure that children wait. “What’s most important for kids, just like adults, is real human connection. Less time alone on the screen means more time to connect, not less," said Julie Scelfo, the founder of Mothers Against Media Addiction, or MAMA, a grassroots group of parents aimed at combatting the harms of social media to children. “I’m confident we can support our kids in interacting in any number of ways aside from sharing the latest meme.” The harms to children from social media have been well documented in the two decades since Facebook’s launch ushered in a new era in how the world communicates. Kids who spend more time on social media, especially as tweens or young teenagers, are more likely to experience depression and anxiety, according to multiple studies — though it is not yet clear if there is a causal relationship. What's more, many are exposed to content that is not appropriate for their age, including pornography and violence, as well as social pressures about body image and makeup. They also face bullying, sexual harassment and unwanted advances from their peers as well as adult strangers. Because their brains are not fully developed, teenagers, especially younger ones the law is focused on, are also more affected by social comparisons than adults, so even happy posts from friends can send them into a negative spiral. Many major initiatives, particularly those aimed at social engineering, can produce side effects — often unintended. Could that happen here? What, if anything, do kids stand to lose by separating kids and the networks in which they participate? Paul Taske, associate director of litigation at the tech lobbying group NetChoice, says he considers the ban “one of the most extreme violations of free speech on the world stage today" even as he expressed relief that the First Amendment prevents such law in the United States "These restrictions would create a massive cultural shift,” Taske said. “Not only is the Australian government preventing young people from engaging with issues they’re passionate about, but they’re also doing so even if their parents are ok with them using digital services," he said. "Parents know their children and their needs the best, and they should be making these decisions for their families — not big government. That kind of forcible control over families inevitably will have downstream cultural impacts.” David Inserra, a fellow for Free Expression and Technology, Cato Institute, called the bill “about as useful as an ashtray on a motorbike” in a recent blog post. While Australia's law doesn't require “hard verification” such as an uploaded ID, he said, it calls for effective “age assurance.” He said no verification system can ensure accuracy while also protecting privacy and not impacting adults in the process. Privacy advocates have also raised concerns about the law's effect on online anonymity, a cornerstone of online communications — and something that can protect teens on social platforms. “Whether it be religious minorities and dissidents, LGBTQ youth, those in abusive situations, whistleblowers, or countless other speakers in tricky situations, anonymous speech is a critical tool to safely challenge authority and express controversial opinions,” Inserra said. A spot check of kids at one mall in the Australian city of Brisbane on Wednesday didn't turn up a great deal of worry, though. “Social media is still important because you get to talk to people, but I think it’s still good that they’re like limiting it,” said Swan Son, a 13-year-old student at Brisbane State High School. extraction.body: BOSTON — For parents who remember growing up with a house phone, going “old school” may be one of the newest technology trends for kids. Some local families are turning to Wi-Fi-enabled house phones as a way for children to call friends without giving them a smartphone or access to social media. For the Gay family in Medway, that means using a device called a Tin Can phone. “One of our neighbors found it, and kind of sent it all out to us and said we should get this for the neighborhood, and we were immediately on board,” said Medway mother Frances Gay. “This was the beginning of the summer. They’ve been using it all summer, and it’s really worked out well.” The phone works over Wi-Fi and allows children to call approved phone numbers. Parents can control which numbers are permitted to call the phone. For Frances and Ed Gay, the device gives their children some independence to communicate with friends without some of the concerns that come with smartphones. “When they first started using it, they’d just pick the phone up. We’d be like, ‘You have to speak,’” Ed Gay said. “I think it’s been great for them to learn communication skills.” The couple hopes alternatives like the house phone will allow them to delay giving their children smartphones and access to social media. “I think the longer we can wait, the better off we are,” Ed Gay said. Concerns grow over social media’s impact on kids The push by some parents to delay social media comes amid growing concern about the effect the platforms can have on children. Dr. James McKowen, a clinical psychologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, sees the negative impacts firsthand. “I work with a lot of parents who, when they try to set limits and boundaries on their phones, their kids get aggressive; they get angry,” McKowen said. “It’s like cutting off their arm in some ways. They just really can’t be separated from their phone.” McKowen said some young people find it difficult to stop using the platforms and that excessive use can interfere with their mood, sleep, time outdoors and socialization. “A decent proportion do find it very hard to stop,” he said. McKowen said social media can also affect developing brains, contributing to issues involving attention spans, impulse control, anxiety and depression. Federal lawmakers consider social media restrictions for children Lawmakers are also considering new restrictions aimed at children’s access to social media. U.S. Rep. Jake Auchincloss is co-sponsoring the “16 and Up Social Media Act,” along with “Parents Over Platforms,” which would establish a national standard prohibiting social media use for children under 16. “These children are functionally laborers in a system of dopamine extraction,” Auchincloss said. Under the proposal described by Auchincloss, parents would enter a child’s birthday into a smartphone. When an app is downloaded, the app would receive an anonymized signal indicating whether the user falls within the permitted age range. “Every time an app is downloaded into the app store, an anonymized age signal is sent up to that app, and all it says is this individual is or isn’t within the age bounds that your app is bound to,” Auchincloss said. McKowen said he believes social media restrictions for young people should be viewed similarly to age restrictions placed on other products. “Just like we think about cigarette use, alcohol use, cannabis use for young people, we’ve got limits on it, we’ve got age restrictions,” McKowen said. “Social media should really be thought of similarly.” State lawmakers in Massachusetts are also considering restrictions on social media. For families like the Gays, broader rules could make it easier for parents who are trying to delay their children’s introduction to social media. “I’d love for this to go into place before this becomes a problem for us,” Frances Gay said. Changes expected for young social media users The changes come as Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, is expected to implement additional restrictions and safety features for minors following a multi-billion-dollar settlement this summer. The lawsuit claimed the social media company made its apps addicting to children on purpose. This is a developing story. Check back for updates as more information becomes available. For families like the Gays, broader rules could make it easier for parents who are trying to delay their children’s introduction to social media.
“I’d love for this to go into place before this becomes a problem for us,” Frances Gay said.

extraction.body: Send this article to your social connections. Send this article to your social connections. Add Boston.com as your preferred source on Google to see more of our stories. The Massachusetts House on Wednesday approved a bill that would bar children under 14 from using social media and require a “bell-to-bell” ban on cellphones in public schools. The measure, which passed 129–25, goes further than the Senate’s version, approved last summer, that banned cellphone use, but did not include the new restrictions on young teens’ access to social media. Under the House bill, children under 14 would be blocked from using social platforms entirely, while 14- and 15-year-olds would need parental permission. Users 16 and older would face no limits. The proposal now heads back to the Senate for further consideration. “The harmful impacts of unregulated technology on our children are something our educators and librarians have long been concerned about,” said Jessica Tang, president of the American Federation of Teachers, Massachusetts, in a statement. Tang continued, “The bills passed by both the House and Senate take important steps to ensure each child has access to a learning experience free of distraction and negative influence.” Under the House bill, social media companies would have to establish age verification systems to vet current and prospective users. School districts would have to implement policies prohibiting cell phone use, with updated policies submitted to the state’s Department of Elementary & Secondary Education by Sept. 1 each year. “This bill will protect children from harmful content and addictive algorithms, and ensure that our students are able to focus in the classroom without the distraction from cell phones,” said House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano, D-Quincy, in a statement. The ban “would be among the most restrictive in the entire country,” Mariano and House Ways and Means Chair Aaron Michlewitz said in a joint statement prior to the vote. The bill’s passage comes as Gov. Maura Healey , Attorney General Andrea Campbell , and many other influential elected officials in Massachusetts have increased their public skepticism of social media companies and the negative impact that they can have on young people. During her State of the Commonwealth address earlier this year, Healey pushed for social media companies to require parental consent and age verification. “These platforms are built with addictive algorithms, and they exploit insecurities, especially in our young people,” Healey said. “We’re going to prevent social media companies from targeting kids for profit. Parents are trying to protect their kids, and we’re going to help them do it.” However, a small coalition of the Massachusetts LGBTQ groups led by the advocacy group Fight for the Future have come out against the age-restriction bans. “Do Massachusetts lawmakers believe that young people have nothing valuable to contribute to society?” questioned Evan Greer, a Boston-based transgender activist and director of Fight for the Future, in a statement. “That’s what this bill seems to say.” Greer argues that the bill would make it less safe for children if they are forced to upload their government ID or submit to a facial recognition scan to post online. The Massachusetts House on Wednesday approved a bill that would bar children under 14 from using social media and require a “bell-to-bell” ban on cellphones in public schools.

The measure, which passed 129–25, goes further than the Senate’s version, approved last summer, that banned cellphone use, but did not include the new restrictions on young teens’ access to social media.
Under the House bill, children under 14 would be blocked from using social platforms entirely, while 14- and 15-year-olds would need parental permission. Users 16 and older would face no limits.
The proposal now heads back to the Senate for further consideration.

“The harmful impacts of unregulated technology on our children are something our educators and librarians have long been concerned about,” said Jessica Tang, president of the American Federation of Teachers, Massachusetts, in a statement.
Tang continued, “The bills passed by both the House and Senate take important steps to ensure each child has access to a learning experience free of distraction and negative influence.”
Under the House bill, social media companies would have to establish age verification systems to vet current and prospective users.
School districts would have to implement policies prohibiting cell phone use, with updated policies submitted to the state’s Department of Elementary & Secondary Education by Sept. 1 each year.

“This bill will protect children from harmful content and addictive algorithms, and ensure that our students are able to focus in the classroom without the distraction from cell phones,” said House Speaker Ronald J. Mariano, D-Quincy, in a statement.
The ban “would be among the most restrictive in the entire country,” Mariano and House Ways and Means Chair Aaron Michlewitz said in a joint statement prior to the vote.

The bill’s passage comes as Gov. Maura Healey , Attorney General Andrea Campbell , and many other influential elected officials in Massachusetts have increased their public skepticism of social media companies and the negative impact that they can have on young people.
During her State of the Commonwealth address earlier this year, Healey pushed for social media companies to require parental consent and age verification.

“These platforms are built with addictive algorithms, and they exploit insecurities, especially in our young people,” Healey said. “We’re going to prevent social media companies from targeting kids for profit. Parents are trying to protect their kids, and we’re going to help them do it.”
However, a small coalition of the Massachusetts LGBTQ groups led by the advocacy group Fight for the Future have come out against the age-restriction bans.

“Do Massachusetts lawmakers believe that young people have nothing valuable to contribute to society?” questioned Evan Greer, a Boston-based transgender activist and director of Fight for the Future, in a statement. “That’s what this bill seems to say.”
Greer argues that the bill would make it less safe for children if they are forced to upload their government ID or submit to a facial recognition scan to post online.
In addition, the term “social media” is so broad, it’s unclear where the line will be drawn for users, Greer said.
“This legislation would have kicked Greta Thuneberg off social media before she organized her first climate protest,” Greer said. “How does that make kids safer?”
Beth Treffeisen is a general assignment reporter for Boston.com, focusing on local news, crime, and business in the New England region.

extraction.body: Parents, the next time you are about to send a quick trivial text message to your students while they’re at school—maybe sitting in a classroom—stop. And think about this: it might take them only 10 seconds to respond with a thumbs-up emoji, but their brain will need 20 minutes to refocus on the algebra or history or physics lesson in front of them— 20 minutes . That was just one of the many findings in a recent report from a 14-country study by UNESCO (United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization) that prompted this headline in the Washington Post : “Schools should ban smartphones. Parents should help.” The study recommends a ban on smartphones at school for students of all ages, and says the data are unequivocal, showing that countries that enforce restrictions see improved academic performance and less bullying. It’s a fraught debate, one that prompts frustration among educators, who say students are less focused than ever as schools struggle to enforce cell phone limitation policies, and rage from some parents, worrying about a possible shooting when they can’t get in touch, who insist they need to be able to reach their children at all times. And, perhaps surprisingly, it prompts a collective yawn from students. BU Today spoke with Renstrom about the latest study and research. Renstrom: The measure affects cell phone use * in school, * not at home or in other places. Reacting as though this prohibits students from using phones at all misses the point—it’s about what students do in a place where learning is the primary objective. The data is clear that phone use in school is problematic and facilitates everything from distractions to cheating to bullying. Introducing measures to support student learning (and teaching) is entirely appropriate and is long overdue. My hope would be that such a measure draws attention to the seriousness of the problems that stem from social media addiction, which isn’t limited to schools. Phones in themselves aren’t bad, of course, but they provide a portal to platforms that facilitate all kinds of harm, including misinformation and mental health problems that stem from addiction and overuse of social media. Schools often set the tone in their policies, so perhaps enacting this one could get parents and students to think more deeply about their phone use in general, which can only be a net positive. Renstrom: Of course. But it is easier said than done. It’s hard to be consistent. We will always have students with some kind of reason, or a note from someone, that gives them access to technology. And then it becomes hard to explain why some people can have it and some people can’t. But student buy-in to the idea is important. Renstrom: I have made the case before that addiction to phones is kind of like second-hand smoking. If you’re young and people around you are using it, you are going to want it, too. Every baby is like that. They want to reach for it, it’s flashing, their parents are on it all the time. Students openly acknowledge they are addicted. Their digital lives are there. But they also know there is this lack of balance in their lives. I do think buy-in is important. But do it as an experiment. Did it work? What changes did it make? Did it make you anxious or distracted during those 50 minutes in class? I did that for years. I surveyed students for a number of semesters; how do you feel about putting your phone in a pouch? They made some predictions and said what they thought about how annoying it was. But at the end, they talked about how those predictions [played out], and whether they were better able to focus. It was very, very clear they were better able to focus. Also interestingly, not a single student left during class to get a drink or go to the bathroom. They had been 100 percent doing that just so they could use their phone. Renstrom: It’s never going to be universal. Different families, different schools. And there is, on some level, a safety issue. I do not blame parents for thinking, if there’s someone with a gun in school, I need a way to reach my kids. What if all the phones are in pouches when someone with a gun comes in? It’s crazy that we even have to consider that. Renstrom: Parents need to stop calling their kids during the day. Stop doing that. What you are doing is setting that kid up so that they are responding to a bot 24-7 when they shouldn’t be. If you’re a kid who gets a text from your parent in class, you are conditioned to respond and to know that [the parent] expects a response. It adds so much anxiety to people’s lives. It all just ends up in this anxiety loop. When kids are in school, leave them alone. Think about what that phone is actually meant for. When you gave them a phone, you said it’s in case of an emergency or if you need to be picked up in a different place. Make those the parameters. If it’s just to confirm, “I’m still picking you up at 3,” then no, don’t do that. Remember when we didn’t have to confirm? There is a time and place for this, for all technology. Renstrom: Studies show kids’ brains, and their gray matter, are low when they are on screens. School is prime habit-forming time. You should not sit in class within view of the professor, laughing while they are talking about World War II. There is a social appropriateness that needs to be learned. Another habit that needs to be addressed is the misconception of multitasking. We are under this misconception we all can do it. And we can’t. You might think, I can listen to this lecture while my sister texts me. That is not supported by science or studies. It is literally derailing you. Your brain jumps off to another track and has to get back on. If you think you have not left that first track, you are wrong. Renstrom: I would like to see both schools and families be more assertive about this. But also to work together. If the parents are anti-smartphone policy, it doesn’t matter if the school is pro-policy. If there is a war between parents and schools, I am not sure much will happen. Some kind of intervention and restriction is better than just ripping it away from kids. The UNESCO study found it is actually even worse for university students. We are all coming at this problem from all different ways. Pouches or banned phones. Or nothing.
