passages: Ford Motor Co. in Dearborn is launching the Ford Privacy Promise to make an “explicit commitment to customers that their vehicle data is safe” and they’re in control of what they share.
As Ford created the Privacy Promise, it surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. consumers — both Ford and non-Ford owners.
It learned that while privacy is important to them, customers understand the value of data sharing.

“Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights,” says Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer and deputy general counsel for data and privacy at Ford.
“With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously.”
Ford says it designs and builds its products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use, storage, and disposal.
This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect a customer’s privacy.
As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.

extraction.body: Ford has introduced a new Privacy Promise, publicly committing to protect customer vehicle data and give owners greater control over the information they share. The initiative comes as connected vehicles collect more personal information, including driving behavior, vehicle diagnostics, and location data.Announced on November 2, the initiative includes a new website that explains Ford's data collection practices and shows customers how to manage their privacy settings through their vehicles or the Ford App..Ford Aims to Build Trust Around Connected Car Data.The automaker said the Privacy Promise is designed to make its data practices easier to understand. Customers can learn what information Ford collects, how it is used, and how they can opt in or out of data sharing.Kristin Jones, Ford's Chief Privacy Officer, said the company wants to communicate its data practices more clearly and help customers understand their privacy choices.The announcement comes as automakers introduce increasingly connected vehicles with features such as remote start, navigation, and driver-assistance technology. A survey cited in the report found that only 14% of US consumers fully understand what data their vehicles collect.Also Read: Ford Fathom vs Slate Truck: Price, Range, Features, Key Differences.Survey Finds Data Privacy is a Major Consumer Concern.Ford surveyed 1,000 consumers to understand their views on vehicle data and privacy. According to Jones, 91% of respondents said data privacy was an important consideration.The survey also found that customers value the benefits of connected technology but want greater control over their information. Respondents identified the ability to adjust privacy settings whenever required as an important factor.Jones said the company wanted to build trust by ensuring customers have access to clear information about their data choices. She also noted that automakers were viewed as more trusted custodians of privacy than several other large organizations handling personal information..Turning Off Data Sharing Could Affect Connected Features.Ford said customers can manage their data-sharing preferences through their vehicle's center display. However, opting out of certain services could affect features that depend on connected vehicle data.For instance, disabling connected services would make real-time navigation and built-in roadside assistance unavailable. Vehicle health information can also help owners receive maintenance updates while supporting research and development for future technologies.The company said it does not sell information about customers' driving behavior to data brokers. Jones reiterated that Ford's objective is to offer products and services that provide value to customers, not to monetize their personal information..Privacy Resources to Expand Beyond US.Ford said the Privacy Promise website will provide information about its privacy practices and available controls. passages: Ford Motor Co. in Dearborn is launching the Ford Privacy Promise to make an “explicit commitment to customers that their vehicle data is safe” and they’re in control of what they share.
As Ford created the Privacy Promise, it surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. consumers — both Ford and non-Ford owners.
It learned that while privacy is important to them, customers understand the value of data sharing.

“Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights,” says Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer and deputy general counsel for data and privacy at Ford.
“With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously.”
Ford says it designs and builds its products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use, storage, and disposal.
This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect a customer’s privacy.
As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.
Ford stresses that it never sells data about how customers drive their vehicle to data brokers.

The company also plans to introduce privacy resources for Lincoln customers and users in Mexico and Canada in the coming weeks, with additional markets to follow.The initiative comes as connected vehicle technology becomes more widespread, making transparency around data collection and customer consent increasingly important..Join our WhatsApp Channel to get the latest news, exclusives and videos on WhatsApp
Ford Motor Co. in Dearborn is launching the Ford Privacy Promise to make an “explicit commitment to customers that their vehicle data is safe” and they’re in control of what they share.
As Ford created the Privacy Promise, it surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. consumers — both Ford and non-Ford owners.
It learned that while privacy is important to them, customers understand the value of data sharing.

“Even for a tech-savvy consumer, it can be hard to understand the relationship between your vehicle, the data it generates, and your privacy and rights,” says Kristin Jones, chief privacy officer and deputy general counsel for data and privacy at Ford.
“With our connected vehicle and app user communities growing every day, Ford takes its responsibility in safeguarding customer data seriously.”
Ford says it designs and builds its products with privacy in mind — from collection of data to its use, storage, and disposal.
This can include privacy-enhancing technologies like anonymizing or aggregating data to further protect a customer’s privacy.
As a result, Ford offers vehicle privacy settings that allow customers to control what data they want to share, subject to the features and services they wish to enjoy.
Ford stresses that it never sells data about how customers drive their vehicle to data brokers.
Ford is launching the Privacy Promise to make an explicit commitment to customers that their vehicle data is safe with us and they’re in control of what they share.
Kristin Jones is Ford's Chief Privacy Officer and Deputy General Counsel, Data & Privacy.

Mizzou Athletics announced a partnership with World Wide Technology that will add a new patch to Mizzou basketball uniforms. Mizzou Athletics and Learfield announced Monday that World Wide Technology will be the new jersey patch partner for Mizzou Basketball. As part of the partnership, the St. Louis based companies' acronym, WWT, will be featured on both the women's and men's uniforms. WWT’s logo will also appear on Norm Stewart Court at Mizzou Arena as part of the Tiger’s expanded partnership. "We are proud to welcome World Wide Technology as a partner of Mizzou Athletics and Mizzou Basketball," said Laird Veatch, Mizzou Director of Athletics. "WWT’s founder and chairman David Steward, its co-founder and CEO Jim Kavanaugh and their team have built an extraordinary company with a global reach and deep Missouri roots. When you have the opportunity to partner with a brand of WWT’s caliber, you put them at the top of your draft board. WWT's investment in our basketball programs demonstrates a strong belief in Mizzou and our commitment to competing for championships. We’re excited to continue to build this partnership with an organization that shares our pride in Missouri and our ambition to demand excellence" said Laird Veatch. Mizzou Athletics announced a partnership with World Wide Technology that will add a new patch to Mizzou basketball uniforms. Mizzou Athletics and Learfield announced Monday that World Wide Technology will be the new jersey patch partner for Mizzou Basketball. As part of the partnership, the St. Louis based companies' acronym, WWT, will be featured on both the women's and men's uniforms. WWT’s logo will also appear on Norm Stewart Court at Mizzou Arena as part of the Tiger’s expanded partnership. "We are proud to welcome World Wide Technology as a partner of Mizzou Athletics and Mizzou Basketball," said Laird Veatch, Mizzou Director of Athletics. "WWT’s founder and chairman David Steward, its co-founder and CEO Jim Kavanaugh and their team have built an extraordinary company with a global reach and deep Missouri roots. When you have the opportunity to partner with a brand of WWT’s caliber, you put them at the top of your draft board. WWT's investment in our basketball programs demonstrates a strong belief in Mizzou and our commitment to competing for championships. We’re excited to continue to build this partnership with an organization that shares our pride in Missouri and our ambition to demand excellence" said Laird Veatch. To report an error or typo, email news@komu.com .

Mizzou Athletics will have a new name displayed on its basketball uniforms this season after announcing a partnership with St. Louis-based World Wide Technology as the jersey patch sponsor for both the men's and women's programs. The company's logo will appear on the uniforms of both teams beginning with the 2026-27 season. WWT branding also will be featured on Norm Stewart Court at Mizzou Arena as part of the expanded agreement. The partnership builds on WWT's existing relationship with the university as Mizzou Athletics' official technology solutions partner. The company has also worked with the University of Missouri System and MU Health Care on technology initiatives involving cybersecurity, artificial intelligence and digital transformation. Mizzou athletic director Laird Veatch said the company's investment reflects its belief in the direction of the university's basketball programs. "WWT's investment in our basketball programs demonstrates a strong belief in Mizzou and our commitment to competing for championships," Veatch said. Founded in 1990, WWT has grown into a global technology solutions provider headquartered in the St. Louis region. The company has more than 14,000 employees and operates in more than 60 locations worldwide. WWT founder and chairman David Steward said the partnership gives the company another opportunity to support its home state. "Mizzou Basketball brings people together and represents the competitive spirit, grit and determination that define our state," Steward said. Men's basketball coach Dennis Gates also welcomed the company's continued support, pointing to Steward's history of investing in the university and its community. "We're grateful for Mr. Steward's support and friendship as we continue to build a championship program in Columbia," Gates said. Women's basketball coach Kellie Harper said having a Missouri-based company support the program is an exciting opportunity for the Tigers. The sponsorship was developed through Mizzou Athletics in collaboration with Learfield's Mizzou Sports Properties. Financial terms of the agreement were not disclosed.

Over many years, WWT has partnered with the university on its technology modernization efforts across all University of Missouri System campuses and University of Missouri Health Care. "Missouri is home, and World Wide Technology is blessed and honored to support the institutions and people who make our state special," said Steward, WWT's founder and chairman. "Mizzou Basketball brings people together and represents the competitive spirit, grit and determination that define our state. Supporting Mizzou Basketball is another way we can give back to our home state and encourage the next generation of leaders on and off the court.” “World Wide Technology is an outstanding example of what can be accomplished through vision and teamwork. I have really appreciated my relationship with Mr. Steward over the years and know how much he values giving back to the community,” Mizzou’s Whitten Family Men's Basketball Head Coach Dennis Gates said. “He has continually demonstrated that with his exceptional work with the Steward Family Foundation and with his partnership at Mizzou. Steward’s support and friendship as we continue to build a championship program in Columbia.” "We're so grateful for World Wide Technology's investment in Mizzou and Mr. Steward’s belief in our programs and student-athletes," Mizzou Women’s Basketball coach Kellie Harper said. "Having a Missouri-based technology company with WWT's reputation and history support our team is incredibly exciting, and we're proud to represent this university and our state together." The sponsorship with World Wide Technology was created with Mizzou Athletics in collaboration with Learfield’s Mizzou Sports Properties. “World Wide Technology is a natural fit for this opportunity. As a Missouri-based industry leader with deep ties to Mizzou, WWT shares a commitment to excellence, innovation and elevating the student-athlete experience,” said Josh Pell, General Manager of Mizzou Sports Properties. “We’re proud to work alongside Mizzou Athletics to bring WWT’s brand to the forefront of Mizzou Basketball and create meaningful connections with Tiger fans.” About World Wide TechnologyWorld Wide Technology (WWT) is a global technology solutions provider helping organizations make a new world happen by turning ambition into real-world outcomes. Founded in 1990, WWT brings together strategy, deep technical expertise and world-class technology partnerships to help public- and private-sector organizations design, build and scale intelligent AI, digital, cybersecurity, cloud and infrastructure solutions. Through its Advanced Technology Center (ATC), a collaborative ecosystem featuring state-of-the-art hardware and software, WWT enables clients and partners to conceptualize, test and validate innovative technology and then deploy solutions at scale using its global integration and distribution capabilities. With more than 14,000 team members and over 60 locations worldwide, WWT's culture— grounded in core values and leadership philosophies— has been recognized by Fortune and Great Place to Work® for its commitment to innovation, trust and creating a great place to work for all. Softchoice, a World Wide Technology company, supports commercial and SMB markets in the U.S. and Canada. About LearfieldLearfield is the leading media and technology company powering college athletics. With ties to over 1,200 collegiate institutions and over 12,000 local and national brand partners, Learfield’s presence in college sports and live events delivers influence and maximizes reach to target audiences. With solutions for a 365-day, 24/7 fan experience, Learfield enables schools and brands to connect with fans through licensed merchandise, game ticketing, donor identification for athletic programs, exclusive custom content, innovative marketing initiatives, student-athlete marketing initiatives , and advanced digital platforms. Since 2008, it has served as title sponsor for the acclaimed Learfield Directors’ Cup, supporting athletic departments across all divisions About Mizzou AthleticsMizzou Athletics supports 450 student-athletes across 20 varsity programs while competing at the highest level of intercollegiate athletics in the Southeastern Conference. Guided by its core values — Earn Trust & Respect, Live Our Will to Win, Dare to Demand Excellence and Believe Every Step Matters — Mizzou is committed to developing championship-level programs, creating transformative student-athlete experiences and uniting the state of Missouri through competitive excellence.COLUMBIA, Mo. – Mizzou Athletics and Learfield today announced St. Louis-based World Wide Technology (WWT) as the new jersey patch partner of Mizzou Basketball. This expands upon WWT’s existing innovative relationship with Mizzou as the University’s Official Technology Solutions Partner of Athletics. As part of the partnership , the WWT brand mark will be featured on the uniforms of both men’s and women’s Tiger basketball programs beginning this fall. WWT’s logo will also appear on Norm Stewart Court at Mizzou Arena as part of the university’s expanded partnership with the St. "We are proud to welcome World Wide Technology as a partner of Mizzou Athletics and Mizzou Basketball," said Laird Veatch, Mizzou Director of Athletics. "WWT’s founder and chairman David Steward, its co-founder and CEO Jim Kavanaugh and their team have built an extraordinary company with a global reach and deep Missouri roots. When you have the opportunity to partner with a brand of WWT’s caliber, you put them at the top of your draft board. WWT's investment in our basketball programs demonstrates a strong belief in Mizzou and our commitment to competing for championships. We’re excited to continue to build this partnership with an organization that shares our pride in Missouri and our ambition to demand excellence."

In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.

Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.

Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.
Some key findings from the report include the following:

Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.

Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.

Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.

Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.

Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.

sources.body: In July and August 2026, MIT Technology Review Insights conducted a global survey of 400 chief data and analytics officers, chief information officers, chief technology officers, chief AI officers, and other senior data and technology executives. Agentic analytics has made real progress, but performance varies sharply depending on the type of insight.

extraction.body: AI analytics agents are generating recommendations faster than organizations can evaluate them. New global research, based on a survey of 400 data and technology executives, explores what separates the organizations getting real business value from agentic analytics from the rest. 48% of agent-generated insights lead to actions that improve the business — up from 37% a year ago, but still leaving more than half unused or not helpful. 55% of executives cite lack of business context as the primary reason agent insights fall short. 60% say orchestrating teams of AI agents will be a primary analyst role within two years. Agentic analytics has made real progress, but performance varies sharply depending on the type of insight. When it comes to describing what happened, agents perform well: 83% of respondents rate their descriptive insights as good or excellent. For prescriptive insights — recommendations on what to do next — only 45% say the same. A small group of organizations, 7% of those surveyed, report that 77% of their agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. What sets them apart isn't a matter of technology. When analytics agents deliver substandard insights, the most common explanation is straightforward: They lack sufficient understanding of the business. “When agents don't have enough understanding of the business needs, requirements and priorities, they struggle to determine the true value of the insights they generate." The research examines how eight industries compare on agent performance. Technology, financial services and retail organizations outperform others in key dimensions — including the share of insights that lead to business improvement. Even when insight quality improves, organizations face a second challenge: determining which insights to trust and act on. Only 24% can evaluate all the insights their agents generate. Most decide on a case-by-case basis, prioritizing by risk or reviewing only when resources allow. That's beginning to change. Two years from now, 53% of executives expect automated evaluation by AI agents to be their primary method — up from 29% today. “Many organizations still rely on expert review and anecdotal testing because evaluating insights' quality is fundamentally harder than evaluating traditional software. The challenge is not just determining whether an answer is correct, but whether it is trustworthy, contextual and valuable." Two years ago, the primary analyst activities were documenting requirements and mapping processes. Today, analysts spend more of their time interpreting AI-generated insights, validating agent outputs and feeding corrections back into the system to improve accuracy over time. The role is shifting from producing analysis to governing, directing and refining it. “Prescriptive insights are hard, because they require a translation step: from 'what will happen' to 'what we should do about it.' This requires the agent to incorporate business constraints, risk preferences and decision authority that are frequently undocumented and contextually variable." In July and August 2026, MIT Technology Review Insights conducted a global survey of 400 chief data and analytics officers, chief information officers, chief technology officers, chief AI officers, and other senior data and technology executives. The survey respondents work in organizations across eight industries. All their organizations earn $500 million or more in annual revenue, with 36% earning over $10 billion annually. In addition to the survey, in-depth interviews with senior technology executives offer firsthand insights into how organizations are striving to improve the quality of AI agent insights. In just a few years, generative AI has changed the face of enterprise analytics, notably by making analytics accessible to users across the organization. Agentic AI promises to do even more, by automating entire workflows and taking actions based on agent insights. But there is a problem: The quality of insights that agents currently generate leaves much to be desired.

Fewer than half of agent-generated insights at the organizations surveyed for this report lead to business improvement. And while most respondents praise the quality of their agents’ descriptive insights, reviews of their prescriptive insights—those on which actions are based—are decidedly mixed.

Failure to produce insights that improve the business deprives organizations of their desired return on investment in agentic analytics. Worse, flawed insights that trigger incorrect actions can cause reputational or financial damage. This report gauges how companies view the quality of the outputs produced by their analytics agents and explores how organizations are seeking to boost insight quality and get their agents working harder for the business.
Some key findings from the report include the following:

Agentic analytics is only just starting to deliver. On average, 48% of insights generated by analytics agents at the surveyed companies lead to actions that improve the business. That is a marked advance from the 37% average the respondents say generated such actions one year ago. But it means that more than half of the insights generated by analytics agents today are still failing to help businesses.

Better quality of insights leads to clear business advantage. At a small cohort of organizations, which we term “insight leaders,” AI agents perform much better than the average. In this group, more than 70% of agent insights lead to actions that improve the business. The insight leaders also give the quality of their agents’ insights higher marks than do the total respondents overall. The quality gap is particularly wide when it comes to prescriptive insights.

Insufficient context reduces insight quality. When analytics agents deliver insights of substandard quality, the main reason is a lack of business context, as cited by 55% of surveyed executives. Fragmented or inaccessible data is the other major factor, according to 45%. Fewer insight leaders say their agents struggle with access to context.

Insight overload further inhibits agent effectiveness. At a majority (52%) of surveyed organizations, analytics agents generate too many insights to be properly evaluated and therefore acted upon. Less than one-quarter (24%) are able to evaluate all agent insights; most do so on a case-by-case basis, and that process is currently human-intensive.

Governance and semantics are areas of focus for improving insights. The surveyed companies are prioritizing initiatives that enable better agent insights by strengthening AI and data governance (cited by 60%). They are also adding a semantic layer to their data architecture (45%). The experts we interviewed agree that the semantic layer is crucial to ensure high-performing agents.

This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

extraction.body: LINCOLN, Neb. ( Nebraska Today ) - The latest results from the 2026 Nebraska Rural Poll show that most rural Nebraskans have used artificial intelligence tools — a sharp increase since the poll first asked about AI in 2024. However, many are still wary of AI’s reliability. Fifty-five percent of rural Nebraskans surveyed have used any AI tool — up from 27% in 2024. Certain groups are more likely than others to have used the tools. At least three-quarters of respondents ages 19 to 39 have used them, compared to just 23% of those 65 and older. Other groups most likely to have used the tools include those with higher education levels or household incomes and women. “The rapid growth in AI use shows that AI is becoming part of everyday life for many rural Nebraskans,” said Heather Akin, associate professor of agricultural and environmental sciences communication at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln. “As AI continues to evolve, it’s important that rural residents have opportunities to explore its uses, recognize its limitations and make informed decisions about when to use it. By supporting access and literacy about AI, Nebraskans can be more prepared to navigate this evolving technology.” Generative AI uses machine learning and deep learning models to create new content — such as text, images, audio, videos or code — in response to what users ask. Examples include ChatGPT, Gemini and DALL-E. Respondents were also asked how interested they are in learning more about different aspects of AI. Many rural Nebraskans surveyed are somewhat or extremely interested in learning about the following: how to protect their privacy when using generative AI (45%), how to evaluate response accuracy (36%), how it can be biased (33%) and how to use it ethically (28%). “The interest rural Nebraskans show in learning about privacy, accuracy and bias shows that they want to understand not just what AI can do, but how to use it responsibly,” said Mary Emery, director of Rural Prosperity Nebraska. “If we can provide accessible learning opportunities, Nebraskans can build confidence in these tools and make informed decisions about when and how AI can best serve their needs.” The “Artificial Intelligence” report and its implications for rural Nebraska will be highlighted during a Rural Poll webinar at noon CST Nov. 18. Register here. The full report can be found on the Nebraska Rural Poll website . The 2026 Nebraska Rural Poll marks the 31st year of tracking rural Nebraskans’ perceptions about policy and quality of life. It is the largest and longest-running poll of its kind. Questionnaires were mailed in April and May to nearly 6,900 Nebraska households, with 881 households from 86 of the state’s 93 counties responding. The poll carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3%. Current and past reports are available here .

Among respondents ages 50-64, 51% indicated that they had ever used AI tools. That’s compared to about 75% of respondents aged 19-39. Akin also said that some respondents may have unknowingly used AI, leading them to respond inaccurately. Heather Akin, associate professor of strategic communication at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, said this increase is in line with national trends.
“We’re seeing just a rapid uptake of those tools over the last year or so, I think in general across the country,” she said.
A 2025 survey from YouGov found that 56% of American adults use AI tools.
Akin said the poll findings were likely a “conservative estimate” of AI use in rural Nebraska because the average age of respondents was about 51.
Among respondents ages 50-64, 51% indicated that they had ever used AI tools. That’s compared to about 75% of respondents aged 19-39.

Akin also said that some respondents may have unknowingly used AI, leading them to respond inaccurately. She pointed to the Google Gemini “AI Overview” results that accompany every Google search as an example.
“I’m not sure whether people always know that they’re using generative AI in their searches, but in fact it’s running in the background,” she said.
The poll found that women were more likely than men to use AI chatbots, although the report did not indicate how large the AI usage gap between men and women was.

Akin said that while she can only speculate as to why women are more likely to use chatbots than men, a June 2026 study from Pew Research Center found the nationwide “gender gap” in chatbot use closed between 2024 and 2026.
Forty-seven percent of women reported having ever used chatbots in 2026, up from 28% in 2024. Meanwhile, men’s chatbot use increased less sharply, from 39% in 2024 to 50% in 2026.
Akin said the closing gender gap could explain why more women than men use chatbots in rural Nebraska.

Akin said AI tools can help people find information in areas where access to medical and legal advice is limited. However, she said this can become harmful when chatbots give out inaccurate information.
A little more than one-third of poll respondents said they were somewhat or extremely interested in learning how to evaluate response accuracy from generative AI.
“Of course, we want to be really cautious and conscious of the accuracy of the information that people get,” Akin said.

The poll results indicated that rural Nebraskans' biggest concern about AI is privacy, with 45% of respondents saying they were somewhat or extremely interested in learning how to protect their privacy when using AI.

“We’re hearing a lot of very valid concerns about it,” Akin said. “I think we’re going to hit a point where, as a society, we kind of have to negotiate how much we’re willing to accept this technology being used.”

Nebraska Extension and Rural Prosperity Nebraska mailed questionnaires to nearly 6,900 Nebraska households in April and May 2026. The poll captured 881 responses from 86 of Nebraska’s 93 counties. Cass, Douglas, Lancaster, Sarpy, Saunders, Seward and Washington counties were not surveyed.

passages: Aaron Glenn lost for the 20th time in 25 games as head coach of the Jets on Sunday, but the former NFL defensive back has no time to fret his future in New York.
According to the embattled coach, there is no fire sale coming before the trade deadline.
The Jets hired Glenn to get the team back to the playoffs, but a stretch of losing seasons could run to 11 in a row.
"There's so much that I think about when it comes to us improving each week that it really doesn't come across my mind, to be honest with you," Glenn said on a media video call Monday.

"There's so much that I think about when it comes to us improving each week that it really doesn't come across my mind, to be honest with you," Glenn said on a media video call Monday. "I understand how this league is. I understand what this business is about, but my first job is each week improving this team. And that's the only thing that I think about." The Jets hired Glenn to get the team back to the playoffs, but a stretch of losing seasons could run to 11 in a row. The Jets (2-6) have lost three consecutive games and now hit the road for a game against the Kansas City Chiefs (5-2) before returning home to face the Buffalo Bills (6-1). The Jets are finding ways to lose close games. Their six losses this season are by a total of 36 points, all but one of them a one-score game. According to the embattled coach, there is no fire sale coming before the trade deadline. With a treasure trove of draft picks from marquee trades for defensive lineman Quinnen Williams and cornerback Sauce Gardner at the trade deadline last year, he believes the Jets will be "in the business of keeping good players," adding running back Breece Hall "will still be here" next week. Glenn said the run of defeats underscores the need for a change in "mindset" or losses will continue piling up. "I mean, that's what this is," Glenn said. "It's a bottom-line business and we have to win, but we still have nine games left. So we still have an opportunity to win nine games."

Bitcoin's (BTC) charts, however, show little sign of a broken bull market. Three signals point that way, from the weekly close to monthly momentum. One group of investors still has reason for caution before the US midterm elections. The Binance hack on October 29 drained about $6.3 billion from 10 blockchains. Binance pledged to cover all losses and began phased withdrawals on November 1. Even so, Bitcoin closed the week down only 2.9%, according to on-chain analyst Willy Woo. Gold fell 3% over the same stretch, per Woo's figures. Woo contrasted this with the FTX collapse, which knocked Bitcoin down 25% in the 2022 bear market. A drop of that size failed to repeat here. Ash Crypto also argues that a 20% drop is normal during a Bitcoin bull market. The hack-week loss stayed far below that threshold. Bitcoin's longer-term chart points in the same direction. Bitcoin posted its 7th straight weekly close above the 50-week moving average (MA), Ash Crypto noted. The streak began in September, when Bitcoin reclaimed the average for the first time in 45 weeks. Alex Thorn, who heads firmwide research at Galaxy, tied that reclaim to past cycle bottoms at the time. "Regaining the 50w MA has historically served as strong confirmation that bear market lows are 'in,'" he said. At press time, Bitcoin traded at $78,307, up 0.65% over the past 24 hours, per BeInCrypto Markets. That puts it about 3.6% above the 50-week MA, which currently stands near $75,602. A slower monthly gauge offers a third reading. Bitcoin gained about 43% across July, August, and September, Coinglass data show. It then closed October down 7.32%, its first monthly loss since June. That loss still left Bitcoin's monthly momentum above a key line, according to analyst PlanB. His chart shows the 14-month relative strength index (RSI) above 50 for a 3rd straight month. RSI measures momentum on a 0 to 100 scale. Readings above 50 mean gains have outweighed losses over the lookback period. PlanB reads the streak as the start of a new bull market. Still, Bitcoin ETF outflows tell a weaker story than the price chart. US spot Bitcoin ETFs lost $643.33 million on October 30, the first full session after the hack. That outflow erased four days of inflows and left the week about $202 million negative. Glassnode data place the average cost basis of US spot ETF holders near $82,308. Bitcoin sits about 4.9% below that line, leaving the average ETF buyer at a loss. Bitcoin also remains 10.4% below its January 1 level, per Coinglass. Those levels frame the next test, which arrives with the midterm vote. US voters head to the polls on November 3. Bitcoin has closed November higher in 10 of 16 years, with a median gain of 10.3%, Coinglass data show. Midterm years split evenly, however, with two November gains and two losses. The losses came in 2018 and 2022, when Bitcoin fell 36.41% and 16.23%. Both were bear market years. A weekly close above the 50-week MA after the vote may separate 2026 from those two years. A move back above $82,308 would put the average ETF holder back in profit. Ash Crypto's monthly analysis marks $87,500 as resistance.
